<fn> converges at some points but does not converge at some other points
questions.why: For each fixed x in [0,1), x^n→0 as n→∞; at x=1, x^n=1 always. So it converges everywhere on [0,1] to a limit function that is 0 on [0,1) and jumps to 1 at x=1 — but that limit is discontinuous even though each fₙ is continuous, which is only possible if the convergence is NOT uniform (uniform limits of continuous functions must stay continuous). Classic textbook example of pointwise-but-not-uniform convergence.

questions.topic: Group theory — elements of a given order in a direct product
questions.question: The number of elements of order 5 in the group Z25 ⊕ Z5 is
questions.why: The subgroup of elements whose order divides 5 is 5Z25 ⊕ Z5, which has 5×5=25 elements. Since 5 is prime, every non-identity element in this order-25 subgroup must have order exactly 5 (order can only be 1 or 5, by Lagrange). Subtract the identity: 25-1=24 elements of order exactly 5.

questions.question: Let F4, F8 and F16 be finite fields of 4, 8 and 16 elements respectively, then
options: F4 is isomorphic to a subfield of F16
F4 is isomorphic to a subfield of F8
F8 is isomorphic to a subfield of F16
F16 is isomorphic to a subfield of F16
questions.why: A finite field F_(2^m) is (isomorphic to) a subfield of F_(2^n) exactly when m divides n. Here F4=F_(2^2) and F16=F_(2^4): 2 divides 4, so F4 IS a subfield of F16. F8=F_(2^3) doesn't fit with either (2∤3 and 3∤4), so F4-in-F8 and F8-in-F16 both fail. Note: the source scan of option 1's subscript is visually ambiguous (looks like it may read "F_1" due to a clipped "6"), but this matches both the math and the marked key, so transcribed with confidence.

questions.topic: System of linear equations — no-solution condition
questions.question: The system of equations kx+y+z=1; x+ky+z=k and x+y+kz=k³ does not have a solution, if k is equal to
questions.why: The coefficient matrix is symmetric with k on the diagonal and 1s off it — its determinant is (k-1)²(k+2). The system fails to have a (unique or consistent) solution exactly at the roots that also break consistency with the RHS; checking k=-2 against the augmented system shows the equations become contradictory (the sum of the LHS terms cannot match the sum of the RHS at that value). Trust the given key; deriving it fully requires checking the rank of the augmented matrix at each root of the determinant, which is standard but lengthy — the reusable takeaway is: determinant=0 is necessary but you must ALSO check the augmented matrix for inconsistency to confirm "no solution" (vs. infinite solutions).

questions.question: The value of x for which the matrix Δ = [[x+λ, x, x], [x, x+λ, x], [x, x, x+λ]] is singular is
questions.why: This matrix has the special form λI + x(all-ones matrix). Its determinant works out to λ²(λ+3x) (a standard result for "constant plus rank-1" matrices). Setting the determinant to 0: since λ≠0 in general, λ+3x=0 gives x=-λ/3.

questions.question: The rank of the matrix [[0,1,-3,-1],[1,0,1,1],[3,1,0,2],[1,1,-2,0]] is
questions.why: [Stage 4 correction:] Row-reduce: row4 = row2+row1 exactly (1,0,1,1)+(0,1,-3,-1)=(1,1,-2,0) — row4 IS a linear combination of rows 1,2, confirmed. But the original draft's claim that "row3 is NOT a combination of rows 1,2" is FALSE: row3=(3,1,0,2) = 1×row1 + 3×row2 = (0,1,-3,-1)+3×(1,0,1,1) = (3,1,0,2), an exact match. So row3 is ALSO dependent on rows 1,2 — only 2 rows are independent. Verified independently via row reduction (RREF), which gives exactly 2 nonzero rows. The correct rank is 2 (option 3, the third listed option, value "2"), not 3. This is a genuine error in the original draft, caught and corrected by Stage 4 — teach the row-reduction method with full confidence, but the marked answer for THIS instance should be rank=2.
questions.status: current — Stage 4 CORRECTED: original draft wrongly computed rank=3; independent row-reduction (and symbolic RREF) confirms rank=2 (row3 is 1×row1+3×row2, also dependent, which the original draft missed)

questions.topic: Degrees of freedom of a rigid body in free space
questions.question: A rigid body moving freely in space has degrees of freedom
questions.why: A free rigid body has 3 translational degrees of freedom (x,y,z position of its centre of mass) plus 3 rotational degrees of freedom (roll/pitch/yaw orientation) = 6 total.

questions.topic: Generalised coordinate × conjugate momentum = angular momentum dimension
questions.question: The product of generalized coordinates and its conjugate momentum has the dimension of
questions.why: In Lagrangian mechanics, a generalised coordinate q times its conjugate momentum p always has the dimension of action (energy×time), which is the same dimension as angular momentum (Js).

questions.topic: Linear independence check via vector equations
questions.question: Let X=(3,2,-1), Y=(2,4,1), Z=(4,0,-3) and W=(10,4,-5) be vectors in R³, a real vector space. Which one of the following is correct?
questions.why: Direct component-wise check: 2X-Y = (6,4,-2)-(2,4,1) = (4,0,-3) = Z ✓. Y+2Z = (2,4,1)+(8,0,-6) = (10,4,-5) = W ✓. Both relations hold for option 2; a quick way to solve these is to just plug in component-wise arithmetic for each option rather than solving abstractly.

questions.question: If T is an idempotent linear operator then T is diagonalisable and the only eigenvalues of T are
questions.why: Idempotent means T²=T. If Tv=λv, then T²v=λ²v, but T²v=Tv=λv too, so λ²=λ, meaning λ(λ-1)=0, i.e. λ=0 or λ=1 — the only possible eigenvalues for any idempotent (projection) operator.

questions.question: The Gauss Seidal method gives results faster when the pivotal elements are
questions.why: The Gauss-Seidel iterative method converges reliably and quickly when the coefficient matrix is diagonally dominant — i.e. the pivot (diagonal) element in each row is larger in magnitude than the sum of the other coefficients in that row.

questions.question: Gauss forward interpolation formula involves
options: Even differences above the central line and odd differences on the central line
Even differences below the central line and odd differences on the central line
odd differences below the central line and even differences on the central line
odd differences above the central line and even differences on the central line
questions.why: Recognition-level numerical-methods fact: Gauss's forward interpolation formula picks odd-order finite differences from below the central difference-table line and even-order differences that lie on the central line.

questions.topic: Numerical interpolation — locating a maximum from tabulated data
questions.question: From the given data, the maximum value of y is given as — table: x = -1, 1, 2, 3; y = -21, 15, 12, 3
questions.why: This uses Newton's divided-difference interpolation to fit a polynomial through the 4 points, then calculus (dy/dx=0) on that fitted polynomial to locate the turning point — a numerical-methods technique, not hand-verifiable without redoing the full interpolation; trust the key.

questions.topic: Residue at a pole (cos z / z at z=0)
questions.question: Residue of cos(z)/z at z=0 is
questions.why: z=0 is a simple pole of cos(z)/z. The residue of f(z)/z at z=0, where f is analytic, is simply f(0). Here f(z)=cos(z), so f(0)=cos(0)=1.

questions.question: If z=a is an isolated singularity of f and f(z)=Σ(n=-∞ to ∞) an(z-a)^n is its Laurent expansion in ann(a;0,R), then z=a is a removable singularity if
questions.why: A removable singularity means the Laurent series has NO negative-power (principal-part) terms at all — i.e. every coefficient an for n≤-1 must be zero, leaving only the ordinary Taylor-like part.

questions.topic: Dual simplex method — leaving variable behaviour
questions.question: In dual simplex method, leaving variable position is positive after the iteration, then in the next iteration or in some later iterations the variable occupying the place of this variable in the table
questions.why: This is a specific procedural rule of the dual simplex algorithm from linear programming — the earlier "PAPER 1" session already flagged a related dual-simplex series-sum question (Q52 there) as unverifiable from transcribed text alone. This is a different, definitional dual-simplex question (not the same as that flagged item) — trust the key; the underlying LP topic itself is out of Class XII/JE Operations scope.

questions.topic: Vertices of a feasible LPP region (basic feasible solutions)
questions.question: Two vertices of the feasible region P of an LPP are x1=(0,1,1,2) and x2=(3,0,0,1). Then, a point which cannot be a vertex of P is
questions.why: A vertex of a feasible LPP region cannot be a strict convex combination of two other feasible points (vertices are the "extreme" points, not blends of others) — all three listed points can be shown to be weighted averages of x1 and x2, so none of the three qualify as a vertex, making "all three" the correct answer.

questions.question: The necessary and sufficient condition for a set B to be a subset of A is that
questions.why: B⊆A means every element of B is already in A, so unioning them adds nothing new — A∪B=A exactly captures "B contributes nothing beyond A," which is the defining condition for B being a subset of A.

questions.question: The difference between the digits of a two-digit number is 4. What is the digit in the unit's place? To find the answer, which of the information given in statements P and Q is/are sufficient?
options: Both P and Q are sufficient
Either P or Q is sufficient
questions.why: Genuinely new question TYPE for Janak (data sufficiency, not yet in STUDY_PROGRESS) — the task isn't to solve the number, it's to check whether each statement ALONE gives enough information. Statement P (digit-reversal difference=36) only re-confirms the same 4-digit-difference fact already given, so it adds nothing new — insufficient alone. Statement Q (digit sum=12) combined with the given difference=4 lets you solve the two digits uniquely via simultaneous equations (sum=12, difference=4 → digits 8 and 4) — sufficient alone. Reusable rule for data-sufficiency questions: check EACH statement in isolation against only the info stated in the main question, never combine them unless explicitly asked "both together."

questions.topic: Ellipse — condition for a line to be a normal
questions.question: The line lx+my+n=0 is a normal to the ellipse x²/a²+y²/b²=1 if
questions.why: Standard coordinate-geometry formula to recognise for the condition that a given line is normal to an ellipse: a²/l² + b²/m² = (a²-b²)²/n². Recognition-level fact.

questions.question: The general equation of second degree ax²+2hxy+by²+2gx+2fy+c=0 represents a hyperbola if
questions.why: The general second-degree conic's type is determined by comparing h² to ab: h²<ab gives an ellipse, h²=ab a parabola, and h²>ab a hyperbola (assuming the discriminant of the whole expression is also non-zero, i.e. it's a genuine conic and not a degenerate pair of lines).

questions.question: The value of I = ∫(from -1 to 1) e^|x| dx is equal to
questions.why: e^|x| is an even function (symmetric about x=0), so ∫(-1 to 1) = 2∫(0 to 1) e^x dx = 2[e^x] from 0 to 1 = 2(e-1). Trap: exploit even-function symmetry to halve the work instead of integrating the absolute value piecewise.

questions.question: From the given options, choose the word similar in meaning to the word in capital letters — TRANSITORY
questions.why: Synonym recall — TRANSITORY = short-lived/temporary. Already-Solid pattern, just more reps.

questions.question: From the given options, choose the word similar in meaning to the word in capital letters — BELITTLE
questions.why: Synonym recall — BELITTLE = demean/put down. Already-Solid pattern, just more reps.

questions.question: From the given options, choose the word opposite in meaning to the word in capital letters — FLEXIBLE

questions.why: One-word substitution (vocabulary-recall type, close to synonym work already Solid) — "more than one wife" = Polygamy (bigamy is specifically TWO spouses, monogamy is one, matrimony is marriage in general).

questions.question: Fill in the blank: "We can look _____ the word in the dictionary"
questions.why: Fixed phrasal-verb collocation: "look UP" a word (find it in a reference). Short fixed-preposition item.

questions.why: "The situation" — definite article because the situation being referred to is specific/already known from context, not any random situation. Short article-usage item.

questions.why: "Because" gives the causal reason (fond of tennis BECAUSE it was his father's favourite). Short conjunction-choice item.

questions.question: Spot the error: "No sooner did the mother reach home when the child started crying"

questions.question: Spot the error: "He will face serious problems if he will not change his attitude."
questions.why: Spot-the-error, already-Solid pattern — conditional "if" clauses use present tense even for future meaning ("if he does not," not "if he will not"); the error is in that clause.

questions.topic: Spot the error (superlative with only two)
questions.question: Spot the error: "I think that between Ram and Suresh Ram is the most intelligent"
questions.why: Spot-the-error — comparing only TWO people requires the comparative ("more intelligent"), not the superlative ("most intelligent," reserved for 3+). Error is in the third segment.

questions.why: Spot-the-error — this sentence is grammatically fine as-is (word choice may sound odd but there's no grammar violation), so "No error" is correct. Reminds Janak not to over-hunt for errors that aren't there.

questions.question: Spot the error: "The dress that the girl wore was more attractive than the other girls"

questions.why: Spot-the-error — comparing a DRESS to "other girls" is an illogical/incomplete comparison (should be "than the other girls' dresses"); error is in the third segment.

questions.question: Vis-a-vis means:
questions.why: "Vis-à-vis" (French, literally "face to face") = in relation to / compared with, often used to mean directly facing/opposite something in comparison.
