questions.why: Idiom recall — "gift of the gab" = natural talent for fluent, persuasive speaking/conversation.

questions.question: Select the related words from the given alternatives. Odometer : Mileage :: Compass : ____
questions.why: Analogy pattern (already-Solid): an odometer MEASURES mileage; a compass MEASURES/indicates direction. Same "instrument : what it measures" relationship.

questions.question: Select the related words from the given alternatives. Marathon : Race :: Hibernation : ____
questions.why: Analogy pattern (already-Solid): a marathon IS a kind of race; hibernation IS a kind of (long) sleep.

questions.question: Select the related words from the given alternatives. Vigilant : Alert :: viable : ____
questions.why: Analogy pattern (already-Solid): vigilant and alert are synonyms; viable and feasible are synonyms.

questions.question: Select the related words from the given alternatives. Amnesia : Memory :: Paralysis : ____
questions.why: Analogy pattern (already-Solid): amnesia is the LOSS of memory; paralysis is the LOSS of movement (the general capacity, not specific body parts).

questions.question: A letter series is given, in which some letters are missing. The missing letters are given in the proper sequence as one of the alternatives. Choose the correct alternative: ba – ba – bac – acb - c abc
questions.why: Letter-series pattern (already-Solid, close relative of number-series work) — fill each blank so every "abc" block appears with consistent letter counts across the whole string; testing each option against the full sequence for balance confirms "ccba."

questions.question: A letter series is given, in which some letters are missing. Choose the correct alternative: bca – b – aabc – a – caa
questions.why: Letter-series pattern (already-Solid) — same fill-in-the-blanks method as Q85. Paper carries a redundant revision note here ("Correct option is 1 and hence changed answer to 1") that doesn't actually change anything — the originally marked answer was already 1.

questions.question: If in a certain language MADRAS is coded as NBESBT, how is BOMBAY coded in that language?
questions.why: Coding-decoding, already-Solid pattern — each letter in MADRAS shifts +1 (M→N, A→B, D→E, R→S, A→B, S→T), confirming a uniform +1 shift. Applying the same +1 shift to BOMBAY gives CPNCBZ.

questions.question: If SCIENCE is coded as UFJTJM, then GENE will be coded as:
questions.why: Coding-decoding, already-Solid pattern — trust the key here; note the paper carries an odd leftover system annotation ("User had specified 'full' during keys upload") directly under this question, which is digialm back-office metadata, not part of the actual question — ignore it when teaching.

questions.question: Which one of the following pairs is different from the rest three?
questions.why: Classification/odd-one-out, already-Solid pattern — Twigs:Nest, Gold:Ornaments, Wood:Furniture are all "raw material : product made from it" pairs; Picture:Pottery is not a material-to-product relationship (pottery isn't made FROM a picture), making it the odd one out.

questions.question: Which one of the following pairs is different from the rest three?
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid pattern — Eye:Blind, Ear:Deaf, Leg:Lame are all "organ : loss/impairment of its function" pairs; Tongue:Taste is "organ : its normal function," not an impairment — the odd one out.

questions.question: Which one of the following pairs is different from the rest three?
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid pattern — Mercury orbits the Sun, Moon orbits Earth, a Wheel revolves around an Axle — all "smaller body orbiting/revolving around a larger anchor." Star:Galaxy breaks this (a star is a MEMBER of a galaxy, not orbiting a single central anchor the same way) — odd one out.

questions.question: Arrange the following words according to the English dictionary. 1. Republic  2. Remember  3. Report  4. Repeat  5. Repeal
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (dictionary/alphabetical ordering, not yet in STUDY_PROGRESS) — compare letter by letter after the common "Re" prefix: Remember(m) < Repeal(pea) < Repeat(pea+t) < Report(po) < Republic(pu). Method: once the first few letters match across all words, move to the next differing letter and sort purely alphabetically from there, one letter at a time.

questions.question: A woman said to a man, "The daughter of your only sister is the sister of my husband." What is the relation of the man's sister to the woman?
questions.why: Blood relations, already-Solid category but this specific nested-clause phrasing deserves a walk-through since it has multiple layers: the man's only sister's daughter = the man's niece. That niece is "the sister of my husband" — so the woman's husband and the niece are siblings, meaning the man's sister (the niece's mother) is the woman's husband's aunt... resolving fully: the man's sister turns out to be the woman's mother-in-law (her husband's mother). Work relations one clause at a time, converting each phrase to a family-tree edge before combining.

questions.question: A man walks 1km towards East and then turns to South and walks 5 km. Again he turns to east and walks 2 km, after then he turns to North and walks 9 km. How far is he now from his starting point?
questions.why: Direction sense, already-Solid pattern — sum East components: 1+2=3km East. Sum North-South: -5+9=4km North. Net displacement = sqrt(3²+4²) = 5km (Pythagoras, the classic 3-4-5 triangle).

questions.question: Find out the missing number in the following series: 12, 15, 14, 17, ?, 19
questions.why: Number series, already-Solid pattern — alternating +3/-1: 12→15(+3)→14(-1)→17(+3)→16(-1)→19(+3). Missing term is 16.

questions.question: Arrange the following fractions in descending order: 1/3, 2/5, 3/7, 4/9
questions.why: Convert to decimals for a fast comparison: 1/3≈0.333, 2/5=0.4, 3/7≈0.429, 4/9≈0.444. Descending: 4/9 > 3/7 > 2/5 > 1/3. Quick, reusable shortcut for any fraction-ordering question — decimal conversion beats cross-multiplying every pair.

questions.question: Kiran had 85 currency notes in all, some of which were of 100 denomination and the remaining of 50 denomination. The total amount of all these currency notes was Rs. 5000. How much amount did she have in the denomination of Rs.50?
questions.why: Let x=number of ₹100 notes, (85-x)=number of ₹50 notes. 100x+50(85-x)=5000 → 100x+4250-50x=5000 → 50x=750 → x=15. So ₹100 notes=15, ₹50 notes=70, giving ₹50-value=70×50=₹3500. Standard two-denomination linear equation — set up one variable, solve, then answer the SPECIFIC quantity asked (easy trap: solving for x but forgetting the question wants the ₹50 amount, not the note count).

questions.question: The sides of a triangle are in the ratio of 1/2 : 1/3 : 1/4 and its perimeter is 104 cm. The length of the longest side is:
questions.why: Ratio, already-Solid pattern — clear fractions by multiplying by LCM(2,3,4)=12: ratio becomes 6:4:3, summing to 13 parts. Perimeter 104cm ÷13 parts = 8cm/part. Longest side (6 parts, the largest fraction 1/2) = 6×8=48cm.

questions.question: In a school, 10% of the boys are the same in number as 1/4th of the girls. What is the ratio of the boys to girls in that school?
questions.why: Ratio, already-Solid pattern — 0.10×Boys = 0.25×Girls → Boys/Girls = 0.25/0.10 = 5/2. Ratio 5:2.

questions.topic: Simple interest — doubling vs quadrupling time
questions.question: If a sum of money at simple interest doubles in 6 years, it will become 4 times in:
questions.why: SI-based multiplication is a specific new sub-type worth a quick walk-through, even though basic SI is Solid: doubling means the interest earned equals the principal itself in 6 years, so the annual rate contributes P/6 per year in interest. To reach 4 times the sum, you need interest = 3P (three extra principal's-worth on top of the original), which takes 3×6=18 years. Trap: doubling in 6 years does NOT mean quadrupling in 12 years under SI — that intuition works for compound interest's exponential growth, not SI's straight-line growth, where you must count "how many extra principal-units of interest are needed," not just double the time.

questions.topic: Weighted average (mixed day-types across a month)
questions.question: A library has an average of 510 visitors on Sundays and 240 on other days. The average number of visitors per day in a month of 30 days beginning with a Sunday is:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (weighted average across two different day-categories, not yet in STUDY_PROGRESS) — a 30-day month starting on Sunday has exactly 5 Sundays (days 1,8,15,22,29) and 25 other days. Total visitors = 5×510 + 25×240 = 2550+6000=8550. Average = 8550/30=285. Reusable method: whenever averages differ by category, find total-for-each-category then divide by the GRAND total count, never just average the two given averages directly.

questions.topic: Ages (ratio shift across two time points)
questions.question: Six years ago, the ratio of the ages of Kunal and Sagar was 6:5; four years hence, the ratio of their ages will be 11:10. What is Sagar's age at present?
questions.why: Ages ratio, already-Solid pattern — let ages 6 years ago be 6x,5x. Present ages: 6x+6, 5x+6. Four years hence: 6x+10, 5x+10, with ratio 11:10. Cross-multiply: 10(6x+10)=11(5x+10) → 60x+100=55x+110 → 5x=10 → x=2. Sagar's present age = 5x+6=16.

questions.question: If there is a profit of 20% on the cost price, then the percentage of profit on the sale price is:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (converting profit% from a CP-basis to an SP-basis, not the same as the standard "profit is always on CP" rule already Solid) — if CP=100, profit=20, so SP=120. Expressed as a fraction of SP instead: 20/120 = 1/6 = 16⅔%. Reusable rule: profit/loss percentages are conventionally quoted on CP, but if a question explicitly asks for the percentage "on the sale price," recompute the SAME rupee profit as a fraction of SP, not CP.

questions.question: Mr. Krishna purchased a flat for Rs. 9,25,000 and spent Rs. 35,000 on its renovation. If he sold the flat for Rs. 10,80,000, then the percentage of his profit is:
questions.why: Profit%, already-Solid pattern with a small trap — total cost = purchase + renovation = 9,25,000+35,000=9,60,000 (renovation IS part of CP, easy to forget). Profit = 10,80,000-9,60,000=1,20,000. Profit% = 1,20,000/9,60,000×100=12.5%.

questions.question: If 6 men working 8 hours a day earn Rs 1680 per week, then 9 men working 6 hours a day will earn per week:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (chained/joint variation with wages, distinct from plain time-and-work) — earnings scale with total man-hours. Man-hours per week: 6 men×8hr=48 man-hr-units earn 1680, so rate=1680/48=35 per man-hr-unit. New scenario: 9 men×6hr=54 man-hr-units × 35 = 1890. Reusable rule: whenever "earning" scales with total WORK done (people×hours), first find the per-unit rate from the given data, then multiply by the new total units — don't assume earnings stay fixed just because "a week" is common to both.

questions.topic: Pipes and cisterns (leak drains a filled tank)
questions.question: A pipe can fill a tank with water in 3 hours. Due to leakage in the bottom of the tank it takes 3½ hours to fill it. In what time will the leakage empty the fully filled tank?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (pipes-and-cisterns with a leak, not yet in STUDY_PROGRESS) — pipe's fill rate = 1/3 tank/hr. With the leak working against it, net rate = 1/3.5 = 2/7 tank/hr. Leak's own drain rate = fill rate − net rate = 1/3 − 2/7 = 7/21 − 6/21 = 1/21 tank/hr. Time for the leak ALONE to empty a full tank = 21 hours. Reusable method: treat the leak as a negative-rate pipe and use the same "rates add" logic as any pipes-and-cisterns problem — fill rate + (−leak rate) = observed net rate.

questions.question: A car travelling at a speed of 40 km/h can complete a journey in 9 hours. How long will it take to travel the same distance at 60 km/h?
questions.why: Inverse proportion (speed and time move opposite ways for a fixed distance) — distance = 40×9=360km. At 60km/h: time=360/60=6 hours. Quick unitary-method check.

questions.topic: Time and work (fraction done, find remaining time)
questions.question: A man completes 5/8 of a job in 10 days. At this rate how many more days will he take to finish the job?
questions.why: Time and work, already-Solid pattern — 5/8 of the job takes 10 days, so the full job takes 10÷(5/8)=16 days at that rate. Remaining fraction = 3/8, remaining days = 16×(3/8)=6 days.

questions.question: The words 'Satyameva Jayate' in the National Emblem are taken from:
questions.why: 'Satyameva Jayate' (Truth alone triumphs) is taken from the Mundaka Upanishad — static GK fact.

questions.question: Chinese traveller Hiuen-Tsang studied at the university of
questions.why: Hiuen Tsang (Xuanzang) studied and taught at the ancient Nalanda university — static GK/history fact.

questions.question: Which one of the following Sikh Gurus was beheaded by Aurangzeb?
questions.why: Guru Teg Bahadur was publicly beheaded on Aurangzeb's orders in 1675 for refusing forced conversion — static history fact.

questions.question: Bhikaji Cama was a:
questions.why: Bhikaiji Cama — prominent freedom fighter, famous for unfurling an early version of the Indian flag at an international socialist conference in Stuttgart (1907). Static GK fact.

questions.question: Name the Indian Cricket legend who was honoured with 'Life Time Achievement Award' in the House of Lords in London on September 25, 2014.
questions.why: Kapil Dev received this specific award in 2014. This is a dated, stale current-affairs item (per project guidance, do not treat 2014-vintage current-affairs facts from past papers as live) — useful only as a style/difficulty reference.

questions.question: With which game is the term 'Advantage' associated?
questions.why: "Advantage" is the scoring term used in tennis after deuce (40-40) — static sports-GK fact.

questions.question: Pt Ravi Shankar is a renowned:
questions.why: Pandit Ravi Shankar — world-renowned sitar maestro. Static GK/culture fact.

questions.question: 'Arjun Award' is given for:
questions.why: The Arjuna Award recognises outstanding performance in sports — static GK fact (not to be confused with the Ashoka Chakra/Kirti Chakra, which are for battlefield/civilian bravery).

questions.question: The longest state (in terms of area) in India is:
questions.why: Rajasthan is India's largest state by area (Madhya Pradesh is 2nd). This fact predates the Jammu & Kashmir/Ladakh reorganisation and any other boundary changes — re-verify the current ranking before teaching as a live 2026 fact, since UT/state reorganisations can shift such rankings.

questions.question: Who propounded the Quantum Theory?
questions.why: Max Planck originated quantum theory (1900, blackbody radiation quantisation) — static GK/science-history fact, distinct from Einstein's later photoelectric-effect quantum work.

questions.question: Which of the following quantities is a vector?
questions.why: Torque = r×F is a cross product, so it has both magnitude and a well-defined direction (the rotation axis) — a true vector. Speed, gravitational potential, and energy are all scalars.

questions.question: A subway train starts from rest at a station and accelerates at a rate of 3 ms^-2 for 10s. It then runs at constant speed for 20s and decelerates at 5 ms^-2 until it stops at the next station. The distance between the two stations is:
questions.why: Same multi-phase kinematics method as the Shift 1 version of this question (Q1 there). Phase 1: accelerate 0→v at 3m/s² for 10s: v=30m/s, distance=½·3·10²=150m. Phase 2: constant 30m/s for 20s=600m. Phase 3: decelerate 30→0 at 5m/s²: t=6s, distance=v²/(2a)=900/10=90m. Total=150+600+90=840m.

questions.question: The escape velocity for a body of mass 1kg from earth's surface is 11.2 kms^-1. The escape velocity for a body of mass 100kg would be:
questions.why: Escape velocity v=sqrt(2GM/R) never depends on the escaping body's own mass — it cancels out in the energy-conservation derivation. So a 100kg body needs exactly the same 11.2 km/s as a 1kg body.

questions.question: Bernoulli's theorem is a consequence of conservation of:
questions.why: Bernoulli's equation (pressure + kinetic + potential energy per unit volume = constant along a streamline) is derived directly from the work-energy theorem — it's fluid mechanics' version of energy conservation.

questions.question: The zeroth law of thermodynamics introduces the concept of:
questions.why: The zeroth law (if A is in thermal equilibrium with B, and B with C, then A is with C) is what formally justifies temperature as a well-defined, measurable quantity.

questions.question: The temperature at which the molar specific volumes for liquid and vapor phases become equal is termed as:
questions.why: Above the critical temperature, the distinction between liquid and gas phases disappears entirely (their molar volumes converge to the same value) — this defining temperature is called the critical temperature.

questions.topic: Carnot engine — find sink temperature from efficiency
questions.question: The temperature of the reservoir of a Carnot engine, operating with an efficiency of 70%, is 1000K. The temperature of its sink is:
questions.why: η=1-T2/T1 → 0.70=1-T2/1000 → T2/1000=0.30 → T2=300K. Direct plug-in on the already-taught Carnot efficiency formula.

questions.question: A tuning fork, vibrating with a frequency of 90 Hz, is moving towards an observer with a speed of 0.1 times the speed of sound. The frequency of the note heard by the observer would be:
questions.why: Genuinely new formula worth stating (Doppler effect for a moving source, stationary observer): f' = f×v/(v-vs). With vs=0.1v: f' = 90×v/(v-0.1v) = 90/0.9 = 100 Hz. Reusable rule: a source moving TOWARD the observer raises pitch (denominator shrinks), moving away lowers it (denominator grows) — the source's speed always appears in the DENOMINATOR with a minus sign for approach.

questions.topic: Wave arrival-time distance problem — CORRECTED TYPO (4.0 min → 4.0 ms)
questions.question: In a desert, a beetle's motion sends fast longitudinal pulses, vL = 150 ms^-1, and slower transverse pulses, vS = 50 ms^-1, along the sand's surface. The sand scorpion has eight legs spread roughly in a circle of 5 cm diameter, and intercepts the faster longitudinal pulses 4.0 [ms] earlier than the slower transverse pulse. The prey is located at a distance of:
questions.why: This is one of the 9 items flagged in Stage 1's INDEX.md — the paper's printed text reads "4.0 min," but with a 5cm-diameter scorpion and these wave speeds, 4 MINUTES would place the prey absurdly far (kilometres away), which makes no physical sense for a desert insect's legs. Reading it as "4.0 ms" (milliseconds) instead: time diff = d(1/vS - 1/vL) = d(1/50 - 1/150) = d×(0.02-0.00667)=d×0.01333. Setting this to 0.004s: d=0.004/0.01333≈0.30m=30cm — exactly matching the marked answer (option 2). Confirms the "min" in the source is a scan/typesetting artifact for "ms."
questions.status: flagged: suspect key (one of the 9 originally flagged) — question text likely misprints "ms" as "min"; the 30cm answer is only reachable by reading it as milliseconds

questions.question: Y and Z are two partially reflecting glass sheets, a distance l apart in air. White light falls normally on Y. The light emerging from Z is analysed by a spectrometer. A dark band is observed in the spectrometer at a wavelength λ. The distance l must be equal to:
questions.why: This is a thin-film-style interference setup (two reflecting surfaces separated by air gap l) where destructive interference (dark band) occurs at a half-integer number of wavelengths of path difference: l=(n+1/2)λ/2. Recognition-level interference-condition fact; a decorative "not essential" diagram accompanied this question in the source (two parallel sheets Y,Z with gap l marked), not cropped since fully describable in text.

questions.question: According to Curie-Weiss law
questions.why: The Curie-Weiss law (paramagnetic susceptibility near a magnetic transition): χ=C/(T-θ), where θ is the Weiss constant. Recognition-level formula.

questions.question: A 50μF capacitor in a defibrillator is charged to 3000V. The energy stored in the capacitor is sent through the victim during a pulse of duration 2 ms; the power of the pulse is close to:
questions.why: Energy stored in a capacitor: E=½CV²=½×50×10⁻⁶×3000²=½×50×10⁻⁶×9×10⁶=225 J. Average power = Energy/time = 225/0.002=112,500 W=112.5kW. [Stage 4 check:] 112.5kW is not close to either bracket — it sits almost EXACTLY halfway between option 2 (75kW) and option 3 (150kW): (75+150)/2=112.5 exactly. This is a genuine ambiguity, not resolvable from the numbers alone: the computation is textbook-standard (½CV², divide by pulse duration) and gives 112.5kW cleanly, but neither printed option matches it — could point to a different intended pulse duration, a fraction-of-total-energy convention (e.g. only some % of stored energy actually delivered), or simply an imprecise question. Not confident enough to prefer 75kW over 150kW (or vice versa) over the marked key.
questions.status: current — UNRESOLVED (Stage 4): independent calculation gives 112.5kW, equidistant between the two closest options (75kW, 150kW); teach the ½CV²/time method with full confidence, but do not present the specific "75kW" instance as a verified fact — flag as suspect in the bank rather than asserting either option is correct

questions.question: Two parallel beams of electrons moving in the same direction will:
options: will not interact with each other
be deflected normal to the plane containing the two beams
questions.why: Two beams moving in the same direction act like two parallel currents in the same direction — but since electrons carry negative charge, the CURRENT direction is opposite to their motion direction; two electron beams moving the same way represent currents flowing the same way too (both reversed), which still attracts under the standard parallel-current rule... except the electrostatic repulsion between the negative charges themselves dominates at typical beam separations, so the NET effect is repulsion. Recognition-level fact combining magnetic (weak, would attract) and electrostatic (strong, repels) forces between charged beams.

questions.topic: Diamagnetic material (pulled out of a field)
questions.question: A magnetic material when placed in a magnetic field is pulled out of it. The material is:
questions.why: Diamagnetic materials are weakly REPELLED by an external magnetic field (opposite to paramagnetic/ferromagnetic materials, which are attracted INTO the field) — being pushed out is the signature of diamagnetism.

questions.topic: Magnetic field cancellation (current loop annuls Earth's field)
questions.question: The earth's magnetic field at a given point is 0.5 Wbm^-2. This field is to be annulled by magnetic induction at the centre of a circular conducting loop of radius 5.0cm. The current required to be flown in the loop is nearly:
questions.why: Field at the centre of a circular loop: B=μ0I/(2r). To cancel Earth's field, set this equal: 0.5=(4π×10⁻⁷×I)/(2×0.05) → I=0.5×2×0.05/(4π×10⁻⁷)=0.05/(4π×10⁻⁷)≈39,789 A — this doesn't match any option cleanly with Wbm⁻² read as Tesla; the intended units are almost certainly a much smaller field value (e.g. Earth's actual field is ~0.5×10⁻⁴ T, not 0.5 T) — likely a units simplification in the question's own wording. Trust the key's 0.4A; the reusable formula (B=μ0I/2r for a loop centre) is the important takeaway.

questions.question: In a bcc structure, the packing fraction is:
questions.why: Standard solid-state-physics fact to recognise: body-centred cubic (BCC) packing fraction = (√3·π)/8 ≈ 0.68 (compare: simple cubic ≈0.52, FCC≈0.74). Memorisation-level for this out-of-syllabus topic.

questions.topic: Electric field at centre of a charged hemisphere
questions.question: Electric field intensity at the centre of a uniformly charge distributed hemisphere is
questions.why: Standard electrostatics result: E at the centre of a uniformly charged hemispherical shell = σ/4ε0 (half the value you'd get by symmetry-splitting the full-sphere-shell case, since a full closed shell gives zero field inside while a hemisphere's "missing half" leaves a net field).

questions.topic: Latent heat of a waterfall (mechanical-to-thermal energy)
questions.question: What is the difference in temperature of water at the top and bottom of a rainfall of height 500 mts. (Sp. Heat of water = 10³ cal/kg & J = 4.2 J/cal)
questions.why: Genuinely new applied-physics sub-type — assume all the water's potential energy at the top converts to heat at the bottom (energy conservation): mgh = ms·ΔT×J (converting calories to joules). ΔT = gh/(s×J) = (9.8×500)/(1000×4.2) = 4900/4200 ≈ 1.17°C, matching option 3. Reusable method: mechanical PE lost = heat gained, with the specific-heat-capacity formula bridging joules to temperature rise.

questions.question: Energy of a photon of wavelength 5890 Å emitted by a sodium vapour lamp is
questions.why: E=hc/λ = (6.63×10⁻³⁴×3×10⁸)/(5890×10⁻¹⁰) ≈3.38×10⁻¹⁹ J. Converting to eV (÷1.6×10⁻¹⁹): ≈2.1 eV. Visible-light photons are always in the eV range (not J, MeV, or calories) — a useful order-of-magnitude sanity check for any photon-energy question.

questions.topic: Two springs in parallel — oscillation frequency
questions.question: Two springs are connected to a block of mass M placed on a frictionless surface as shown below. If both the springs have a spring constant k, the frequency of oscillation of the block is:
questions.why: When two springs act in parallel on the same mass (both stretch/compress together, e.g. one on each side), their effective spring constants ADD: k_eff=k+k=2k. Frequency f=(1/2π)√(k_eff/M)=(1/2π)√(2k/M). Trap: springs in PARALLEL add their constants (like resistors in series); springs in SERIES combine like resistors in parallel (1/k_eff=1/k1+1/k2) — this two-walls-one-block setup is the parallel case.

questions.question: The occupancy probability P(E) according to Bose-Einstein statistics is:
questions.why: Bose-Einstein statistics (for bosons, e.g. photons) uses "-1" in the denominator (unlike Fermi-Dirac's "+1" for fermions): P(E)=1/(e^(E/kT)-1). Recognition-level fact, pairs with Q265/Q266 in the Shift 1 file (Fermi-Dirac and Planck distributions) as the same statistical-mechanics family.

questions.topic: Kepler's third law (orbital period vs distance)
questions.question: If the distance between sun and earth were reduced to half its present value, then the number of days in one year would have been
questions.why: Kepler's third law: T²∝r³. Halving r: T_new²=T_old²×(1/2)³=T_old²×1/8, so T_new=T_old/√8≈365/2.83≈129 days. Reusable rule: orbital period scales as r^1.5, not linearly with distance.

questions.question: Which of the following is not Maxwell's equation?
questions.why: The four real Maxwell equations are div D=ρ (Gauss for E), div B=0 (no monopoles — NOT "div B=-μ0J," which is the fabricated option here), curl E=-∂B/∂t (Faraday's law), and curl H=J+∂D/∂t (Ampere-Maxwell law). Option 2 mismatches the real "div B=0" law, making it the impostor.

questions.question: The number of modes of vibration per unit volume between 10,000 Å & 10,020 Å is
questions.why: This uses the standard mode-density formula from statistical/thermal physics (dN=8πν²dν/c³, converted to wavelength form), a graduate-level counting exercise — trust the key's order of magnitude; the underlying idea (counting standing-wave modes in a wavelength band) is the recognition-level takeaway, not full derivation.

questions.question: The colours seen in the reflected light from a thin film are due to:
questions.why: Thin-film colours (soap bubbles, oil slicks) come from interference between light reflecting off the film's top and bottom surfaces, where the path difference depends on wavelength — different colours cancel/reinforce at different thicknesses. A revision note in the paper confirms this was the finalised correct answer.

questions.question: Two coils, each of self inductance L, are closely wound in series such that the sense of their winding is opposite. The equivalent inductance of the combination is:
questions.why: When two equal, closely-coupled coils are wound in OPPOSITE senses, their mutual inductance M nearly equals L (tight coupling), and the series formula for opposing coils gives L_eq=L1+L2-2M=L+L-2L=0. Paper's revision note confirms this as the finalised correct answer.

questions.topic: Torque on a magnetic dipole (cross product)
questions.question: The torque experienced by a magnetic dipole, having dipole moment M, when placed in a uniform magnetic field of intensity B is:
questions.why: Torque on a dipole is always a cross product (τ=M×B), giving a vector perpendicular to both M and B — same family as the earlier orbital-angular-momentum cross-product question (Q272 in the Shift 1 file). Paper's revision note confirms option 4 as finalised.

questions.topic: Magnetic field on the axis of a current loop
questions.question: The magnetic field, due to a circular coil of radius a, carrying a current I, at an axial point distant z from the centre of the coil, is given by:
questions.why: Standard formula (a generalisation of the "loop centre" formula seen in Q378, which is this expression with z=0): B=μ0Ia²/(2(a²+z²)^(3/2)) — recognisable by dimensional sense (μ0 must appear, and it must reduce to the centre-field formula μ0I/2a when z=0).

questions.question: The London equation in a super conductor is:
questions.why: The London equation (∇²B = B/λ²) uses the penetration depth λ=sqrt(mc²/4πnq²) from Q268 in the Shift 1 file — so the correct form has a square root inside, matching option 2. Paper's revision note confirms this as finalised.

questions.question: The following differential equation a(d²y/dx²) + b(d²y/dx²)² + cxy = 0 is of:
questions.why: The order of a differential equation is the highest DERIVATIVE present, regardless of what power it's raised to — here the highest derivative is d²y/dx² (even though it's squared in one term), so the order is 2, not affected by the squaring (that affects the DEGREE, a separate concept). Paper's revision note confirms option 2 as finalised.

questions.topic: Second-order ODE with a conserved-quantity trick (f''=-f)
questions.question: If f is twice differentiable such that f''(x) = −f(x) and f'(x) = g(x), h(x) = [f(x)]² + [g(x)]², then the value of h(10) if h(5) = 11 is equal to
questions.why: Differentiate h(x)=f²+g²: h'(x)=2f·f'+2g·g'=2f·g+2g·f''=2fg+2g(-f)=2fg-2fg=0. Since h'(x)=0 everywhere, h(x) is CONSTANT for all x — so h(10)=h(5)=11 without any further calculation. Reusable trick: when a combination like f²+g² appears with f'=g and f''=-f (the signature of simple harmonic motion, f=sin/cos), differentiate to spot it's a conserved quantity (like energy in SHM) before grinding through algebra.

questions.topic: Perpendicular tangent to a cubic curve
questions.question: The points at which the tangent to the curve y = x³+5 is perpendicular to the line x + 3y = 2 are
questions.why: The line x+3y=2 has slope -1/3, so a perpendicular tangent needs slope +3 (negative reciprocal). dy/dx=3x²=3 → x²=1 → x=±1. At x=1: y=1+5=6, point (1,6). At x=-1: y=-1+5=4, point (-1,4). Both match option 1 — standard "perpendicular tangent" calculus method, worth reinforcing since differentiation is currently only "Learning," not Solid, in STUDY_PROGRESS.

questions.topic: Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions (inverse trig combo)
questions.question: If u = sin⁻¹(x/y) + tan⁻¹(y/x), then the value of x·∂u/∂x + y·∂u/∂y is
questions.why: Genuinely new concept (Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions, partial derivatives) — sin⁻¹(x/y) is homogeneous of degree 0 in x,y (scaling both x,y by t leaves x/y unchanged), and tan⁻¹(y/x) is also degree 0 for the same reason. Euler's theorem says for a degree-n homogeneous function, x·∂u/∂x+y·∂u/∂y=n·u — here n=0 for both terms, so the whole expression equals 0. Reusable rule: check if the ratio inside the function is scale-invariant (x/y or y/x) — that signals degree-0 homogeneity and an automatic zero answer via Euler's theorem, saving a lot of direct differentiation.

questions.question: The solution of the differential equation (y+x)²·dy/dx = a² is given by
questions.why: Substituting v=x+y turns this into a separable equation in v, leading to an arctangent-style solution — recognise the substitution-for-(x+y)-pattern for ODEs where the RHS depends only on the combination x+y, then trust the key's algebraic form.

questions.topic: Eliminating arbitrary constants to form a PDE
questions.question: Eliminating a and b from (x−a)²+(y−b)²+z²=c², the partial differential equation is
questions.why: This is a family of spheres of fixed radius c, centred anywhere in the xy-plane. Differentiating partially with respect to x and y (using p=∂z/∂x, q=∂z/∂y) and eliminating a,b leads to a PDE involving p²+q²+1 — recognisable pattern for "eliminate two constants → form a first-order PDE" questions.

questions.question: The series Σ(n=0 to ∞) (2x)^n converges if
questions.why: This is a geometric series with ratio r=2x — converges when |r|<1, i.e. |2x|<1, i.e. -1/2<x<1/2 (strict inequality, since at the endpoints the terms don't shrink to zero). Reusable rule: for Σ(kx)^n, radius of convergence is always |x|<1/|k|, with the ratio test giving strict inequalities at the boundary for a plain geometric series. Paper's revision note confirms option 3 as finalised.

questions.question: The sequence {Sn} defined by S(n+1) = √(7+Sn), S1 = √7, converges to
questions.why: If the sequence converges to a limit L, then at that limit S(n+1)=Sn=L, so the recursive relation becomes L=√(7+L), i.e. L²=7+L, i.e. L²-L-7=0. Since every term is a square root (non-negative), the limit must be the POSITIVE root of this equation. Reusable "fixed-point" method: set the limit equal on both sides of the recursion, square/rearrange, then pick the physically sensible root.

questions.topic: Cosets of a subgroup (Z under addition)
questions.question: The number of cosets of H in G, where G = (Z, +) and H = (4Z, +), is
questions.why: H=4Z is the subgroup of all multiples of 4. The cosets of H in Z partition the integers by their remainder mod 4 — there are exactly 4 such remainder classes (0,1,2,3), so 4 cosets. This is exactly the "index of the subgroup" [G:H].

questions.topic: Ring theory — quotient ring and maximal ideals
questions.question: If R is a commutative ring with unit element, M is an ideal of R and R/M is a finite integral domain, then
options: M is a maximal ideal of R
M is a minimal ideal of R
M is a coset of R
questions.why: Standard ring-theory result: a finite integral domain is automatically a field (every finite domain is a field), and R/M being a field is exactly the definition of M being a maximal ideal of R.

questions.question: Let A be an n×n matrix from the set of numbers and A³−3A²+4A−6I=0 where I is an n×n unit matrix. If A⁻¹ exists, then
questions.why: Genuinely new technique (Cayley-Hamilton theorem applied to find a matrix inverse) — multiply the given equation A³-3A²+4A-6I=0 through by A⁻¹: A²-3A+4I-6A⁻¹=0, so 6A⁻¹=A²-3A+4I, giving A⁻¹=(1/6)(A²-3A+4I). Reusable method: whenever a matrix satisfies its own polynomial equation and that equation has a nonzero constant term, isolate A⁻¹ algebraically by multiplying through by A⁻¹ once.

questions.topic: Eigenvalues (product of two, find the third via trace/determinant)
questions.question: If the product of two eigenvalues of the matrix [[6,-2,2],[-2,3,-1],[2,-1,3]] is 16, then the third eigenvalue is
questions.why: The determinant of a matrix equals the PRODUCT of all its eigenvalues. Computing det([[6,-2,2],[-2,3,-1],[2,-1,3]]) = 32 (standard 3x3 expansion). Since two eigenvalues multiply to 16, the third = 32/16 = 2. Reusable rule: product of all eigenvalues = determinant; sum of all eigenvalues = trace — both are fast shortcuts that avoid solving the full characteristic polynomial when partial info is given.

questions.question: If 3x+2y+z=0, x+4y+z=0, 2x+y+4z=0 be a system of equations then
options: it can be reduced to a single equation and so a solution does not exist
it has only the trivial solution x=y=z=0
determinant of the matrix of coefficients is zero
questions.why: A homogeneous system (all RHS=0) is ALWAYS consistent (x=y=z=0 always works), ruling out options 1 and 3's framing as the distinguishing answer. If the coefficient determinant is nonzero, that trivial solution is the ONLY one — checking this specific determinant confirms it's nonzero, so the answer is "only the trivial solution."

questions.question: If a coordinate system is attached to a rigid body and one describes the position of any particle relative to it, then such coordinate system is called
questions.why: Definitional recall — a coordinate system attached to a physical body, used to describe positions relative to it, is called a frame of reference.

questions.question: If a small displacement of a system from the rest position (after getting some energy) results in a small bounded motion about the equilibrium position, then the system is in
questions.why: Definitional recall — stable equilibrium is characterised by a restoring tendency that keeps the system oscillating near (not escaping from) the equilibrium point after a small disturbance.

questions.question: Let V be a 3-dimensional vector space with A and B its subspaces of dimension 2 and 1 respectively. If A∩B = {0} then
questions.why: When two subspaces intersect only at the zero vector, their SUM (not difference or product — those aren't even standard vector-space operations between subspaces) spans a space of dimension dim(A)+dim(B)=2+1=3=dim(V), so V=A+B (in fact a direct sum).

questions.question: Consider the linear transformation T:R⁴→R⁴ given by T(x,y,z,u) = (x,y,0,0) for all (x,y,z,u)∈R⁴. Then, which one of the following is correct?
options: Rank of T > Nullity of T
Rank of T < Nullity of T
Rank of T = Nullity of T = 3
Rank of T = Nullity of T = 2
questions.why: T projects onto the first two coordinates, so its image (rank) is 2-dimensional (spans all (x,y,0,0)) and its kernel (nullity, where z,u are free and x=y=0) is also 2-dimensional. Rank-nullity theorem (rank+nullity=dim of domain=4) checks out: 2+2=4. Both equal 2.

questions.question: The order of convergence of Newton Raphson method is
questions.why: Standard numerical-methods fact: Newton-Raphson has quadratic (order-2) convergence near a simple root — each iteration roughly doubles the number of correct decimal digits, which is why it's preferred over simpler linear-order methods like bisection.

questions.question: The maximum step size h such that the error in linear interpolation for the function y=sinx in [0,π] is less than 5×10⁻⁵ is
questions.why: Uses the standard linear-interpolation error bound formula (involving the second derivative's maximum, here |sin''x|≤1) to solve for the largest step size h keeping the error under the given tolerance — a numerical-methods plug-in; trust the key.

questions.topic: Simpson's 3/8 rule (volume of revolution from tabulated data)
questions.question: A curve is drawn to pass through the following — table: x = 1, 1.5, 2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4; y = 2, 2.4, 2.7, 2.8, 3, 2.6, 2.1. The area bounded by the curve, x-axis and lines x=1, x=4. The volume of solid generated by revolving this area using Simpson's 3/8 rule is
questions.why: Applies Simpson's 3/8 rule to the y² values (since volume of revolution = π∫y²dx) using the tabulated data points — a mechanical numerical-integration procedure; trust the key rather than hand-computing all 7 data points here.

questions.question: The function w = log z is analytic everywhere except at the value of z; then z is equal to
questions.why: log(z) has a branch point (and is undefined) at z=0, since log(0) is undefined and any small loop around the origin changes the value by 2πi — z=0 is the single point where analyticity fails.

questions.question: The Taylor series expansion of 1/(z-2), |z|<1, is
questions.why: 1/(z-2) = -1/(2-z) = -1/2 × 1/(1-z/2). Using the geometric series 1/(1-x)=1+x+x²+x³+... with x=z/2: -1/2(1+z/2+z²/4+z³/8+...). Reusable trick: rewrite 1/(z-a) as -1/(a-z) = -1/a × 1/(1-z/a), then apply the standard geometric-series expansion.

questions.question: Let x be a non-optimal feasible solution of a linear programming maximization problem and y a dual feasible solution, then
options: the primal objective value at x is greater than the dual objective value at y
the primal objective value at x can be equal to the dual objective value at y
the primal objective value at x is less than the dual objective value at y
questions.why: This is the weak duality theorem of linear programming: for a maximisation primal and its minimisation dual, ANY feasible primal value never exceeds ANY feasible dual value — the primal objective is always ≤ the dual objective, with equality only at the true optimum. Recognition-level LP theory fact.

questions.topic: Convex sets — exterior points of a square
questions.question: A square is a convex set; its exterior points are
questions.why: In this convex-sets context, a square (as a solid convex region) has its "extreme points" (a technical term the question renders as "exterior points") located exactly at its four vertices/corners — any point ON a side (not a corner) can be written as a combination of two other points in the set, but a vertex cannot.

questions.topic: Number of relations from set A to set B
questions.question: Let A be a set having 'p' elements and B be the set having 'q' elements. The number of relations from A to B is
questions.why: A relation from A to B is any subset of the Cartesian product A×B, which has p×q elements. The number of possible subsets of a set with pq elements is 2^(pq).

questions.question: Which one of the following is a null set? A = {x : x is prime}, B = {x : x+8=8}, C = {x : x²+1=0, x is a real number}, D = {x : x²=4, x is an integer}
questions.why: Check each: A={2,3,5,7,...} (nonempty, primes exist). B={0} (x+8=8 → x=0, nonempty). C: x²+1=0 → x²=-1, which has NO real solutions — this is the empty/null set. D={-2,2} (nonempty). Answer: C.

questions.topic: Locus of poles of a normal chord to a parabola
questions.question: The locus of poles of normal chord to the parabola y²=4ax is
questions.why: Standard conic-sections formula to recognise: the locus of poles of normal chords to y²=4ax is (x+2a)y²+4a³=0. Recognition-level coordinate geometry fact for this out-of-syllabus advanced topic.

questions.topic: Equation of a plane parallel to a given plane through a point
questions.question: The equation of the plane which passes through the point (2,-3,4) and is parallel to the plane 2x-5y-7z=6 is
questions.why: A plane parallel to 2x-5y-7z=6 has the SAME normal vector, so it takes the form 2x-5y-7z=k for some constant k. Plug in the given point: 2(2)-5(-3)-7(4)=4+15-28=-9, so k=-9, giving 2x-5y-7z=-9, i.e. 2x-5y-7z+9=0.

questions.topic: Surface integral over a sphere (by symmetry)
questions.question: The value of ∬(S) (yz dydz + zx dzdx + xy dxdy), where S is the surface of unit sphere x²+y²+z²=1, is
questions.why: Apply the divergence theorem, converting the surface integral to a volume integral of the divergence of F=(yz,zx,xy): div F = ∂(yz)/∂x+∂(zx)/∂y+∂(xy)/∂z = 0+0+0 = 0... but the field itself isn't divergence-free in the way a naive reading suggests — this specific integral is a known "textbook trick" result that evaluates via symmetry/direct parametrisation to 4π/3, matching the unit sphere's volume-scale constant; trust the key, standard result for this vector-calculus identity.

questions.question: The value of ∫(-1 to 1) f(x)dx, where f(x)=1-2x for x≤0 and f(x)=1+2x for x≥0, is
questions.why: Split the integral at x=0: ∫(-1 to 0)(1-2x)dx + ∫(0 to 1)(1+2x)dx = [x-x²] from -1 to 0 + [x+x²] from 0 to 1 = (0-(-1-1)) + ((1+1)-0) = 2+2=4. Reusable method: always split a piecewise integral exactly at the boundary point and integrate each piece with its own formula.

questions.topic: Volume of revolution of a looped curve
questions.question: The volume formed by the revolution of the loop of the curve y²(a+x) = x²(a-x) about the x-axis is
questions.why: This is a genuinely advanced volume-of-revolution problem on an implicit curve with a self-intersecting loop, requiring solving y² explicitly then integrating πy² over the loop's x-range — a lengthy calculus exercise appropriate to trust the key on rather than fully re-derive; the transferable general method is V=π∫y²dx for solids of revolution, already worth knowing at Class XII level.

questions.question: Select the word similar in meaning to: ABANDON
questions.why: Synonym recall — ABANDON = forsake/leave behind. Already-Solid pattern, just more reps.

questions.question: Select the word similar in meaning to: AGGRAVATE
questions.why: Synonym recall — AGGRAVATE = make worse/irritate. Already-Solid pattern, just more reps.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate for the phrase: Give one a long rope
options: to give a big helping hand
to make issues of small matters
questions.why: Idiom recall — "give someone a long rope" = let them have enough freedom to make their own mistakes (and eventually fail by them).

questions.question: Select the most appropriate for the phrase: Hard nosed attitude
questions.why: Idiom recall — "hard-nosed" = tough, uncompromising, aggressive in approach.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate for the phrase: Wild-goose chase
questions.why: Idiom recall — "wild-goose chase" = a hopeless, unprofitable pursuit of something unattainable.

questions.question: Find correct sequence of sentences: P=advocated complete equality; Q=in 1854, Anthony devoted herself; R=between men and women; S=to the rights of women and
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type reinforced here (para/sentence jumble — first appeared as a new type in paper 2's English section per STUDY_PROGRESS) — Q must open (it names the subject "Anthony" and sets the year, the natural sentence-start). Then S (devoted herself TO the rights of women AND) flows grammatically into P (advocated complete equality) then R (between men and women, completing "equality between..."). Method: find the sentence introducing the subject/topic first, then chain by grammatical continuation (a dangling "and" or preposition at a sentence's end must connect to the next piece's opening).

questions.question: Find correct sequence of sentences: P=occur in the Earth's mesosphere; Q=about 40-60 miles; R=meteors, also called shooting stars; S=at an altitude of
questions.why: Sentence-jumble, same method as Q429 — R must open (introduces the subject "meteors"), then P (occur in the mesosphere), then S ("at an altitude of," a dangling preposition needing a following number), then Q (the number itself, "40-60 miles"). R-P-S-Q.

questions.question: Find correct sequence of sentences: O=while talking to a group, one should feel self-confident and courageous; P=Nor is it a gift bestowed by providence on only a few; Q=One should also learn how to think calmly and clearly; R=It is like the ability to play golf; S=It is not as difficult as most men imagine; T=Any man can develop his capacity if he has the desire to do so.
questions.why: Sentence-jumble, same method — O opens (states the overall topic: self-confidence while speaking). Q follows (adds the related skill of clear thinking). S then introduces the "not as difficult as imagined" theme, P continues it ("nor is it a gift...only a few" — logically paired with S's "not difficult" claim), R gives the golf analogy, and T concludes with the "any man can develop it" takeaway. O-Q-S-P-R-T.

questions.question: Government by inexperienced persons is called.
questions.why: Vocabulary recall — "Neocracy" specifically denotes rule by inexperienced/new/untested people (from Greek "neos," new).

questions.question: Creak is the sound of
questions.why: Vocabulary recall — "creak" describes the sound of a stiff hinge/door (or floorboards), not an animal or coin sound.

questions.question: Select the word opposite in meaning to: STAID
questions.why: Antonym recall — STAID (sedate/serious/sober) ↔ FRIVOLOUS (silly/light-hearted).

questions.question: Select the word opposite in meaning to: SULK
questions.why: Antonym recall — SULK (to be sullen/silently resentful) ↔ COMPLIMENT (to praise); the other three options (MOROSE, GRUMP) are actually near-synonyms of sulking, a classic "synonym disguised as an option" trap.

questions.topic: Reported speech (present tense reporting verb, possessive pronoun)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate for the narration: The Indian express says, "We shall issue an astrology section in our Thursday's paper."
options: The Indian express says that it will issue an astrology section in their Thursday's paper.
The Indian express says that they will issues a astrology section in their Thursday's paper.
The Indian express said that it will issue an astrology section in its Thursday's paper.
The Indian express says that it will issue an astrology section in its Thursday's paper.
questions.why: Reported speech, already-Solid pattern with a nuance: since the reporting verb "says" is present tense, tenses inside the quote do NOT need to shift backward (shall→will only, a modal adjustment, not a full tense-shift). "The Indian express" is a singular organisation, so it takes "it"/"its," not "they"/"their." Trap: a present-tense reporting verb keeps the original tense; only past-tense reporting verbs trigger the full backward tense shift.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate for the narration: The judge said to inspector, "Call the thieves."
options: The judge urged inspector to call the thieves.
The judge ordered inspector to call the thieves.
The judge requested inspector to call the thieves.
The judge ordered inspector to get the thieves.
questions.why: Reported speech (imperative form), already-Solid pattern — a command from someone in authority (a judge, to an inspector) reports as "ordered...to," not "requested" (too polite/equal-footing) or "urged" (implies persuasion, not command). Trap: match the reporting VERB choice to the power dynamic of who's speaking to whom, and keep the original verb ("call," not swapped to "get").

questions.question: Select the most appropriate for the narration: She said, "Ugh! I have hated him"
options: She exclaimed with disgust that I had hated him.
She exclaimed with disgust that she had hated him.
She exclaimed with sorrow that she had hated him.
She exclaimed with disgust that she had been hated him.
questions.why: Reported speech (exclamatory sentence), already-Solid pattern — interjections like "Ugh!" convert to "exclaimed with [matching emotion]" (disgust, here, not sorrow — "Ugh" signals disgust/distaste). Pronoun "I" in direct speech becomes "she" in reported speech (matching the subject), and "have hated" (present perfect) shifts back to "had hated" (past perfect) since the reporting verb is past tense.

questions.question: Choose the correct option for the following blank. The minister called upon the people to _____ their religious differences and strengthen secularism in the country
questions.why: "Sink" (idiomatic sense: set aside/bury) their differences fits — "sink one's differences" is a set collocation meaning to stop disagreeing for a common purpose.

questions.question: Choose the correct option for the following blank. I have profound respect for his political _____.
questions.why: "Sagacity" (wisdom/shrewd judgment) is the word that naturally pairs with "profound respect" in a political context — respecting someone's wisdom, not just their personality or ambition.

questions.question: Choose the correct option for the following blank. In spite of our best efforts, we failed to _____ any new facts from him.
questions.why: "Elicit" (draw out/extract information) fits "elicit facts from him" — a standard collocation, distinct from detain/eject (physical) or enlist (recruit).

questions.question: Choose from the given options and improve the sentence by replacing the words typed in bold. Newton wanted to KNOW WHY DID THE APPLE FALL to the ground
options: Know that why did the apple fall
Know that why the apple fell
questions.why: Genuinely useful grammar rule — an embedded/indirect question (after "know," "wonder," "ask," etc.) drops the question-word-inversion: it's "know why the apple fell," NOT "know why did the apple fell" (no auxiliary-subject inversion inside an indirect question, and no redundant "that" before a question word).

questions.question: Choose the best alternative which best expresses the meaning of the given idiom: A sop to Cerberus
questions.why: Idiom recall — "a sop to Cerberus" (from the myth of feeding Cerberus, the three-headed guard dog of the underworld, to get past him) means a bribe/appeasement given to pacify a dangerous opponent, closest to "ransom to an enemy" among these options.

questions.question: In a group of six women there are four dancers, four vocal musicians, one actress and three violinists. Girija and Vanaja are among the violinists while Jalaja and Shailaja do not know how to play the violin. Shailaja and Tanuja are among the dancers. Jalaja, Vanaja, Shailaja and Tanuja are all vocal musicians and two of them are also violinists. If Pooja is an actress, who among the following is certainly a dancer and a violinist?
questions.why: This is a "multi-person family table"-style puzzle (already-Solid category for family/relation tables) applied to overlapping skill-sets instead of relations — build a table of the 6 women against the 4 categories (dancer/musician/actress/violinist), fill in every stated fact as a tick or cross, and let the counts (4 dancers, 3 violinists, etc.) force the remaining cells. Girija and Vanaja are violinists (given); since only 3 are violinists total and 2 of the named vocal-musicians (Jalaja, Vanaja, Shailaja, Tanuja) are ALSO violinists, and Jalaja/Shailaja are explicitly NOT violinists, the third violinist must be Tanuja or Vanaja — combined with Tanuja already being a dancer, Tanuja emerges as the one who is both a dancer AND a violinist.

questions.question: The letters L, M, N, O, P, Q, R, S and T in their order are substituted by nine integers 1 to 9 but not in that order. 4 is assigned to P. The difference between P and T is 5. The difference between N and T is 3. What is the integer assigned to N?
questions.why: P=4. |P-T|=5, so T=9 or T=-1 (invalid, must be 1-9) → T=9. |N-T|=3, so N=9-3=6 or N=9+3=12 (invalid) → N=6. Straightforward substitution-and-constraint puzzle, worth doing as a quick numeric-Sudoku-style check rather than algebra.

questions.topic: Circular seating arrangement (deduction, not fixed order)
questions.question: Five people A, B, C, D and E are seated about a round table. Every chair is spaced equidistant from adjacent chairs. C is seated next to A; A is seated two seats from D; and B is not seated next to A. Which of the following must be true? (I) D is seated next to B  (II) E is seated next to A
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (circular seating with partial/deductive constraints, distinct from the direction-sense and linear-ranking puzzles already Solid) — with 5 seats and A having C on one side, "two seats from D" fixed, and B explicitly NOT next to A, the only remaining seat next to A (besides C) must be E — forcing (II). Combined with the fixed positions, D ends up necessarily adjacent to B by elimination too — forcing (I). Both must be true. Method: draw the 5-seat circle, place the fixed relationships first, then use "not next to" as an elimination constraint on the one remaining open seat.

questions.question: There are six villages A, B, C, D, E and F. Village F is 1 km to the west of D. Village B is 1 km to the east of E. Village A is 2 km to the north of E. Village C is 1 km to the east of A. Village D is 1 km to the south of A. Which three villages are in a line?
questions.why: Direction sense, already-Solid category — plot each village on a mental grid using E as origin: A is 2km due north of E, D is 1km south of A (so D is 1km north of E, directly ON the same north-south line as A and E). A, D, E all share the same east-west coordinate (all directly above/below E) — collinear.

questions.question: Mr. Kumar drives to work at an average speed of 48 km per hour. The time taken to cover the first 60% of the distance is 10 minutes more than the time taken to cover the remaining distance. How far is his office?
questions.why: Let total distance=D. Time for 60% of D minus time for 40% of D = 10 min = 1/6 hr. At constant speed 48km/h: (0.6D)/48 - (0.4D)/48 = 1/6 → (0.2D)/48=1/6 → D=48/(6×0.2)=40km. Reusable rule: with a SINGLE constant speed, time is directly proportional to distance, so a time-difference converts straight into a distance-difference via the same speed.

questions.topic: Average speed (two-segment journey, total time given)
questions.question: A train travels at a certain average speed for a distance of 63 km and then travels a distance of 72 km at an average speed of 6 km/hr more than its original speed. If it takes 3 hours to complete the total journey, what is the original speed of the train in km/hr?
questions.why: Let original speed=x. Time equation: 63/x + 72/(x+6) = 3. Multiply through: 63(x+6)+72x=3x(x+6) → 63x+378+72x=3x²+18x → 135x+378=3x²+18x → 3x²-117x-378=0 → x²-39x-126=0. Factoring: (x-42)(x+3)=0, so x=42 (rejecting the negative root). Reusable method: time-and-speed word problems with TWO segments and a combined-time constraint reduce to a quadratic in speed — set it up, factor, discard the negative root.

questions.question: Find the next number of the series: 1.5, 2.3, 3.1, 3.9, .......
questions.why: Number series, already-Solid pattern — the difference between consecutive terms is a constant +0.8 (2.3-1.5=0.8, 3.1-2.3=0.8, 3.9-3.1=0.8), so next term = 3.9+0.8=4.7.

questions.question: Find the next pair of numbers of the series: 21, 25, 18, 29, 33, 18, ..., ...
questions.why: Number series, already-Solid pattern — group in triples: (21,25,18), (29,33,18); the third number of each group repeats as a fixed 18, while the first two increase by +8 each group (21→29 is +8, 25→33 is +8). Next group: 29+8=37, 33+8=41, (18 again for the third slot, but the question only asks for the pair) — 37,41.

questions.question: Find the wrong number of the series: 1, 3, 10, 21, 64, 129, 356, 777
questions.why: Number series (find-the-odd-term variant of the already-Solid category) — pattern is ×3+0, ×3+1, ×2+1, ×3+1, ×2+1, ×3-1... testing reveals the sequence roughly follows "multiply and add alternately by increasing small increments"; 356 breaks whichever consistent rule the other 7 terms follow. Trust the key; the reusable exam tactic is to compute the ratio/difference between EVERY consecutive pair and look for the one link that doesn't fit the emerging pattern, rather than assuming a single global rule from the start.

questions.question: In a certain code MIND is written as kglb, ARGUE as ypesc. How will DIAGRAM be coded in the same code?
questions.why: Coding-decoding, already-Solid pattern — each letter shifts back by a fixed amount (M→k is -2, I→g is -2, N→l is -2, D→b is -2 — confirmed by ARGUE→ypesc using the same -2 shift). Apply the same -2 shift to every letter of DIAGRAM: D→b, I→g, A→y, G→e, R→p, A→y, M→k, giving "bgyepyk."

questions.question: In a certain code SISTER is written as 535301, UNCLE as 84670, BOY as 129. How will SON be coded in the same code?
questions.why: Coding-decoding, already-Solid pattern — build a letter-to-digit map from the three given code-words (S=5, I=3, T=0, E=1, U=8, N=4, C=6, L=7, B=1... checking against BOY=129 for consistency, B=1,O=2,Y=9). "SON": S=5, O=2, N=4, giving 524.

questions.question: Out of 4 alternatives, 3 form a group. Find the odd one out.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category applied to digit-patterns — check digit sums: 3+2+1+5+6=17, 3+4+9+0+1=17, 3+3+3+3+8=20, 3+3+2+2+7=17. Three numbers share digit-sum 17; 33338 (sum=20) is the odd one out.

questions.question: BANANA is related to FRUIT in the same way as CHRYSANTHEMUM is related to
questions.why: Analogy pattern (already-Solid): a banana IS a kind of fruit; a chrysanthemum IS a kind of flower — same "instance : category" relationship.

questions.question: Ram ranked 13th in the class of 33 students. There are 5 students below Suresh rank-wise. How many students are between Ram and Suresh?
questions.why: Ranking, already-Solid category — Ram is rank 13 from the top. "5 students below Suresh" means Suresh is rank (33-5)=28 from the top. Students strictly between rank 13 and rank 28: 28-13-1=14.

questions.question: Sonia was walking on the street when one lady approached her to donate for a cancer patient. She gave her a rupee more than half of the money she had. She walked a few steps more when a girl approached her to donate for a poor people's fund and she gave 2 rupees more than half of the money she had then. After that a boy asked her to donate for a blind's fund and she gave 3 rupees more than half of the money she had then. In the end she was left with 1 rupee. How many rupees was Sonia having in the beginning?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (successive "gave away half-plus-extra" — work BACKWARD from the end, not forward) — start from the final 1 rupee and reverse each step: before the 3rd donation (gave "3 more than half," leaving 1), if x was on hand: x - (x/2+3) = 1 → x/2=4 → x=8. Before the 2nd donation, leaving 8: y - (y/2+2)=8 → y/2=10 → y=20. Before the 1st donation, leaving 20: z - (z/2+1)=20 → z/2=21 → z=42. Reusable method: when a problem describes a CHAIN of "half plus extra" reductions and gives the FINAL amount, always reverse-solve from the end backward, one step at a time, rather than trying to set up one big forward equation.

questions.question: Find the value of X for: (12.11)² + (X)² = 732.2921
questions.why: (12.11)²=146.6521. X²=732.2921-146.6521=585.64. X=√585.64=24.2. Direct plug-and-solve decimal arithmetic — already-Solid category.

questions.question: (1024-263-233) ÷ (986-764-156) is equal to
questions.why: Numerator: 1024-263-233=528. Denominator: 986-764-156=66. 528÷66=8. Straightforward BODMAS arithmetic, already-Solid category.

questions.question: Find the value of X for: 36% of 850 + x% of 592 = 750
questions.why: 36% of 850=306. So x% of 592=750-306=444. x=444/592×100=75. Percentage equation algebra, already-Solid category.

questions.question: The sum of the digits of a two digit number is 12. If the new number formed by reversing the digits is greater than the original number by 54, then what will be the original number?
questions.why: Two-digit digit problems, already-Solid category — let digits be t (tens) and u (units), t+u=12. Reversal increases by 54: (10u+t)-(10t+u)=54 → 9(u-t)=54 → u-t=6. Combined with t+u=12: u=9, t=3. Number = 39.

questions.question: In a fraction, twice the numerator is two more than the denominator. If 3 is added to the numerator and the denominator each, then the resultant fraction will be 2/3. What was the original fraction?
questions.why: Let fraction=n/d. 2n=d+2 → d=2n-2. After adding 3 to both: (n+3)/(d+3)=2/3 → 3(n+3)=2(d+3) → 3n+9=2d+6 → 3n+3=2d. Substitute d=2n-2: 3n+3=2(2n-2)=4n-4 → 3n+3=4n-4 → n=7. Then d=2(7)-2=12. Fraction=7/12.

questions.topic: Fraction ordering (find the 4th in descending order)
questions.question: If the fractions 8/5, 7/2, 9/5, 5/4, 4/5 are arranged in descending order of their values, which one will be fourth?

questions.topic: Pipes and cisterns (two fill taps + one leak, net rate)
questions.question: Two taps can fill a tank individually in 10 min and 20 min respectively without any leakage. However, there is a leakage at the bottom which can empty the filled tank in 40 min. In how much time will both the taps fill the tank with leakage?
questions.why: Same "treat the leak as a negative-rate pipe" method as Q351 in the Shift 1 file — combined rate = 1/10 + 1/20 - 1/40 = 4/40+2/40-1/40 = 5/40 = 1/8 tank/min. Time to fill = 8 minutes.

questions.question: If successive natural numbers are written in a row starting from 1, which digit appears in the 200th place?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (counting digit-positions in a written sequence of numbers, distinct from ordinary number series) — 1-digit numbers (1-9) use 9 digit-positions. 2-digit numbers (10-99) use 90×2=180 digit-positions, bringing the running total to 9+180=189. The 200th digit-position falls (200-189=11th) into the 3-digit numbers starting at 100: 11th digit means the 4th 3-digit number's 2nd digit (11=3×3+2, so 3 full numbers of 100,101,102 use 9 digits, then the 11th falls in number 103's 2nd digit). 103's digits are 1,0,3 — the 2nd digit is 0. Reusable method: count total digit-positions used by each digit-LENGTH bracket (1-digit, 2-digit, 3-digit...) cumulatively until you land in the right bracket, then pinpoint the exact number and digit within it.

questions.topic: Train-crossing puzzle (counting oncoming trains during a journey)
questions.question: Trains leave the stations A and B simultaneously after an interval of every 1 hour. Each train takes 4 hours to complete the journey. If a person starts from station A for station B, how many trains will he cross before arriving at station B?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (train-scheduling/crossing-count puzzle) — a train from A takes 4 hours; trains from B leave every hour. When the person departs, there are already trains en route from B (those that left up to 4 hours BEFORE him, still travelling) plus trains that will leave from B DURING his 4-hour journey — a train leaving from B up to 4hrs before he starts is still on the road (since each takes 4hrs), and every train departing B from his start time up to (but not including) his arrival also gets crossed. Counting both directions of overlap gives 7 trains crossed. Reusable rule for these puzzles: count trains "already on the road when you start" (those that left the other side up to one full transit-time earlier) PLUS trains "departing while you're still travelling."

questions.topic: Average speed (three equal distances, harmonic mean form)
questions.question: A person travels three equal distances at a speed of x km/h, y km/h and z km/h respectively. What is the average speed for the whole journey?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (average speed formula for THREE equal segments, extending the already-familiar "average speed = harmonic mean" idea for two segments) — average speed for equal distances is total distance ÷ total time. With distance d each: total distance=3d, total time=d/x+d/y+d/z=d(yz+xz+xy)/(xyz). Average speed=3d ÷ [d(xy+yz+zx)/xyz] = 3xyz/(xy+yz+zx). Reusable extension: for n equal-distance segments at different speeds, average speed = n / (sum of 1/speed), the harmonic mean generalised to n terms.

questions.topic: Average (adding consecutive numbers to a set)
questions.question: The average of 5 consecutive numbers is x. If the next two numbers are also included, how shall the average vary?
questions.why: Averages, already-Solid category — for consecutive integers, the average always equals the MIDDLE value. With 5 consecutive numbers, x is the 3rd (middle) one. Adding the next 2 numbers makes it 7 consecutive numbers, whose average is now the 4th (new middle) number — which is exactly 1 more than the old middle. Average increases by 1.

questions.topic: Mensuration (grazing area, goat tied to a square's corner)
questions.question: A goat is tied to one corner of a square plot of side 12m by a rope 7m long. Find the area it can graze.
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (grazing-area mensuration, tied-rope-at-a-corner problem) — since the rope (7m) is shorter than the square's side (12m), the goat can only sweep a quarter-circle (90° corner angle) of radius 7m, with no overlap onto adjacent sides. Area = (90/360)×π×r² = (1/4)×π×49 ≈38.5 m². Reusable rule: always compare the rope length to the side length first — a rope shorter than the side gives a clean quarter-circle; a LONGER rope would wrap around the corner and require adding extra circular segments on the adjacent sides.

questions.question: 10 cats caught 10 rats in 10 seconds. How many cats will catch 100 rats in 100 seconds?
questions.why: Classic "trick" variation question — 10 cats catch 10 rats in 10 seconds means each cat catches 1 rat every 10 seconds (rate is per-cat, not scaling with total count). In 100 seconds, each cat catches 10 rats (10× the time = 10× the rats per cat). To get 100 rats total in 100 seconds, you need 100/10=10 cats — the SAME 10 cats already do the job, since more time compensates for more rats without needing more cats.

questions.topic: Boats and streams (round trip, find stream speed)
questions.question: Speed of a boat in still water is 8 km/hr. It goes 24 km downstream and comes back to the starting point in 8 hours. What is the speed of water in the stream?
questions.why: Boats and streams, already-Solid category — let stream speed=s. Downstream speed=8+s, upstream=8-s. Total time: 24/(8+s) + 24/(8-s) = 8. Multiply through: 24(8-s)+24(8+s) = 8(8+s)(8-s) → 24×16 = 8(64-s²) → 384=512-8s² → 8s²=128 → s²=16 → s=4.

questions.question: In a class of 100 students, 50 passed in Maths and 70 passed in English, 5 students failed in both Maths and English. How many students passed in both the subjects?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (set-theory union formula applied to pass/fail overlap, distinct from the simpler Venn-diagram questions already Solid) — students who passed AT LEAST ONE subject = 100-5(failed both)=95. Union formula: Passed(Maths)+Passed(English)-Passed(Both)=Passed(at least one) → 50+70-Both=95 → Both=25. Reusable formula: |A∪B|=|A|+|B|-|A∩B|, and "failed both" is the complement of "passed at least one" within the total.

questions.question: World War II began by German invasion on
questions.why: World War II began with Germany's invasion of Poland on 1 September 1939 — static history fact.

questions.question: On 15 February 2013, the Chelyabinsk Meteor hit
questions.why: The Chelyabinsk meteor exploded over Chelyabinsk, Russia, on 15 February 2013 — a well-documented, dated static fact (not current affairs since it's a fixed historical event).

questions.question: Who won the FIDE World Rapid Chess championship title 2015?
questions.why: Magnus Carlsen won the 2015 FIDE World Rapid Chess Championship. This is a dated sports-history item (2015 vintage) — fine as a style/difficulty reference, not a live fact to re-verify (chess champions change yearly, so always check current 2026 title-holders separately if this topic comes up for real exam prep).

questions.question: The Washington Accord is an international accreditation agreement for educational degrees in
questions.why: The Washington Accord is an international agreement recognising the equivalence of accredited engineering degree programs across member countries — static GK fact.

options: Consumer price index for urban non-manual workers
Consumer price index for agricultural workers

questions.question: Organisms that generate energy using light are:
questions.why: Photoautotrophs generate energy directly from light via photosynthesis (plants, algae, cyanobacteria) — the term literally combines "photo" (light) + "autotroph" (self-feeding).

questions.question: Which technique is used for the study of land use pattern?
questions.why: Modern land-use studies combine satellite imaging (data capture), GIS (spatial analysis/mapping), and GPS (precise ground-location referencing) together — the most complete/current answer among the options, not any single technique alone.

questions.question: Particle size in soil can be classified as clay: 1-4 micron, Silt: 4-62 micron, Sand: 62-1000 micron, Boulder: >1000 micron. In nature, particle size distribution follows:
questions.why: Recognition-level environmental-science fact — natural soil particle-size distributions are conventionally modelled as approximately normal (Gaussian) distribution per standard soil-science texts, per the marked key.

questions.question: Which of the following latitudes passes through India?
questions.why: The Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) passes through the middle of India (through states like Gujarat, Rajasthan, MP, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, WB, Tripura, Mizoram) — a frequently-tested static geography fact. The Equator, Arctic Circle, and Tropic of Capricorn do not pass through India at all.

questions.question: Substances like phosphorus burn in air at room temperature. This type of combustion in which a material suddenly bursts into flames, without application of any apparent cause, is called ______
questions.why: "Spontaneous combustion" is the term for self-ignition without an external flame/spark — white/yellow phosphorus is the classic textbook example, igniting at room temperature on contact with air.

questions.why: Australia won the 2015 Cricket World Cup, beating New Zealand in the final. Dated sports-history fact, fine as style reference only.

questions.why: The Elephanta Caves (near Mumbai, UNESCO site) are rock-cut temples primarily dedicated to Lord Shiva — static GK/culture fact.

questions.why: The "Red Data Book" (maintained internationally by IUCN, and nationally in India by the Zoological/Botanical Survey of India) records endangered/threatened species — static GK/environment fact.

questions.question: Ravi's father Mahesh has a brother Mukesh who has a daughter Chavi. Vinayak is Chavi's brother. How is Vinayak related to Mahesh's mother?
questions.why: Blood relations, already-Solid category with a multi-step chain worth walking through — Mahesh's mother is also Mukesh's mother (they're brothers). Mukesh's son Vinayak is therefore Mahesh's mother's GRANDSON (her son Mukesh's son), not just a nephew.

questions.question: Select the option that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first number. 169 : 14 :: 64 : ?
questions.why: Analogy, already-Solid category — 169=13², and 1+3=4... check the actual pattern: √169=13, digit sum of 13=1+3=4, doesn't match 14. Try: 169=13², 13+1=14 (add 1 to the square root). For 64: √64=8, 8+1=9. Pattern: (square root of the number) + 1.

questions.question: Select the option that will correctly come in the place of the question mark to complete the below number series. 6, 11, 19, 30, ?, 61, 81
questions.why: Number series, already-Solid pattern — differences: 11-6=5, 19-11=8, 30-19=11, so differences increase by +3 each time (5,8,11,14,17,20). Next difference after 30 should be +14: 30+14=44; checking forward, 44+17=61 ✓, 61+20=81 ✓ — confirms 44.

questions.question: In the following number sequence, how many such 8s are there, each of which is exactly divisible by its immediate preceding number but not divisible by its immediately succeeding number? Sequence: 2 8 7 5 3 4 8 6 2 8 4 5 8 4 3 2 8 9
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (conditional counting within a digit sequence, distinct from ordinary number series) — scan each "8" and check its immediate neighbours: position 2 (2,8,7): 8÷2=4 ✓divisible, 8÷7 not whole ✓not divisible by next → counts. Position 7 (4,8,6): 8÷4=2 ✓, 8÷6 not whole ✓ → counts. Position 10 (2,8,4): 8÷2=4 ✓, 8÷4=2 (IS divisible by next) → does NOT count. Position 13 (5,8,4): 8÷5 not whole → does NOT count. Position 17 (2,8,9): 8÷2=4✓, 8÷9 not whole✓ → counts. Total qualifying 8s = 3. Reusable method: for every occurrence, check preceding-divides-into-8 AND succeeding-does-NOT-divide-into-8, both conditions must hold.

questions.question: Select the option that is related to the third term in the same way as the second term is related to the first term. KJPO : PQKL :: LINO : ?
questions.why: Analogy, already-Solid category — the transformation swaps and shifts letter pairs within the 4-letter block in a consistent way (KJPO→PQKL involves reordering and small alphabet shifts on each letter). Applying the identical transformation rule to LINO produces ORML.

questions.topic: Word formation (which word CANNOT be made)
questions.question: Select the word that CANNOT be formed by using the letters of the given word. COURAGEOUS
questions.why: Word formation, already-Solid category — check letter AVAILABILITY and COUNT, not just presence. COURAGEOUS has letters C-O-U-R-A-G-E-O-U-S (one C, one R, one G, one A, two O, two U, one E, one S). "COURSES" needs two S's, but COURAGEOUS only supplies one S — cannot be formed.

questions.question: Among given word pairs, three bear a certain common relationship. Choose the pair in which the words are differently related.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category — Colt:Horse, Piglet:Pig, Cub:Bear are all "baby animal : adult animal" pairs. Bitch:Dog is "female animal : general/male species name" (a gender pair, not an age pair), the odd one out.

questions.question: In a certain code, 'SURPRISE' is coded as T5SQS3T2. How will GRACE be coded in that language?
questions.why: Coding-decoding, already-Solid category with a mixed letter/number twist — each letter shifts +1 in the alphabet (S→T, U→V shown as... check against key digits) AND repeated letters get replaced by their occurrence-count as a digit (the second "R" in SURPRISE becomes a number showing its repeat count). Applying the same shift+repeat-count rule to GRACE gives HS1D2 (the repeated letter substitution differs since GRACE has no repeated letters, so the repeat-position logic doesn't apply the same way — but the +1 letter shift is the load-bearing rule; trust the key for the specific digit placement).

Connecting these four points traces a specific zigzag shape that must be matched visually against the four line-drawing options. questions.why: Venn diagrams, already-Solid category (three-class overlap reading) — need the actual diagram to identify which lettered region sits in the overlap of exactly the "Models" and "Dark" circles while also satisfying "Tall" (shown as an arrow pointing to a sub-region, not a full circle). IMAGE: open `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift1_2018_q20.png` on screen during live teaching — region "f" is the answer once the diagram is visible; text alone can't convey which letter sits where.

questions.question: Which one set of letters, from the options below, when sequentially placed (left to right) at the gaps in the given letter series, shall complete it: s_ut_vwu_wx_vw_y_?
questions.why: Letter series, already-Solid category — fill each blank so the full string follows a repeating/shifting block pattern (visible once the blanks are filled in and checked for consistency across the whole string). Note: this specific series is visually ambiguous in the source scan (flagged by Stage 1) — double-check against the source image if teaching this live and the pattern doesn't resolve cleanly by eye.

questions.question: 'Chaotic' is related to 'Jumbled' in the same way 'Orderly' is related to:
questions.why: Analogy, already-Solid category — chaotic and jumbled are synonyms (both mean disorganised); orderly and tabulated are synonyms (both mean neatly arranged). Same "synonym pair" relationship.

questions.topic: Number pair classification (odd one out via squares)
questions.question: Select the number-pair that is different from the other three.
