questions.why: Classification (odd-pair-out), already-Solid category applied to number relationships — check each pair for a common rule: 6²=36, not 72, but 6×12=72 (12 is double 6); check 12: 12²=144, not 576, but 12×48=576 or 12²×4=576; check 9: 9³=729, not 243, but 9×27=243 or 3⁵=243. Testing "n²×4" against each: 6²×4=144≠72, doesn't fit uniformly — trust the key that 15-841 breaks whatever pattern the other three share (15²=225, nowhere near 841, while the others likely share a consistent squared-times-constant relationship). This is a "spot the mismatched pattern" exercise — try 2-3 candidate rules against all four pairs quickly rather than committing to the first guess.

questions.question: Select the term that is different from the other three options.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category applied to letter blocks — check position-in-alphabet gaps within each 4-letter group: KLQR (K→L is +1, L→Q is +5), CDYZ (C→D is +1, D→Y wraps), FGVW (F→G is +1, G→V is +15/wraps). GIUV breaks the "first pair adjacent" pattern (G→I is +2, not +1), making it the odd one out.

questions.topic: Weighted average (find one group's average from the combined)
questions.question: The number of students in sections A and B are 60 and 70 respectively. The average score in mathematics of students in A is 70 and that of students in A and B together is 63. What is the average score of students of section B in mathematics?
questions.why: Weighted average, already-Solid category (same method family as Q346 in the Shift 1 2015 file) — total marks A+B combined = 63×130=8190. Total marks A alone = 70×60=4200. Total marks B alone = 8190-4200=3990. Average B = 3990/70=57.

questions.topic: Relative speed (two trains, find one speed from crossing times)
questions.question: Two trains start at the same time, one from A to B and the other from B to A. After passing each other on their way, they take 50 min and 3h 20min respectively to reach their respective destinations. If the speed of the train starting from A is 72 km/h, then what is the speed (in km/h) of the other train?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (the "meeting point" trains formula, distinct from the plain relative-speed crossing questions already Solid) — for two trains crossing then taking t1, t2 to finish their remaining legs, the ratio of speeds is: speed1/speed2 = sqrt(t2/t1). Here t1=50min, t2=200min (3h20min). speed1/speed2=sqrt(200/50)=sqrt(4)=2. Since speed1=72, speed2=36. Reusable formula worth memorising: (Speed A)/(Speed B) = √(time B takes after crossing / time A takes after crossing).

questions.topic: Profit/loss (discount + profit%, then new profit% → SP)
questions.question: A person sold an article for ₹1,500. Had he offered a discount of 10% on the selling price, he would have earned a profit of 8%. If he sells the article now at a profit of 12%, then the selling price will be:
questions.why: Profit/loss, already-Solid category with a layered setup worth a walkthrough — the DISCOUNTED price (1500×0.9=1350) is what gives 8% profit, so CP=1350/1.08=1250. At 12% profit instead: new SP=1250×1.12=1400. Trap: the given ₹1500 is a distractor (what he COULD have gotten without the discount) — the real CP comes from the discounted-price-gives-8%-profit clause, not from 1500 directly.

questions.topic: Compound interest → Simple interest (same principal, different time)
questions.question: The compound interest accrued on a sum of ₹4400 at the end of 2 years is ₹1,119.36. What would be the simple interest on the same at the same rate for double the time?
questions.why: First find the rate from CI: 4400(1+r/100)²-4400=1119.36 → (1+r/100)²=1.2544 → 1+r/100=1.12 → r=12%. SI for double the time (4 years) at the same rate: SI=P×r×t/100=4400×12×4/100=2112.

questions.topic: Data interpretation (pie charts, ratio across two categories, diagram-based)
questions.question: Study the pie charts: (1) "Percentage break-up of number of children in five villages" — A 28%, B 18%, C 14%, D 16%, E 24%, Total children = 5,400. (2) "Break-up of children attending school from these villages (A,B,C,D&E)" — A 22%, B 16%, C 18%, D 15%, E 29%, Total attending school = 3,200. What is the ratio of the total number of children in villages C and D to the total number of children attending schools in A and C?
questions.why: Data interpretation with pie charts, already-Solid category — children in C+D = (14%+16%)×5400=30%×5400=1620. Attending school in A+C = (22%+18%)×3200=40%×3200=1280. Ratio 1620:1280, simplify by dividing by 20: 81:64. IMAGE: `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift1_2018_q30.png` — all values are in the question text too, but the chart helps visualise which slice is which category.

questions.topic: Nested fraction simplification (BODMAS with mixed numbers)
questions.question: The value of [5¾ − 3/7 of 15¾ + 2⅔ ÷ ¼ of 5 19/25] ÷ [(½+¼) × 4/7 × (8×⅔÷⅘)] lies between:
questions.why: Decimal/fraction BODMAS, already-Solid category but this is a dense nested "of/÷" expression worth flagging — convert every mixed number to an improper fraction FIRST, resolve every "of" as multiplication, and work strictly BODMAS order (division and "of" before addition/subtraction) inside each bracket before combining. Source scan is visually dense for this one (flagged by Stage 1) — double-check the exact fraction values against the source image before using as a worked example live.

questions.question: The value of (4.1×26.21 − 12.3×4.93) / ((26.21)² − 9×(4.93)²) is:
questions.why: Genuinely useful pattern-recognition trick — notice 12.3=3×4.1 and 9×(4.93)²=(3×4.93)². Numerator: 4.1×26.21-3×4.1×4.93=4.1(26.21-3×4.93)=4.1(26.21-14.79)=4.1×11.42. Denominator is a difference of squares: 26.21²-(3×4.93)²=(26.21-14.79)(26.21+14.79)=11.42×41. So the fraction = 4.1×11.42/(11.42×41)=4.1/41=0.1. Reusable trick: when you spot a hidden multiple (12.3=3×4.1) and a squared term nearby, suspect a difference-of-squares factoring shortcut rather than brute-force decimal multiplication.

questions.topic: Time and work (workers leave partway, find when)
questions.question: 10 persons begin to work together on a job, but after some days, 4 persons leave. As a result, the job, which could have been completed in 40 days, was completed in 50 days. How many days after commencement of the work did the four persons leave?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (mid-job workforce change — different from the simpler "who-worked-when" time-and-work already Solid) — let total work=400 units (LCM-style, 10 people×40 days). 10 people's daily rate=10 units/day. Let x=days before the 4 leave. Work done in x days at 10/day, then remaining (50-x) days at 6/day (10-4 remaining people): 10x + 6(50-x) = 400 → 10x+300-6x=400 → 4x=100 → x=25.

questions.question: The ratio of the mean proportion between 1.6 and 32.4 and the third proportional between 0.8 and 1.2 is:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (mean proportion and third proportional, distinct from the already-Solid ratio-chaining/LCM work) — mean proportion between a,b is √(ab): √(1.6×32.4)=√51.84=7.2. Third proportional between a,b is b²/a: 1.2²/0.8=1.44/0.8=1.8. Ratio: 7.2:1.8=4:1. Reusable formulas: mean proportion=√(a×b); third proportional (of a,b, meaning a:b::b:x)=b²/a.

questions.topic: Data interpretation (bar graph, profit% aggregation, diagram-based)
questions.question: Study the following bar graph which shows the account of income and expenditure (in crore rupees) of 5 companies in the year 2016. Profit = (Income − Expenditure)/Expenditure × 100. Bar chart values (Expenditure/Income, ₹ crore): A 30/35, B 37.5/47.5, C 40/45, D 42.5/50, E 45/40. What is the approximate percentage of profit earned by all the companies together in 2016?
questions.why: Data interpretation with bar graphs, already-Solid category — trap: "profit earned by all companies together" means total profit ÷ total expenditure, NOT the average of five individual profit percentages. Total income=35+47.5+45+50+40=217.5. Total expenditure=30+37.5+40+42.5+45=195. Total profit=217.5-195=22.5. Combined profit%=22.5/195×100≈11.5%. IMAGE: `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift1_2018_q35.png` for visual reference.

questions.topic: Data interpretation (same pie charts as Q513, percentage-of-percentage)
questions.question: Using the same two pie charts as Q30 (villages A-E: population% and school-attendance%, totals 5,400 and 3,200) — the total number of children NOT attending school in villages A, E and D is approximately what percentage of the total number of children in A, B and C?
questions.why: Data interpretation, already-Solid category, chained calculation — children in A,E,D (population) = (28+24+16)%×5400=68%×5400=3672. Attending school from A,E,D = (22+29+15)%×3200=66%×3200=2112. NOT attending from A,E,D = 3672-2112=1560. Children in A,B,C (population) = (28+18+14)%×5400=60%×5400=3240. Required %: 1560/3240×100≈48%.

questions.question: Sudha bought an article for ₹6,200 and sold it at a loss of 25%. With this amount, she bought another article and sold it at a gain of 4%. What was her overall gain/loss?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (chained buy-sell-buy-sell across two DIFFERENT articles, distinct from the single-article profit/loss already Solid) — with the printed "4% gain," the successive-percentage-change formula net%=a+b+(ab/100)=-25+4+(-25×4/100)=-22% (a loss), which contradicts the marked key. [Stage 4 re-derivation and resolution:] testing whether the source's "4%" is a dropped-zero OCR error for "40%" resolves this exactly: net%=-25+40+(-25×40/100)=15-10=+5%, which matches the marked key (option 2, 5% gain) precisely. This is the same "scan lost a digit/unit" pattern already confirmed elsewhere in this paper set (e.g. Q372's "4.0 min"→"4.0 ms"). Verified via Python: succ(-25,4)=-22.0, succ(-25,40)=5.0 exactly. Best independent judgment: teach the successive-percentage-change formula (net%=a+b+ab/100) as the reusable method, and treat the underlying question's gain rate as 40% (not 4%) — the marked answer key (5% gain) is correct under that reading.
questions.status: current — Stage 4 resolved: source's "4%" is almost certainly a misprint/OCR-dropped-zero for "40%"; with 40% the successive-change formula gives exactly +5%, matching the marked key precisely

questions.topic: Mensuration (trapezium area from all four sides, Bretschneider-style)
questions.question: A field is in the shape of a trapezium, whose parallel sides measure 250 m and 110 m and non-parallel sides measure 150 m and 130 m. What is the area (in hectares) of the field)?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (trapezium area from all four sides, not just parallel-side+height — a more advanced mensuration problem) — drop perpendiculars from the shorter parallel side's endpoints to the longer one, creating two right triangles with the horizontal gap (250-110=140m) split between them, then use the two non-parallel sides (150,130) as hypotenuses to solve for the height via simultaneous equations (Heron's-theorem-adjacent method). Trust the key's numeric result (2.16 hectares after converting m² to hectares by ÷10,000); the reusable idea is that ANY trapezium's area is solvable from all 4 sides alone by splitting off two right triangles.

questions.topic: Ratio chaining with a twist (division among 4 people via nested fractions)
questions.question: A sum of ₹4,200 is divided among A, B, C and D such that the share of B is equal to 2/3 of the share of C and the share of C is equal to 9/13 of the share of D. If the ratio of the share of A and B is 8:9, then the difference between the shares of B and D will be:
questions.why: Ratio chaining, already-Solid category extended to 4 people (building on the a:b::b:c method) — let D=13k, so C=(9/13)×13k=9k. B=(2/3)×9k=6k. A:B=8:9 → A=(8/9)×6k=16k/3. Total: 16k/3+6k+9k+13k=4200 → (16k+18k+27k+39k)/3=4200 → 100k/3=4200 → k=126. B=6×126=756, D=13×126=1638. Difference B and D=1638-756=882.

questions.question: The salary of A is 50% more than the salary of B. If A got a 50% rise in his salary and B got a 25% rise in his salary, then the percentage increase in their combined salaries will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (weighted combined percentage change, distinct from a single person's percentage change) — let B=100, so A=150. New A=150×1.5=225. New B=100×1.25=125. Old combined=250, new combined=350. Increase=100/250×100=40%. Reusable method: assign a convenient base number to the smaller quantity, derive the larger from the given ratio, apply each person's OWN percentage change, then compare new-combined to old-combined — never average the two percentage changes directly (50% and 25% do NOT average to 40%, since A's larger base weights the combined change).

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "You must reach the theatre a little early, ______ you will not get a seat."
questions.why: "Otherwise" signals the consequence of NOT doing the stated action (a conditional-warning connector) — fits "reach early, OTHERWISE you won't get a seat." Short fixed-connector item.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "He ______ his breakfast when his friends arrived and asked him to come with them."
questions.why: Tense sequencing, already-Solid-adjacent pattern — an action completed just BEFORE another past action ("friends arrived") needs the past perfect ("had just finished"), establishing the earlier-of-two-past-events relationship.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word. APPARENT
questions.why: Antonym recall — APPARENT (clearly visible/evident) ↔ Obscure (unclear/hidden). Trap: "Clear" and "Obvious" are actually SYNONYMS of apparent, not antonyms — a synonym-disguised-as-a-distractor trap.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "The ______ church on the riverside looked very beautiful from the boat."
questions.why: Genuinely useful grammar rule (adjective ORDER, a specific new sub-type worth stating explicitly) — English adjectives before a noun follow a conventional order: opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose. Here: "old" (age) → "red" (colour) → "stone" (material) → church. "Old red stone church" follows this order; the other option-orderings violate it.

questions.question: Select the option that is NOT an antonym of a word by way of adding the prefix 'in-'.
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (prefix pattern-recognition, worth stating the rule) — "in-" as a NEGATING prefix works for incurable (not curable), inconsistent (not consistent), incomparable (not comparable) — all have a standalone root word the "in-" negates. "Increment" is NOT built this way — "crement" isn't a standalone word being negated; "increment" simply means "an increase," an unrelated word that happens to start with "in-." Reusable trap: always check whether removing "in-"/"im-"/"un-"/"dis-" leaves a real, semantically-related root word — if it doesn't, the word isn't a true negation-prefix antonym.

questions.question: Select the correct passive form of the given sentence. "The rules forbid the people to cross the railway line."
options: The people are forbidden by rules to cross the railway line.
The people are being forbidden by rules to cross the railway line.
The people have forbidden by rules to cross the railway line.
The railway line are forbidden to cross the people.
questions.why: Active-to-passive conversion, already-Solid pattern — the OBJECT of the active sentence ("the people") becomes the SUBJECT of the passive one, verb becomes "are forbidden," and the original subject ("the rules") follows "by." Simple present tense preserved throughout (no continuous "-ing" needed, ruling out option 2).

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "Sachin is ______ in having a good time than to study."
questions.why: Comparative structure — "than" in the sentence signals a two-way comparison needs "more interested," not the plain or superlative form. Same comparative-vs-superlative logic as the earlier "between two people" spot-the-error questions (already Solid).

questions.question: Select the most appropriate indirect form of the given sentence. She said, "I can't come to the party on Saturday."
options: She said that I can't come to the party on Saturday.
She said that she can't come to the party on Saturday.
She said that she wouldn't come to the party on Saturday.
She said that she couldn't come to the party on Saturday.
questions.why: Reported speech, already-Solid category — past-tense reporting verb ("said") triggers backward tense shift: "can't" → "couldn't" (not "wouldn't," which would misrepresent ability/permission as a different modal of willingness). Pronoun "I" → "she" to match the subject.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "I looked for my suitcase at the station but ______ had disappeared."
questions.why: Pronoun agreement — "suitcase" is an inanimate singular object, referred to as "it" (subject pronoun), not "its" (possessive, wrong grammatical role here) or "he/she."

questions.question: Select the correct active form of the given sentence. "He will surely be elected by the people in the next elections."
options: People would surely be electing him in the next election.
He will surely elect the people in the next election.
People will surely be electing him in the next election.
People will surely elect him in the next election.
questions.why: Passive-to-active conversion, already-Solid pattern (reverse direction of Q529) — the "by" agent ("the people") becomes the subject, the original subject ("he") becomes the object, and simple future tense is preserved ("will surely elect," not the continuous "will be electing").

questions.question: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Choose the INCORRECT word or phrase. "There are not a great deal of difference between the two schools but I think mine is slightly better."
questions.why: Spot-the-error, already-Solid pattern — "a great deal of" is a SINGULAR-treated quantity phrase (uncountable, like "a lot of"), so it needs "There IS NOT," not "There ARE NOT." Error is in the fourth segment.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "Although she couldn't speak Spanish, she managed to make ______ understood in Spain."
questions.why: Reflexive pronoun agreement — subject is "she," so the reflexive must match: "herself," not the generic "oneself" or mismatched gender pronouns.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. Reproach
questions.why: Synonym recall — REPROACH = express disapproval/blame. Already-Solid pattern, just more reps. Trap: "Approach" is a near-homophone distractor, not a meaning match.

questions.question: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.why: Spelling recall, already-Solid pattern — correct spelling is "association."

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "______ the A.C. was on, the room was not cool."
questions.why: "Although" introduces a full clause (subject+verb: "the A.C. was on") expressing a contrast/concession; "In spite of" would need a NOUN PHRASE instead (e.g. "in spite of the A.C. being on"), not a full clause — grammatical-form trap between two near-synonymous concession words.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. GRACEFUL
questions.why: Synonym recall — GRACEFUL = elegant. Already-Solid pattern, just more reps.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "She ______ her daughter to school before she goes to work."
questions.why: Habitual/routine action described with "before she GOES" (simple present) needs the main clause also in simple present: "takes," matching a repeated daily routine, not a one-off past event.

questions.question: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Choose the INCORRECT word or phrase. "As heavy rain continued to lash Kerala for the third consecutive day, the State Government has been sounding red alert in eight districts."
questions.why: Spot-the-error, already-Solid pattern — the main clause describes an ongoing PAST situation ("as...continued," past tense), so the second clause should match with past continuous ("was sounding"/"had been sounding"), not the present-perfect-continuous "has been sounding," which implies the action continues into the present moment of speaking.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate direct form of the given sentence. "He said that he was not feeling well and that he wanted to go to bed."
options: He said, "He was not feeling well. He wanted to go to bed."
He said, "I am not feeling well. I want to go to bed."
He said, "I am not feeling well and that I want to go to bed."
He said, "I was not feeling well. I wanted to go to bed."
questions.why: Reverse reported-speech conversion (indirect→direct), same skillset as the already-Solid direct→indirect direction — reverse the tense shift (past→present, since we're recovering the ORIGINAL words at the time they were spoken) and reverse the pronoun shift ("he"→"I"). Also drop the connecting "that" (not used in direct quotes) and split into separate sentences matching natural spoken structure.

questions.question: Select the wrongly spelt word.
questions.why: Spelling recall, already-Solid pattern (reverse framing — find the WRONG one, not the correct one) — "mortguage" is misspelt; correct is "mortgage" (silent "t," no "u").

questions.question: Which of the following materials is used for the generation of ultrasonic waves by using magnetostriction effect?
questions.why: Magnetostriction (a material's dimensions changing in a magnetic field) is a property of ferromagnetic materials specifically (e.g. nickel), used to generate ultrasonic waves by rapidly oscillating the applied field.

questions.topic: Trapezoidal rule (numerical integration from a small table)
questions.question: Consider the below data: x: 0, 1, 2; f(x): 4, 3, 12. The value of ∫(0 to 2) f(x)dx by the Trapezoidal rule will be:
questions.why: Trapezoidal rule with step h=1: Integral ≈ h/2 × [f(x0)+2f(x1)+f(x2)] = 1/2×[4+2(3)+12] = 1/2×[4+6+12]=1/2×22=11. Reusable formula: trapezoidal rule weights the FIRST and LAST points once, and every MIDDLE point twice, then multiplies by h/2.

questions.question: For what value of λ do the simultaneous equations 2x+3y=1, 4x+6y=λ have infinite solutions?
questions.why: The second equation is exactly 2× the first equation's LHS (4x+6y=2×(2x+3y)). For infinite solutions, the RHS must scale the same way: λ must equal 2×1=2. Reusable rule: two linear equations have infinite solutions only when EVERY coefficient (including the constant) scales by the same factor.

questions.topic: De Broglie wavelength — shortest for given kinetic energy
questions.question: Which of the following particles in motion, having the same kinetic energy, has the shortest wavelength?
questions.why: De Broglie wavelength λ=h/√(2mKE) — for FIXED kinetic energy, λ is inversely proportional to √mass. The alpha particle is by far the heaviest of the four (≈4 atomic mass units, vs ≈1 for neutron/proton and ≈1/1836 for electron), so it has the SHORTEST wavelength. Reusable rule: heavier particle + same KE → shorter de Broglie wavelength.

questions.question: A positron is an anti-particle of an electron, having the same mass but opposite charge to the electron. Then the minimum energy released in annihilation of matter of a pair of an electron and a positron is nearly:
questions.why: Each electron (and positron) has rest-mass energy of 0.511 MeV (E=mc²). When a pair annihilates, BOTH masses convert to energy: total = 2×0.511≈1.02 MeV. Trap: don't forget to double the single-particle rest energy — both particles vanish, not just one.

questions.topic: Exact differential equations (testing the exactness condition)
questions.question: Consider two differential equations: I: e^y dx + (xe^y + 2y)dy = 0.  II: x dy + 2y² dx = 0. Which of the following statements is correct?
options: Both I and II are exact differential equations.
I is not exact but II is an exact differential equation.
Neither I nor II are exact differential equations.
I is exact but II is not an exact differential equation.
questions.why: Genuinely new concept (testing exactness of a first-order ODE, M dx+N dy=0 is exact iff ∂M/∂y=∂N/∂x) — for equation I: M=e^y, N=xe^y+2y. ∂M/∂y=e^y, ∂N/∂x=e^y — EQUAL, so I is exact. For equation II: M=2y², N=x. ∂M/∂y=4y, ∂N/∂x=1 — NOT equal (unless y=1/4), so II is not exact. Reusable test: always compute ∂M/∂y and ∂N/∂x and compare — this single check decides exactness before attempting any solution method.

questions.topic: Forming a PDE by eliminating constants (exponential-trig form)
questions.question: A partial differential equation derived from the equation z = a·e^(by)·sin(bx) will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type — z=a·e^(by)·sin(bx) satisfies Laplace's equation, a well-known result for this exact functional form (harmonic function). Differentiating twice: ∂²z/∂x²=-ab²e^(by)sin(bx), ∂²z/∂y²=ab²e^(by)sin(bx) — these two are exact negatives, so summing them gives 0, i.e. ∂²z/∂x²+∂²z/∂y²=0.

questions.question: The value of ∫ e^x/(e^(2x)−4) dx will be ______, where C is an arbitrary constant.
questions.why: Substitute u=e^x, du=e^x dx: ∫du/(u²-4), a standard 1/(u²-a²) form integrating to (1/2a)log|(u-a)/(u+a)|+C with a=2: (1/4)log|(u-2)/(u+2)|+C = (1/4)log|(e^x-2)/(e^x+2)|+C. Reusable trick: whenever e^x appears alongside e^(2x), substitute u=e^x to reduce it to a standard algebraic integral form.

questions.topic: Ultrasonic pulse-echo flaw detection (timing to distance)
questions.question: Ultrasonic pulse echo technique, a non-destructive ultrasonic testing, is employed for possible flaw detection in a metallic bar of thickness 30 cm. If the arrival times of the ultrasonic pulses are 45 μs and 90 μs respectively, the distance of the flaw from the end of the steel bar at which the ultrasonic pulse initially enters, will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new applied-physics sub-type — the pulse's speed in the bar can be found from the FULL round-trip echo (bar's far end, 90μs for 2×30cm=60cm): speed=60cm/90μs=0.667 cm/μs. The FLAW echo arrives at 45μs (round trip to the flaw and back): flaw distance = speed×time/2 = 0.667×45/2≈15 cm. Reusable method: pulse-echo distance = (speed × round-trip time)/2, since the pulse travels TO the reflector and back.

questions.question: In an experimental arrangement of a Fresnel's biprism, monochromatic light of wavelength λ is used to produce an interference fringe pattern. On introducing a thin, transparent glass sheet of refractive index 1.50 and thickness 7 microns in the path of one of the interfering beams, the central fringe of the pattern is shifted to the position of the 6th bright fringe. Then the wavelength λ of the monochromatic light used is nearly:
questions.why: Fringe shift formula (same family as Q275 in the Shift 1 2015 file): shift in fringe-widths = (μ-1)t/λ. Setting this to 6 (shifted to the 6th fringe): 6 = (0.5×7000nm)/λ → λ=3500/6≈583nm, closely matching option 4 (581nm, small rounding).

questions.topic: General solution of a nonlinear first-order PDE (Charpit-style)
questions.question: General solution of the partial differential equation x(y²+z)∂z/∂x − y(x²+z)∂z/∂y = (x²−y²)z will be:
options: φ(xyz, x²+y²−2z) = 0, where φ is an arbitrary function.
φ(x+y+z, x²+y²) = 0, where φ is an arbitrary function.
φ(x²+y²+z², x+y+z) = 0, where φ is an arbitrary function.
φ(x+y−z, xy+yz+zx) = 0, where φ is an arbitrary function.
questions.why: This is a Lagrange-type PDE solved via the auxiliary/Charpit equations, identifying two independent invariant combinations (xyz and x²+y²-2z) that stay constant along the characteristic curves — recognition-level answer for this graduate PDE topic; trust the key, the underlying method (find two functionally independent invariants from the auxiliary equations, express the general solution as an arbitrary function of both) is the transferable idea.

questions.question: A biased six-faced dice when thrown is thrice as likely to show an odd number as an even number. If it is thrown twice, then the probability that the sum of the two numbers thrown is odd will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (biased-dice probability, distinct from anything in STUDY_PROGRESS) — P(odd)=3/4, P(even)=1/4 (since odd is 3× as likely and they must sum to 1). Sum of two throws is odd only if ONE throw is odd and the OTHER is even (odd+even=odd; odd+odd=even; even+even=even). P(sum odd) = P(odd,even)+P(even,odd) = (3/4×1/4)+(1/4×3/4) = 3/16+3/16=6/16=3/8. Reusable rule: "sum is odd" always means exactly one of the two values is odd — compute both orderings and add.

questions.topic: Square root of a prime is irrational
questions.question: Let p be a prime number. Then √p is:
questions.why: Standard proof-by-contradiction result (already implicitly known from Class X/XI number theory) — the square root of any prime number is always irrational; this is a generalisation of the classic "√2 is irrational" proof.

questions.topic: Particle nature of light (Compton effect + photoelectric effect)
questions.question: Which of the following pairs of phenomena illustrate the particle nature of the electromagnetic radiation?
questions.why: The Compton effect (photon scattering off electrons, transferring momentum like a particle collision) and the photoelectric effect (light ejecting electrons only above a threshold FREQUENCY, not intensity — a particle/quantum behaviour) are the two classic phenomena demonstrating light's particle nature. Bragg's diffraction, by contrast, demonstrates light's WAVE nature.

questions.question: The frequency of ultrasonic waves is:
options: Greater than 20 Hz and less than 20 KHz
questions.why: Definitional recall — ultrasonic waves are sound waves with frequency ABOVE the human audible range, i.e. more than 20 kHz. (Below 20 Hz is infrasonic; 20Hz-20kHz is the audible range.)

questions.question: The value of ∫(0 to 1) sin⁻¹(x)/x dx is:
questions.why: A known closed-form definite integral result (evaluated via series expansion of sin⁻¹x/x or a Feynman-trick parametric-differentiation approach) equal to (π/2)log 2 — a graduate-level integral to recognise/trust rather than derive live.

questions.topic: Optical rotation (specific rotation, concentration and tube length)
questions.question: A sugar solution in a tube of length 2.0 dm produces optical rotation of 12°. The sugar solution is then diluted to one half of its initial concentration. If the dilute solution is contained in another tube of length 3.0 dm, the optical rotation produced by it will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new applied-physics formula — optical rotation θ = [specific rotation]×length×concentration, so θ∝(length×concentration). Original: θ1=k×2×c=12°, so k×c=6. New: concentration halved (c/2), length tripled to 3.0: θ2=k×3×(c/2)=1.5×(k×c)=1.5×6=9°. Reusable rule: rotation is proportional to the PRODUCT of tube length and concentration, so compute the ratio of (new length×new concentration) to (old length×old concentration) and scale the original angle by that ratio.

questions.topic: Standard matrix of a linear transformation (from basis images)
questions.question: The standard ordered basis of R³ is {e1,e2,e3}. Let T:R³→R³ be the linear transformation such that T(e1)=7e1−5e3, T(e2)=−2e2+9e3, T(e3)=e1+e2+e3. The standard matrix of T is:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (building a transformation matrix from images of basis vectors) — the standard matrix of T has T(e1), T(e2), T(e3) as its COLUMNS: T(e1)=(7,0,-5), T(e2)=(0,-2,9), T(e3)=(1,1,1). Writing these as columns gives [[7,0,1],[0,-2,1],[-5,9,1]]. Reusable rule: the matrix of a linear transformation is ALWAYS built by placing each basis vector's image as a column, in order.

questions.question: Which of the following equations correctly represents the momentum p of a photon of Energy E?
questions.why: Standard relativistic photon relation (a massless particle): p=E/c. Directly from E=pc for massless particles (a special case of E²=(pc)²+(mc²)² with m=0).

questions.topic: Group velocity vs particle velocity (matter waves)
questions.question: The group velocity of matter waves associated with a moving particle is:
questions.why: For matter waves (de Broglie waves), the GROUP velocity (the speed of the overall wave packet) equals the actual velocity of the moving particle — this is what makes matter waves physically meaningful (phase velocity, by contrast, can exceed light speed and doesn't represent the particle's real motion).

questions.topic: Relativistic electron speed from total energy
questions.question: The speed of a fast moving electron, having total energy of 2 MeV, is nearly:
questions.why: Total relativistic energy E=γmc², with rest energy mc²=0.511 MeV. γ=E/mc²=2/0.511≈3.91. From γ=1/√(1-v²/c²): v/c=√(1-1/γ²)=√(1-1/15.29)=√(0.9346)≈0.967, matching "0.97c." Reusable method: find γ from total-energy÷rest-energy, then solve v/c=√(1-1/γ²).

questions.question: The value of ∫ 1/((x+1)√(x²−1)) dx will be ______, where C is an arbitrary constant.
questions.why: A standard integral-table form involving 1/((x+a)√(x²-a²)) — resolvable via a trig or hyperbolic substitution (x=sec θ) into a form that integrates to a square-root expression. Recognition-level result; trust the key.

questions.topic: Contour integration (residue theorem on a circle)
questions.question: The value of ∮(C) 1/(Z²+4) dZ where C is |Z−2i|=1 will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new concept (residue theorem for complex contour integration) — 1/(Z²+4) has poles at Z=±2i. The contour |Z-2i|=1 is a small circle around Z=2i ONLY (Z=-2i is far outside). Residue at Z=2i: lim(Z→2i)(Z-2i)/((Z-2i)(Z+2i))=1/(4i). By the residue theorem, the integral = 2πi × residue = 2πi/(4i)=π/2. Reusable method: identify which poles lie INSIDE the given contour, compute the residue there, multiply by 2πi.

questions.question: Which of the following materials behaves as a dielectric?
questions.why: Mica is a classic insulating/dielectric material (used in capacitors); Tungsten and Copper are metals (conductors), Germanium is a semiconductor — none of those three are dielectrics.

questions.question: The value of lim(x→0) (x·sin(1/x)) is:
questions.why: Genuinely useful technique (squeeze/sandwich theorem) — sin(1/x) always stays bounded between -1 and 1, no matter how wild it oscillates as x→0. So -|x| ≤ x·sin(1/x) ≤ |x|, and since both bounds →0 as x→0, the squeeze theorem forces the limit to be 0. Reusable rule: whenever a bounded oscillating function (sin/cos of something blowing up) is multiplied by something shrinking to 0, the limit is 0 by squeezing — no need to worry about the oscillation itself.

questions.question: The ratio of the amplitudes of the electric field and magnetic field strengths has the same dimensions as that of:
questions.why: E/B has units of velocity (E/B=c for EM waves in vacuum) but when properly analysed in terms of E/H (magnetic field strength, not flux density), the ratio carries the dimensions of impedance (Ohms) — this is the basis of the "impedance of free space" concept (≈377Ω).

questions.question: For a non-relativistic particle, the ratio of phase velocity to group velocity of de Broglie waves is:
questions.why: For a non-relativistic free particle, phase velocity vp=E/p while group velocity vg=dE/dp; using E=p²/2m gives vg=p/m (the actual particle velocity) and vp=p/2m — exactly half of vg. Ratio vp:vg=1:2.

questions.topic: Polarisation demonstrates transverse nature of light
questions.question: Which of the following phenomena establishes the transverse nature of light waves?
questions.why: Only TRANSVERSE waves can be polarised (their oscillation direction can be restricted to one plane) — longitudinal waves cannot. That light CAN be polarised is the classic proof that light is a transverse wave.

questions.question: Ultrasonic waves, propagating through a medium, can be detected by:
questions.why: Piezoelectric crystals (like quartz) generate a voltage when mechanically stressed by pressure waves — the standard detection method for ultrasonic waves, the reverse of how they're also often generated.

questions.topic: Complex line integral (parametrise the straight-line path)
questions.question: The value of the integral ∫(0 to 1+i) (x−y+ix²) dZ along the straight line from z=0 to Z=1+i will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new technique (line integral along a specified path in the complex plane) — parametrise the line z=t(1+i) for t from 0 to 1, so x=t,y=t,dz=(1+i)dt. Substitute into (x-y+ix²)dz = (t-t+it²)(1+i)dt = it²(1+i)dt. Integrate: i(1+i)∫(0 to 1)t²dt = i(1+i)×(1/3) = (i+i²)/3 = (i-1)/3, matching option 3. Reusable method: for a straight-line path, always parametrise as z=z0+t(z1-z0), substitute x,y in terms of t, then do an ordinary single-variable integral.

questions.question: The general solution of dx/y² = dy/x² = dz/(x²y²z²) will be:
options: x²+2y²=C1, x³−3z=C2 (where C1, C2 are arbitrary constants)
questions.why: From dx/y²=dy/x²: cross-multiply to get x²dx=y²dy, integrate both sides: x³/3=y³/3+const, giving x³-y³=C1. From dx/y²=dz/(x²y²z²): using the first relation to eliminate one variable then integrate the remaining separable equation gives the second invariant x³+3z⁻¹=C2 (after appropriate substitution). Recognition-level for this Lagrange-auxiliary-equation family (same technique as Q279, Q397 in earlier files) — trust the key's final form.

questions.question: Let A be a non-singular diagonalisable matrix of order 3 with eigenvalues λ1, λ2, λ3. A⁻¹ is diagonalisable if:
questions.why: A⁻¹ can only exist if A is NON-SINGULAR, meaning NO eigenvalue is zero (a zero eigenvalue makes the determinant zero, which makes A singular/non-invertible). Options 1, 2, and 4 each list a zero eigenvalue among the three, ruling them out — only option 3 has all three eigenvalues nonzero.

questions.topic: Complete solution of a Clairaut-type PDE
questions.question: A complete solution of the partial differential equation x·∂z/∂x + y·∂z/∂y − z = (∂z/∂x)(∂z/∂y) will be:
options: z = ax+by−ab, where a, b are arbitrary constants.
z = x²+y²−2ab, where a, b are arbitrary constants.
z = ax²+by²+abxy, where a, b are arbitrary constants.
z = ax−by+ab, where a, b are arbitrary constants.
questions.why: This PDE is a Clairaut-type equation (of the form z=xp+yq+f(p,q), where p=∂z/∂x, q=∂z/∂y) — its complete solution is always found by directly substituting p=a, q=b (arbitrary constants) into the ORIGINAL equation: z=ax+by-ab (from the RHS term becoming ab when p=a,q=b). Reusable rule: any PDE in Clairaut form z=xp+yq+f(p,q) has complete solution z=ax+by+f(a,b) by direct substitution — no actual solving required, just pattern recognition.

questions.question: The solution of the difference equation u(n+3) − 4u(n+2) + u(n+1) + 6u(n) = 0 will be:
options: un = C1(−1)^n + C2(2)^n + C3(3)^n (where C1, C2, C3 are constants)
questions.why: Genuinely new concept (linear difference/recurrence equations, the discrete analogue of linear ODEs) — form the characteristic equation by substituting un=r^n: r³-4r²+r+6=0. Testing small integer roots: r=-1: -1-4-1+6=0 ✓. r=2: 8-16+2+6=0 ✓. r=3: 27-36+3+6=0 ✓. Roots are -1,2,3, giving the general solution un=C1(-1)^n+C2(2)^n+C3(3)^n. Reusable method: for a linear constant-coefficient difference equation, substitute un=r^n, solve the resulting polynomial for r, and each distinct real root contributes one term C·r^n — directly parallel to the auxiliary-equation method for ODEs.

questions.question: Maximum angle of diffraction in a plane transmission diffraction grating is:
questions.why: The grating equation d·sinθ=nλ requires sinθ≤1, so the maximum physically possible diffraction angle is 90° (sinθ=1) — beyond that, no further order can be observed.

questions.question: The value of ∫(0 to 2π) ∫(0 to π/4) ∫(0 to 1) r² sinθ dr dθ dφ will be:
questions.why: Separate the three independent integrals: ∫(0 to 1)r²dr=1/3. ∫(0 to π/4)sinθ dθ=[-cosθ] from 0 to π/4=1-cos(π/4)=1-√2/2=(2-√2)/2. ∫(0 to 2π)dφ=2π. Multiply: (1/3)×(2-√2)/2×2π = (2π/3)×(2-√2)/2 = (π/3)(2-√2) = (√2π/3)(√2-1) after factoring √2 out of (2-√2)=√2(√2-1). Matches option 4. Reusable method: this is a "separable" triple integral (each limit depends only on its own variable), so split into three independent single integrals and multiply the results.

questions.topic: Complex locus (circle from a modulus equation)
questions.question: The curve represented by Z·Z̄ + (1+i)Z + (1−i)Z̄ = 0 will be:
options: a circle with centre at (−1,1) and radius √2
an ellipse with semi-major axis 2 and semi-minor axis 1
questions.why: With z=x+iy, ZZ̄=x²+y² and expanding the linear terms in terms of x,y produces a standard circle equation x²+y²+2x-2y=0 (after simplification), which completes the square to (x+1)²+(y-1)²=2 — a circle centred at (-1,1) with radius √2.

questions.question: Which of the following is the energy quantum of radiation?
questions.why: Vocabulary/definitional recall — a "photon" is the quantum (discrete packet) of electromagnetic radiation energy. (A "phonon," by contrast, is the quantum of lattice VIBRATION/sound energy in a solid — an easy sound-alike trap.)

questions.topic: Optical rotation (circular birefringence, angle from index difference)
questions.question: The refractive indices of quartz crystal for right-handed and left-handed circularly polarized light of wavelength 762.9 nm are 1.5391 and 1.5392 respectively. The angle of rotation produced by the crystal plate of thickness 0.5 mm is:
questions.why: Genuinely new formula — optical rotation from circular birefringence: θ=(π×t×(nL-nR))/λ, converted to degrees. With t=0.5mm=5×10⁻⁴m, Δn=0.0001, λ=762.9×10⁻⁹m: θ(radians)=π×5×10⁻⁴×0.0001/(762.9×10⁻⁹)≈0.206 rad ≈11.8°, matching option 2. Reusable formula: rotation angle depends on the DIFFERENCE between the two circular-polarisation refractive indices, scaled by thickness and inversely by wavelength.

questions.topic: Linear independence via the Wronskian (three exponential solutions)
questions.question: The solutions e^x, e^−x, and e^2x of d³y/dx³ − 2d²y/dx² − dy/dx + 2y = 0 will be:
options: linearly dependent for x∈[−2,2] and linearly independent elsewhere.
linearly independent for x∈[−1,1] and linearly dependent elsewhere.
linearly independent on every real interval.
linearly dependent for all real x.
questions.why: Genuinely new concept — solutions to a linear ODE with DIFFERENT characteristic roots (here 1,-1,2, all distinct) are always linearly independent everywhere (their Wronskian is never zero, since it involves a nonzero exponential factor times a nonzero Vandermonde-style determinant of the distinct roots). Reusable rule: distinct-root exponential solutions to a linear ODE are linearly independent on EVERY real interval, never just a limited range.

questions.question: The wavelength produced by a He-Ne laser corresponds to the transition in:
options: most favourable to He atoms than Ne atoms
questions.why: In a He-Ne laser, helium atoms are excited by the electrical discharge and TRANSFER their energy to neon atoms via collisions — but the actual laser light EMISSION (the transition producing the characteristic wavelength) happens in the neon atoms only. Helium's role is purely as an energy-pumping intermediary.

questions.question: If 3, 5 are the eigenvalues of a square matrix A of order 2, then the eigenvalues of the matrix A³ will be:
questions.why: Reusable rule worth stating explicitly: if λ is an eigenvalue of A, then λ^k is an eigenvalue of A^k, for any positive integer power k (same eigenvector, cubed eigenvalue). Here: 3³=27, 5³=125.

questions.question: The solution of the differential equation x²·d²y/dx² − x·dy/dx + y = log x will be:
options: y = C1 + C2·x·log x + x²·log x
y = (C1·x + C2·log x)x + log(2x) + 2 (where C1, C2 are arbitrary constants)
questions.why: Genuinely new equation family (Euler-Cauchy / equidimensional ODE, solved via the substitution x=e^t which turns it into a constant-coefficient ODE in t) — the complementary function comes out as (C1+C2·t)x=(C1+C2·log x)x (a repeated-root case), plus a particular integral matching log x+2. Recognition-level result for this out-of-syllabus ODE family; the key transferable idea is the x=e^t substitution trick for any x²y''+xy'+... equation.

questions.question: In order to investigate the internal atomic structure of crystals, we make use of:
questions.why: X-rays have wavelengths comparable to the spacing between atoms in a crystal lattice (~angstroms), which is required for diffraction to reveal atomic structure (Bragg's law) — visible/UV/IR wavelengths are far too long for this purpose.

questions.topic: Entire functions (sinh and cosh of a complex variable)
questions.question: For a complex variable z=x+iy, which of the following statements is true?
options: Both sinh Z and cosh Z are entire functions.
Neither sinh Z nor cosh Z are entire functions.
sinh Z is entire but cosh Z is not an entire function.
sinh Z is not entire but cosh Z is an entire function.
questions.why: sinh(z) and cosh(z) are both built from e^z (sinh z=(e^z-e^-z)/2, cosh z=(e^z+e^-z)/2), and e^z is entire (analytic everywhere in the complex plane, no singularities) — so both sinh and cosh are also entire, same as their real-analysis counterparts sin/cos.

questions.question: A ray of light is incident on a transparent medium at an angle of 60°. The reflected ray of light is found to be completely polarised. Then the refractive index of the transparent medium is nearly:
questions.why: Brewster's law: when reflected light is completely polarised, the incidence angle is the Brewster (polarising) angle θB, and n=tan(θB). tan(60°)=√3≈1.73. Reusable formula worth memorising: refractive index = tangent of the polarising angle.

questions.question: A metre stick moves along its length with a certain speed. The apparent length of the moving metre stick as measured by a stationary observer on the ground is found to be 98 cm. Then the velocity v of the metre stick in terms of the speed of light in vacuum c will be:
questions.why: Length contraction formula: L=L0√(1-v²/c²). 0.98=1×√(1-v²/c²) → 0.9604=1-v²/c² → v²/c²=0.0396 → v/c=√0.0396≈0.199≈0.19c. Reusable formula: contracted length = rest length × √(1-v²/c²) — solve backward for v when given the contracted length.

questions.question: Which of the following materials exhibits the piezoelectric effect?
questions.why: Quartz is the classic piezoelectric crystal (generates voltage under mechanical stress, and vice versa) — Copper, Aluminium, and Iron are all simple metals with no piezoelectric property.

questions.question: The experimental evidence that the electron exhibits wave-like characteristics was first provided by:
questions.why: De Broglie THEORISED matter waves (1924); Davisson and Germer EXPERIMENTALLY confirmed electron diffraction (1927), proving electrons behave as waves — the key distinction is theory vs. experimental proof.

questions.question: Newton's rings can be obtained in:
options: both transmitted and reflected light systems
any light system with narrow source of light
questions.why: Newton's rings (thin-film interference between a plano-convex lens and a flat glass plate) can be observed in BOTH reflected light (the standard setup, dark centre) and transmitted light (complementary pattern, bright centre) — the two patterns are complementary (where one is dark, the other is bright).

questions.question: If f(0)=3, f(1)=5, f(3)=21, then the unique polynomial of degree 2 or less using Newton's divided-difference interpolation will be:
questions.why: Verify by plugging x=0,1,3 into each candidate: option 3 (2x²+3): f(0)=3✓, f(1)=2+3=5✓, f(3)=18+3=21✓. All three points match perfectly. Reusable exam shortcut: with only 3 data points and 4 answer options, it's often FASTER to just plug all 3 x-values into each candidate polynomial and check for matches than to build the full divided-difference table from scratch.

questions.question: The 2nd approximation to a root of the equation x²−x−1=0 in the interval (1,2) by the Bisection method will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new numerical-methods technique — bisection repeatedly halves the interval, keeping the half where the function changes sign. f(1)=1-1-1=-1, f(2)=4-2-1=1 (sign change confirmed). 1st approximation (midpoint): x=1.5, f(1.5)=2.25-1.5-1=-0.25 (still negative) → root is in (1.5,2). 2nd approximation (midpoint of new interval): x=(1.5+2)/2=1.75. Reusable method: each bisection step takes the midpoint of whichever half retains the sign change, narrowing the bracket every iteration.

questions.topic: Curie law applies to paramagnetic materials only
questions.question: The Curie law, χ = C/T, expressing susceptibility χ varying with absolute temperature T, is obeyed by:
questions.why: Curie's law (χ=C/T, susceptibility inversely proportional to temperature) applies specifically to PARAMAGNETIC materials; ferromagnetic materials instead follow the Curie-WEISS law (χ=C/(T-θ), with a shifted transition temperature θ) above their Curie point, and diamagnetic susceptibility is essentially temperature-independent.

questions.topic: Iron for electromagnets and transformer cores
questions.question: Which of the following materials is most suitable for making electromagnets and the core of a transformer?
questions.why: Iron (specifically soft iron, easily magnetised and demagnetised) is the standard core material for electromagnets and transformers — it has high permeability but low retentivity (doesn't stay magnetised once the field is removed), ideal for rapidly-changing AC applications.

questions.question: Which of the following optical phenomena CANNOT convert unpolarised light to plane polarised light?
questions.why: Double refraction (birefringence), scattering, and reflection (at Brewster's angle) can all selectively filter/orient the electric field direction, producing polarised light. Diffraction (bending around obstacles/through slits) does not selectively filter polarisation direction — it cannot polarise light.

questions.question: The Poynting vector of electromagnetic waves has the same dimensions as that of:
questions.why: The Poynting vector S=E×H represents the rate of energy flow per unit area (power per unit area) of an electromagnetic wave — its dimensions are exactly those of power density (W/m²).

questions.topic: Real analysis (identify the false statement — Cauchy sequences)
questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: The series Σ(n=1 to ∞) 1/n² is convergent.
A Cauchy sequence of real numbers need not be bounded.
A sequence of real numbers is convergent if and only if it is a Cauchy sequence.
If <xn> is a convergent sequence of real numbers, then <xn> is a Cauchy sequence.
questions.why: Genuinely new concept-check (Cauchy sequences, real analysis) — a fundamental theorem states every Cauchy sequence of REAL numbers IS necessarily bounded (this is a standard, provable result, part of why completeness of R makes Cauchy=convergent). So the claim "need not be bounded" is FALSE, which is exactly why it's the correct pick for "which statement is false." Reusable fact worth memorising: Cauchy sequence of reals ⟹ bounded ⟹ (by completeness of R) convergent.

questions.question: The length of the curve y = x^(3/2) over the interval [0,1] will be:
questions.why: Arc length formula: L=∫√(1+(dy/dx)²)dx. dy/dx=(3/2)√x, so (dy/dx)²=(9/4)x. L=∫(0 to 1)√(1+9x/4)dx. Substitute u=1+9x/4, du=(9/4)dx: L=(4/9)∫√u du=(4/9)×(2/3)u^(3/2)=(8/27)u^(3/2) evaluated from u=1 to u=13/4... working through the constants gives the final form (1/27)[(13)^(3/2)-8]. Reusable formula: arc length = ∫√(1+(y')²)dx, then substitute for any power-function y'.

questions.topic: Linear (in)dependence of vector sets in R³
questions.question: Consider two subsets of R³ given as S1 = {[2,3,1],[1,0,5],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]} and S2 = {[1,0,0],[0,1,1],[0,0,0]}. Which of the following statements is true?
options: S1 is linearly dependent but S2 is linearly independent.
Both S1 and S2 are linearly independent.
S1 is linearly independent but S2 is linearly dependent.
Both S1 and S2 are linearly dependent.
questions.why: Two quick reusable shortcuts (no computation needed): ANY set of MORE than 3 vectors in R³ is automatically linearly dependent (S1 has 4 vectors — too many for a 3-dimensional space, so it must be dependent). ANY set CONTAINING the zero vector is automatically linearly dependent (S2 includes [0,0,0] — the zero vector alone breaks independence). Both S1 and S2 are dependent, for two DIFFERENT structural reasons.

questions.question: The p-series Σ(n=1 to ∞) 1/n^p diverges for:
questions.why: Standard p-series test (worth memorising as a reusable rule): Σ1/n^p converges when p>1, and diverges when p≤1 (including the harmonic series case p=1). So it diverges for 0<p≤1.

questions.question: In which state is Madai festival celebrated?
questions.why: The Madai festival (a tribal harvest/hunting festival) is celebrated in Chhattisgarh — static GK/culture fact.

questions.question: As per Economic Survey 2017-18, the service sector contributed ______ to India's GVA (Gross Value Added) in 2017-18.
questions.why: Dated Economic Survey statistic (2017-18 vintage) — service sector contributed 55.2% of GVA per that specific survey year. Re-verify current sectoral GVA contribution separately before quoting as live; use only as style reference.

questions.question: The President has the power to promulgate ordinances under ______ of the Constitution of India.
questions.why: Article 123 gives the President power to promulgate ordinances when Parliament is not in session — static polity/GK fact.

questions.question: With whom has the Government of India entered into an agreement for a flexible financing arrangement to accelerate research towards early development of biopharmaceuticals under the National Biopharma Mission?
questions.why: The National Biopharma Mission's flexible-financing arrangement was with the World Bank (dated to this 2018 scheme announcement). Dated policy fact, style reference only.

questions.question: Indu Malhotra recently became the ______ woman lawyer to be directly elevated from the Bar to the Supreme Court as a judge.
questions.why: Justice Indu Malhotra (2018) was the first woman lawyer directly elevated from the Bar (not via the High Court route) to the Supreme Court. Dated appointment-history fact, useful as static trivia but not to be confused with a "current" judge status.

questions.question: Which of the following hockey players won the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna award in 2017?
questions.why: Sardara Singh won the Khel Ratna in 2017 (hockey category). Dated sports-award fact, style reference only.

questions.question: Which of the following is correct?
options: The total number of Fundamental Duties provided by Article 51A of the Constitution of India is 15.
questions.why: Article 51A lists 11 Fundamental Duties (originally 10, with the 86th Amendment in 2002 adding an 11th about parents/guardians providing education) — static polity fact worth memorising directly.

questions.question: It takes ______ full grown trees to make one tonne of paper.
questions.why: Standard environmental-awareness trivia fact: roughly 17 full-grown trees are needed to produce one tonne of paper — a commonly cited conservation statistic.

questions.question: Who among the following introduced the 'Doctrine of Lapse'?
questions.why: Lord Dalhousie introduced the Doctrine of Lapse (annexation policy denying adopted heirs succession rights to princely states) — static colonial-history fact.

questions.question: Which of the following is the basic unit of inheritance in living organisms which controls the transfer of hereditary characteristics from parents to offspring?
questions.why: A gene is the basic functional unit of heredity (a segment of DNA, carried on a chromosome, within a cell) — static biology definitional fact, worth distinguishing from the broader terms DNA/chromosome/cell.

questions.question: Select the option that is related to the third term in the same way as the second term is related to the first term: ACEG : ZXVT :: BDFH : ?
questions.why: Analogy, already-Solid category — ACEG (letters skip by 2: A,C,E,G) maps to ZXVT, which is each letter's alphabet-mirror (A↔Z, C↔X, E↔V, G↔T, using the 27-minus-position mirror rule). Applying the same mirror to BDFH (B↔Y, D↔W, F↔U, H↔S) gives YWUS.

questions.question: Select the option that is different from the other three.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category — check letter-position gaps within each 5-letter group: JKMPT (+1,+2,+3,+4), DEGJN (+1,+2,+3,+4), HIKNR (+1,+2,+3,+4) — three groups share the same "+1,+2,+3,+4" spacing pattern. FGIKP breaks this (spacing is +1,+2,+2,+4), making it the odd one out.

questions.question: 'Flabby' is related to 'Toned' in the same way as 'Weak' is related to:
questions.why: Analogy, already-Solid category — flabby and toned are antonyms; weak and robust are antonyms. Trap: "Week" is a homophone distractor of "weak," not a related word at all.

questions.topic: Classification (odd number out, primes vs composites)
questions.question: Select the number that is different from the other three numbers.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category — 13, 3, and 17 are all PRIME numbers; 9 is composite (3×3), the odd one out.

questions.question: Choose the option that will correctly replace the question mark (?) in the below number series. 15, 35, 63, ?, 143
questions.why: Number series, already-Solid pattern — notice each term is n(n+4) for n=3,5,7,9,11: 3×7=21? Doesn't fit directly; try differences: 35-15=20, 63-35=28, ?-63=?, 143-?=?. Second differences constant: 28-20=8, so next difference=28+8=36, giving ?=63+36=99; check: 143-99=44, and 44-36=8 ✓ (constant second difference confirmed). Answer 99.

questions.question: If all the vowels are removed from the English alphabet, which letter would be ninth to the right of the sixth letter from the left?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (modified-alphabet position counting, distinct from plain letter-series work) — remove A,E,I,O,U from the 26-letter alphabet, leaving 21 consonants: B,C,D,F,G,H,J,K,L,M,N,P,Q,R,S,T,V,W,X,Y,Z. The 6th letter from the left in this reduced list is H. Counting 9 places to the right of H: H(6th)→...→9 more positions lands on S (15th in the reduced list). Reusable method: rebuild the modified alphabet list explicitly first, THEN count positions on that new list — don't try to count directly on the original 26-letter alphabet.

questions.topic: Classification (odd number out, primes vs composite)
questions.question: Select the number that is different from the other three options.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category — same pattern as Q617: 13, 11, 7 are prime; 9 is composite, the odd one out.

questions.question: Five children are standing in a single queue, one after another, facing the stage. R is nearest to the stage. S is standing ahead of P and is not before or after T. Q is just after R and T is not standing near Q. Who is at the end of the line?
questions.why: Ranking/linear-order puzzle, already-Solid category applied to a queue instead of a height/marks ranking — R is 1st (nearest stage). "Q is just after R" → Q is 2nd. "S not before/after T" means S and T are not adjacent. "T not standing near Q" rules out T being 1st or 3rd (adjacent to Q's position 2). Working through the remaining positions (3,4,5) for S,P,T with the given adjacency constraints places T at the very end (5th, furthest from stage).

questions.question: Given below are two statements and two conclusions. Consider these statements to be true even if they seem factually absurd. Read the conclusions and decide which of the given conclusions logically follow(s). Statements: A. All tables are chairs. B. All chairs are racks. Conclusions: 1. All racks are tables. 2. All chairs are tables.
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type worth stating the rule explicitly (syllogism, not yet a named Solid concept though closely related to Venn-diagram/classification logic already Solid) — draw nested circles: Tables⊂Chairs⊂Racks (all tables are chairs, all chairs are racks). Conclusion 1 ("all racks are tables") reverses the containment direction — FALSE, since Racks is the LARGEST circle, containing chairs and tables, not the other way round. Conclusion 2 ("all chairs are tables") also reverses a containment (Chairs is bigger than Tables, so not every chair is necessarily a table) — FALSE. Neither follows. Reusable rule: in a chain "All A are B, All B are C," you can ONLY validly conclude "All A are C" (forward direction) — never reverse any single link's containment.

questions.question: Select the option that is related to the third number in the same way as the second number is related to the first number. 7 : 64 :: 12 : ?
questions.why: Analogy, already-Solid category — check 7→64: (7+1)²=64 ✓ (add 1, then square). Apply to 12: (12+1)²=169.

questions.topic: Word analogy (odd pair out, synonym relationships)
questions.question: Identify the word-pair that is different from the other three.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category — Dynamic:Energetic, Authoritarian:Dominating, Wimpy:Feeble are all SYNONYM pairs. Tough:Tender is an ANTONYM pair, the odd one out.

questions.topic: Word formation (which word CANNOT be made)
questions.question: From the given options, select the word that CANNOT be formed using the letters of the given word. ADMIRATION
questions.why: Word formation, already-Solid category — check letter availability from ADMIRATION (A,D,M,I,R,A,T,I,O,N: two A's, two I's, one each of D,M,R,T,O,N). "ADMIRE" needs an E, which ADMIRATION doesn't contain at all — cannot be formed.

questions.question: Pointing to a photograph, Somen said, "His mother is my mother-in-law's son's only sister." How is Somen related to the person in the photograph?
questions.why: Blood relations, already-Solid category, worked through step by step — "my mother-in-law's son" is Somen's wife's brother (brother-in-law). That person's "only sister" is Somen's wife herself (his own wife is her brother's only sister). So "his mother" (the photograph person's mother) = Somen's wife. That makes the person in the photograph Somen's own child, so Somen is the FATHER of the person in the photo.

questions.question: In a certain code language 'ADMIT' is written as 'YVMQF'. How will 'TRAIN' be written in the same code language?
questions.why: Coding-decoding, already-Solid category — each letter of ADMIT shifts by a DIFFERENT amount to reach YVMQF (A→Y is -4, D→V is -8, M→M is 0, I→Q is +8, T→F is... check wraparound), suggesting a position-dependent shift rather than a uniform one. Trust the key's derived pattern applied consistently to TRAIN, giving FHYQM.

questions.topic: Calendar reasoning (day-of-week shift within a month)
questions.question: If the fifth day of a month is 4 days earlier to Friday, what day will it be on the twenty-first day of that month?
questions.why: Calendar reasoning, already-Solid category — "4 days earlier than Friday" means Monday (Fri-4=Mon). So the 5th is a Monday. From the 5th to the 21st is 16 days later. 16 mod 7 = 2 (since 7 days = same weekday), so the 21st is 2 days after Monday: Wednesday.

questions.topic: Data interpretation (pie charts, gender ratio across disciplines, diagram-based)
questions.question: Study the pie charts: (1) "Total Number of Students = 3,200" — Arts 27%, Management 20%, Science 30%, Commerce 17%, Engineering 6%. (2) "Total Number of Girls = 1,800" — Arts 12%, Management 19%, Science 37%, Commerce 24%, Engineering 8%. What is the ratio of the total number of girls in the Engineering and Science disciplines to the total number of boys in Arts, Engineering and Science?
questions.why: Data interpretation, already-Solid category, but this variant needs a BOYS calculation derived indirectly (total minus girls per discipline) — Girls in Engineering+Science = (8%+37%)×1800=45%×1800=810. Total students in Arts+Engineering+Science = (27%+6%+30%)×3200=63%×3200=2016. Girls in those same three disciplines = (12%+8%+37%)×1800=57%×1800=1026. Boys in Arts+Engineering+Science = 2016-1026=990. Ratio: 810:990, simplify by dividing by 90: 9:11. IMAGE: `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift2_2018_q19.png`. Trap: the question asks for BOYS in one group but only girls'-pie data is given directly — must subtract girls from the TOTAL population pie to get boys per discipline.

questions.question: The ratio between the number of students in class I and II is 8:5, that between the number of students in class II and III is 3:4, and that between the number of students in class III and IV is 7:8. If the difference between the number of students in class II and IV is 33, then the number of students in class III is:
questions.why: Ratio chaining, already-Solid category, extended to a triple-chain — make the shared terms match across all three ratios (already-Solid LCM method): I:II=8:5, II:III=3:4, III:IV=7:8. Match II (5 and 3, LCM=15): I:II=24:15, II:III=15:20. Match III (20 and 7, LCM=140): scale II:III by 7 → 105:140, III:IV scale by 20 → 140:160. Combined chain: I:II:III:IV = 168:105:140:160 (after aligning I:II=24:15 scaled by 7 too: 168:105). Difference II-IV = 105-160 is negative, so use |IV-II|=55 parts=33 → 1 part=0.6. III=140×0.6=84.

questions.topic: Mensuration (cylinder melted and recast into a cone)
questions.question: A solid metallic right circular cylinder of base diameter 16 cm and height 2 cm is melted and recast into a right circular cone of height three times that of the cylinder. The curved surface area of the cone will be: (Use π=3.14)
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (volume-conservation "melted and recast" mensuration, distinct from simple ratio-scaling already Solid) — volume is conserved: cylinder volume=πr²h=π×8²×2=128π. Cone height=3×2=6cm. Cone volume=πR²(6)/3=2πR²=128π → R²=64 → R=8cm (same radius as cylinder, coincidentally). Cone slant height l=√(R²+h²)=√(64+36)=√100=10cm. Curved surface area=πRl=3.14×8×10=251.2 cm². Reusable method: "melted and recast" always means volumes are EQUAL — set the two volume formulas equal and solve for the new shape's unknown dimension.

questions.topic: Relative speed (train crosses platform, then a man crosses it separately)
questions.question: A 240 m long train, moving at an average speed of 54 km/h, crosses a platform in 30 s. A man crosses the same platform in 120 s. What is the speed (in km/h) of the man?
questions.why: Relative speed, already-Solid category with a two-part setup — first find platform length: train speed=54km/h=15m/s. Distance covered in 30s (train length + platform length)=15×30=450m. Platform length=450-240=210m. Man crosses only the platform (210m) in 120s: speed=210/120=1.75 m/s=1.75×3.6=6.3 km/h.

questions.question: If [√50+√98+√72]/[5√2−√18] − (√75+√108−√147) = a+b√3, then the value of √(4a−7b) will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (surd simplification with nested radicals, find embedded coefficients) — simplify each root to its simplest radical form: √50=5√2, √98=7√2, √72=6√2 (numerator sums to 18√2). √18=3√2 (denominator: 5√2-3√2=2√2). First fraction=18√2/2√2=9. Second part: √75=5√3, √108=6√3, √147=7√3 → 5√3+6√3-7√3=4√3. Combined: 9-4√3=a+b√3, so a=9, b=-4. √(4×9-7×(-4))=√(36+28)=√64=8. Reusable method: always reduce every surd to its SIMPLEST radical form first (pull out perfect-square factors), then combine like terms by their radical part.

questions.topic: Compound interest (two equal sums borrowed a year apart)
questions.question: Anita borrowed two equal sums at the beginning of two successive years at 10% compound interest. At the end of the second year, she paid ₹12,474 to settle her debts. How much did she borrow each year?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (staggered-loan compound interest, two different maturity periods for equal principals) — let each borrowed amount=P. The FIRST year's loan accrues interest for 2 full years: P×1.1². The SECOND year's loan accrues for only 1 year: P×1.1. Total owed: P(1.21+1.1)=P×2.31=12474 → P=12474/2.31=5400. Reusable method: when sums are borrowed at DIFFERENT times but settled together, each amount compounds for its OWN specific duration — set up separate terms, don't assume both compound for the same number of years.

questions.topic: Profit/loss chain (buy at loss, repair cost, sell at profit → find original CP)
questions.question: Person A sold a car to B at a loss of 28%. B spent ₹2,520 on its repair and sold it to C for ₹70,875, thus earning a profit of 12.5%. How much had A paid to buy the car?
questions.why: Profit/loss chain, already-Solid category with an added repair-cost layer (same "renovation is part of CP" trap as Q349 in the Shift 1 2015 file) — B's total cost = purchase price from A + repair = X. B's SP=70,875 at 12.5% profit: X×1.125=70875 → X=63,000. So B PAID A + 2520 repair = 63,000 → B paid A = 60,480. This 60,480 is A's selling price, which represents A's CP at a 28% LOSS: A's CP×0.72=60,480 → A's CP=84,000.

questions.topic: Profit/loss (find discount% from markup% and actual profit%)
questions.question: A trader marks his goods such that he earns a profit of 30% on its cost. He then sells it by offering a discount of x% on its marked price. If his actual profit is 9.85%, then the value of x is:
questions.why: Profit/loss, already-Solid category — let CP=100. Marked price (30% markup)=130. After discount x%: SP=130×(1-x/100). Actual profit is 9.85%, so SP=109.85. Solve: 130(1-x/100)=109.85 → 1-x/100=0.845 → x/100=0.155 → x=15.5.

questions.topic: HCF with common remainder (find x, then x+y mod 33)
questions.question: Let x be the greatest number such that when it divides 5892, 6105 and 6531, the remainder in each case is y. When (x+y) is divided by 33, the remainder will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (HCF-of-differences with a common but UNKNOWN remainder, distinct from the plain HCF-distribution already Solid, since y isn't given directly) — the greatest divisor giving the SAME remainder on all three numbers is the HCF of their pairwise DIFFERENCES: HCF(6105-5892, 6531-6105)=HCF(213,426)=213 (since 426=2×213). So x=213. Find y: 5892÷213 gives remainder y (compute 213×27=5751, 5892-5751=141, so y=141). x+y=213+141=354. 354÷33=10 remainder 24. Reusable rule: "same remainder for multiple numbers, find the greatest divisor" always means HCF of the PAIRWISE DIFFERENCES, not the numbers themselves.

questions.question: The income of A is 20% more than that of B, and the income of C is 10% less than the sum of the incomes of A and B. If the income of C is ₹19,800, then by what percentage is the income of C more than the income of B?
questions.why: Percentage chaining, already-Solid category extended to 3 linked people — let B=100, A=120 (20% more). A+B=220. C=90% of 220=198. Given C=19,800 actual, scale factor=19800/198=100, so B actual=100×100=10,000. C is more than B by: (19800-10000)/10000×100=98%.

questions.question: A sum of ₹8,690 is divided among A, B and C such that 2/5 of A, 4/9 of B and 6/11 of C are equal. What is the difference between A and C?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (equal-fractional-shares ratio, distinct from the direct ratio-chaining already Solid) — if 2A/5=4B/9=6C/11=k, then A=5k/2, B=9k/4, C=11k/6. Find a common multiple to express as integer ratio: LCM of denominators (2,4,6)=12. A=5k/2×(12/12)=30k/12, B=9k/4×(3/3)=27k/12, C=11k/6×(2/2)=22k/12. Ratio A:B:C=30:27:22, sum=79 parts=8690 → 1 part=110. Difference A-C=(30-22)×110=8×110=880.

questions.topic: Pipes and cisterns (fill then drain, staggered start)
questions.question: Tap A can fill an empty tank in 10 h while tap B can empty a fully-filled tank in 12 h. Tap A is turned on first. After 2 hours, Tap B is also turned on. What will be the total time (in hours) taken to fill the tank?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (staggered-start pipes-and-cisterns, distinct from the simultaneous-start version already worked in Q351/Q465) — in the first 2 hours, only A works: fills 2×(1/10)=1/5 of the tank. Remaining=4/5. Once both are on, net rate=1/10-1/12=(6-5)/60=1/60 per hour (very slow, since B nearly cancels A). Time to fill remaining 4/5 at this net rate: (4/5)÷(1/60)=48 hours. Total time=2+48=50 hours.

questions.topic: Average (batsman innings, average dropping after new scores)
questions.question: The average score of a batsman for a certain number of innings was 42 runs. In the next five innings he scored 20, 35, 25, 10 and 40 runs and his average for all the innings came down by 5. How many innings did he play in all?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (average shift from adding a batch of new values, algebraic setup) — let original innings=n, original total=42n. New 5 innings total=20+35+25+10+40=130. New average=42-5=37, over (n+5) innings: 42n+130=37(n+5) → 42n+130=37n+185 → 5n=55 → n=11. Total innings=n+5=16.

questions.question: The value of [1.331×21.9×1.24 / (16.5×0.121×7.3×0.62)] × [2.8×1.3̄6 / 31.8̄1] is:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (dense decimal arithmetic combined with recurring-decimal notation) — spot hidden multiples: 1.331=11×0.121, 21.9≈3×7.3, 1.24≈2×0.62, letting large chunks of numerator/denominator cancel via ratio (11×3×2 type factoring), dramatically simplifying before touching a calculator's worth of decimals. Trust the key's final simplified value; the reusable skill is factoring out hidden common-ratio relationships between numerator and denominator terms in decimal-heavy expressions, exactly like Q515 in the Shift 1 2018 file. This is the 15th and last General Aptitude question.

questions.topic: Nested fraction/"of" expression (BODMAS with mixed numbers)
questions.question: The value of {(4/5) of [7/8(1/4+5/4+3/2)] / (1¾+½)} of (2 16/17 ÷ 7/9) is:
questions.why: Same skillset as Q514 in the Shift 1 2018 file (dense nested "of/÷" BODMAS) — convert every mixed number to an improper fraction first, resolve each "of" as multiplication, and work strictly inside-out through the brackets. Note: this question was skipped in the initial numbering pass of this file and inserted here out of strict source order (it belongs between the surd-simplification question and the compound-interest question above) — content and source mapping are both correct, only its position in this file is appended rather than interleaved. Source scan is visually dense for this one (flagged by Stage 1) — double-check the exact fraction values against the source image (shift2_2018/page_008.png) before using as a worked example live.

questions.question: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Choose the INCORRECT word or phrase. "If the water level in Periyar rises alarmingly, more people from the banks of Periyar in Ernakulam District were evacuated."
questions.why: Spot-the-error, already-Solid pattern — the "if" clause is present tense ("rises"), describing a hypothetical/future condition, so the main clause needs future tense ("will be evacuated"), not past tense ("were evacuated") — tense mismatch is the error.

questions.question: Select the option that is NOT an antonym of another word by way of adding the prefix 'im-'.
questions.why: Same rule as Q528 in the Shift 1 2018 file — impassive, impertinent, imperceptible all negate a real standalone root word by adding "im-." "Impression" is not built this way (removing "im-" leaves "pression," not a real related word) — it's simply an unrelated word starting with "im-."

questions.question: Select the correct passive form of the given sentence. "Somebody has stolen the manhole cover in our lane."
options: The manhole cover in our lane has been stolen.
The manhole cover in our lane is being stolen.
The manhole cover in our lane had been stolen.
Our lane in the manhole cover has been stolen.
questions.why: Active-to-passive, already-Solid pattern — present perfect active ("has stolen") converts to present perfect passive ("has been stolen"). A vague active subject ("somebody") is simply dropped in the passive.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "She didn't buy the second-hand study table because ______ top was chipped off."
questions.why: Possessive pronoun agreement — "top" belongs TO the table, so the possessive "its" (not the subject pronoun "it") goes directly before the noun "top."

questions.question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. DUBIOUS
questions.why: Synonym recall — DUBIOUS = doubtful/uncertain. Already-Solid pattern; the other three options are near-ANTONYMS, testing whether the meaning was actually understood.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "______ I didn't speak French, I managed to make myself understood."
questions.why: Same grammatical-form rule as Q538 — "Even though" introduces a full clause (subject+verb); "In spite of" would require a noun phrase instead.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "There is heavy fog at the Delhi airport. The plane, ______, has been diverted."
questions.why: "Therefore" signals the logical consequence of the fog — fits the two-sentence cause-and-effect structure, unlike "because" (which needs to join clauses directly).

questions.question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. RECIPROCATE
questions.why: Synonym recall — RECIPROCATE = to respond in kind. The four "Re-" prefixed options sounding similar is the trap, testing precise meaning not prefix-matching.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "I was exhausted last night after driving, so I went to bed ______ than usual."
questions.why: "Than usual" signals a two-way comparison, requiring the comparative "earlier," not the plain form or superlative.

questions.question: Select the wrongly spelt word.
questions.why: Spelling recall — "geniune" is misspelt; correct is "genuine" (i and u are swapped).

questions.topic: Tense (habitual routine in a subordinate clause)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "As soon as he ______ home, he sits and talks to his children asking them about their day."
questions.why: Same habitual-routine rule as Q540 — the main clause is present tense ("sits and talks," a repeated habit), so "as soon as he comes" matches.

questions.question: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Choose the INCORRECT word or phrase. "In India most people wears both their traditional clothes and western dresses."
questions.why: Spot-the-error, already-Solid pattern — "most people" is plural, so it needs "wear," not "wears."

questions.topic: Reported speech → direct speech (present-tense reporting verb)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate direct form of the given sentence. "Addressing the students, the professor said that it gave him great pleasure to be interacting with them."
options: Addressing the students, the professor said, "It gives me great pleasure to be interacting with you."
...said, "It gave him great pleasure to be interacting with them."
...said, "It gives him great pleasure to be interacting with you."
