...said, "It has given him great pleasure to be interacting with them."
questions.why: Reverse reported-speech conversion — reverse the tense ("gave"→"gives") and both pronouns ("him"→"me," "them"→"you"), since the professor now speaks directly TO the students.

questions.topic: Reported speech (past-tense reporting verb, full backward shift)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate indirect form of the given sentence. He wrote, "It is time we thought about settling this deal."
options: He wrote that it was time they thought about settling that deal.
He wrote that it was time we thought about settling that deal.
He wrote that it is time we thought about settling this deal.
He wrote that that is time they thought about settling that deal.
questions.why: "Wrote" is past tense, triggering full backward shift: "is"→"was," "this"→"that." "We" shifts to "they" per the marked key's context (writer reporting about a group excluding the current speaker).

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "The flat ______ is very nice but the entrance to the colony is crowded and dirty."
questions.why: "The flat" is a singular inanimate subject, so it needs "itself."

questions.topic: Tense (past perfect for a long-duration state, ended by a sudden event)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "The old Neem tree which ______ in our compound for fifty years suddenly crashed to the ground last night."
questions.why: A long-standing state BEFORE a specific past event ("crashed...last night") needs past perfect ("had stood") — same pattern as Q525.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word. OBSTRUCTED
questions.why: OBSTRUCTED ↔ Unhindered. Trap: "Blocked" is a near-synonym distractor.

questions.question: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.why: Correct spelling is "commission" (double M, double S).

questions.question: Select the correct active form of the given sentence. "If he is elected by people in the next election, he will be greatly surprised."
options: If people are electing him in the next election, he is greatly surprised.
If he elected the people in the next election, he will be greatly surprised.
If people elected him in the next election, he will be greatly surprised.
If people elect him in the next election, he will be greatly surprised.
questions.why: The "if" clause active form uses simple present ("elect"), matching the original passive's simple present ("is elected"); the main clause keeps its future tense unchanged.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "She looked very graceful in her ______ sari."
questions.why: Same adjective-order rule as Q527 — age/condition → colour → material: "new" → "green" → "cotton" → sari.

questions.topic: Gauss-Seidel iterative method (one iteration by hand)
questions.question: The approximate solution of the system of simultaneous equations 2x−5y+3z=7; x+4y−2z=3; 2x+3y+z=2, by applying the Gauss-Seidel method one time (using initial approximation x=0, y=0, z=0), will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new numerical-methods technique — Gauss-Seidel solves for each variable in turn, IMMEDIATELY using each newly-updated value (unlike Jacobi, which waits for the full sweep). Rearrange: x=(7+5y-3z)/2, y=(3-x+2z)/4, z=2-2x-3y. From x=y=z=0: x=3.5 (use immediately), y=(3-3.5)/4=-0.125 (use immediately), z=2-7+0.375=-4.625. Reusable rule: Gauss-Seidel always uses the MOST RECENTLY updated values within the same iteration.

questions.topic: Euler-Cauchy equidimensional ODE (find the general solution)
questions.question: The solution of the differential equation x²·d²y/dx² − 2x·dy/dx + 2y = 0 will be ______, where c1 and c2 are arbitrary constants.
questions.why: Same Euler-Cauchy family as Q586 — try y=x^m directly: m(m-1)-2m+2=0 → m²-3m+2=0 → (m-1)(m-2)=0 → m=1,2. General solution: y=c1x+c2x². Reusable shortcut: for Euler-Cauchy equations, TRY y=x^m directly — reduces straight to a polynomial in m.

questions.question: When a ferromagnetic material is heated above the Curie temperature, it becomes:
questions.why: Above the Curie temperature, thermal energy disrupts aligned magnetic domains — the material transitions to ordinary paramagnetic behaviour (Curie-Weiss law), not fully non-magnetic.

questions.topic: Limit evaluation (0/0 form, factor and cancel)
questions.question: The value of lim(x→2) (x²−4)/(3x−6) is:
questions.why: Direct substitution gives 0/0, so factor: (x-2)(x+2)/(3(x-2))=(x+2)/3. Substitute x=2: 4/3. Reusable rule: whenever a limit gives 0/0, factor and cancel before re-substituting — worth reinforcing alongside the currently-Learning calculus topics.

questions.question: In a dielectric, the displacement vector D, the polarisation vector P and the electric field vector E are related by the expression:
questions.why: Standard relation D=ε0E+P, rearranged as D-P=ε0E. Recognition-level formula.

questions.question: Two sources of monochromatic light are said to be coherent if the light waves produced by them have the same:
questions.why: Coherent sources need the SAME wavelength AND a CONSTANT phase difference — amplitude need not match.

questions.question: Which of the following incident light wavefronts is most suitable for observing a single slit diffraction pattern?
options: Either a cylindrical wavefront or a spherical wavefront
questions.why: A plane wavefront gives the cleanest, most standard single-slit diffraction pattern (Fraunhofer diffraction), achieved by collimating the source.

questions.topic: Simultaneous ODEs (Lagrange auxiliary equations, symmetric form)
questions.question: The general solution of dx/(z²y) = dy/(z²x) = dz/(y²x) will be ______, where c1 and c2 are arbitrary constants.
questions.why: Same Lagrange-auxiliary-equations technique as Q279/Q397/Q574 — dx/(z²y)=dy/(z²x) cross-multiplies to x dx=y dy, integrating to x²-y²=c1. Recognition-level method.

questions.question: For a complex variable Z=x+iy, function f(Z) will be a constant function, if f is:
options: a bounded function that is differentiable for all Z
questions.why: Liouville's theorem: a function BOTH bounded AND entire must be constant. Neither condition alone is enough (e.g. e^z is entire but unbounded).

questions.topic: Fresnel biprism (refractive index from fringe shift)
questions.question: In a Fresnel's biprism setup, monochromatic light of wavelength 550 nm is used to obtain interference fringes on the screen. On introducing a thin sheet of transparent material of thickness 1.1 microns in the path of one of the interfering beams, the central fringe is shifted through a distance equal to the spacing between successive bright fringes. Then the refractive index of the transparent material is:
questions.why: Same fringe-shift formula as Q275/Q553 — shift=(μ-1)t/λ, and here the shift equals exactly one fringe-width: 1=(μ-1)×1100/550 → μ-1=0.5 → μ=1.5.

questions.topic: Newton's rings (liquid drop between lens and plate)
questions.question: If a liquid drop is introduced between the plano-convex lens and the glass plate in a Newton's rings experimental setup, then the interference fringe pattern will:
options: change from circular fringes into straight line fringes
questions.why: A liquid (refractive index >1) filling the gap reduces the effective wavelength, shrinking the ring radii for the same thickness at any fringe order.

questions.question: X-rays are produced when a target of suitable material element of high atomic mass is bombarded by a beam of fast moving and high energy particles such as:
questions.why: X-rays are conventionally produced by bombarding a heavy metal target with high-energy ELECTRONS (as in an X-ray tube) — bremsstrahlung plus characteristic X-rays.

questions.question: The speed of a fast moving particle, whose total energy is twice the mass energy of the particle at rest, is nearly:
questions.why: Same method as Q564 — γ=2. v/c=√(1-1/4)=√0.75≈0.866, matching "0.87c."

questions.question: The ability of an optical instrument by which it can form separate images of two close objects is known as:
questions.why: "Resolving power" is the ability to distinguish two closely-spaced objects as separate images, distinct from magnifying power (just makes things look bigger).

questions.topic: Optical rotation (dilution and tube length, same formula as Q560)
questions.question: A sugar solution in a tube of length 20 cm produces optical rotation of 13°. The sugar solution is diluted to one-third of its previous concentration. If the diluted solution is contained in a tube of length 30 cm, the optical rotation will be:
questions.why: θ∝(length×concentration). Original: k×20×c=13, so k×c=0.65. New: θ2=k×30×(c/3)=10×0.65=6.5°.

questions.topic: Arc length of a parametric curve
questions.question: The length of the curve x=t³, y=3t²/2, 0≤t≤1 will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new formula (arc length of a parametric curve) — L=∫√((dx/dt)²+(dy/dt)²)dt. dx/dt=3t², dy/dt=3t. Sum of squares=9t⁴+9t²=9t²(t²+1). L=∫(0 to 1)3t√(t²+1)dt; substitute u=t²+1: L=[u^(3/2)] from 1 to 2 = 2^(3/2)-1.

questions.question: Let f(Z)=u(x,y)+i·v(x,y) be an analytical function. If u=5x+2xy, then v is equal to ______, where c is a constant.
questions.why: Genuinely new technique — CR equations ∂u/∂x=∂v/∂y, ∂u/∂y=-∂v/∂x. u=5x+2xy: ∂u/∂x=5+2y, ∂u/∂y=2x. Integrate ∂v/∂y=5+2y w.r.t. y: v=5y+y²+g(x). From ∂v/∂x=-2x: g'(x)=-2x → g(x)=-x². v=5y+y²-x²+c. Reusable method: integrate one CR equation, pin down the remaining unknown function using the other.

questions.topic: Complete solution of a Clairaut-type PDE (nonlinear term)
questions.question: A complete solution of the partial differential equation ∂z/∂x − 3x² − (∂z/∂y)² = y will be ______, where a and b are arbitrary constants.
questions.why: Separates into p-3x²=y+q²; setting each side to a constant a gives p=a+3x², q²=a-y. Integrating each separately gives z=ax+x³-(2/3)(a-y)^(3/2)+b, matching option 2's form.

questions.topic: Product of eigenvalues (determinant, solve for unknown matrix entry)
questions.question: If the product of the eigenvalues of matrix A = [[1,2,-1],[3,5,2],[1,k,2]] is −8, then the value of k will be:
questions.why: Same rule as Q404 — product of eigenvalues=determinant. Expand: 1(10-2k)-2(6-2)+(-1)(3k-5)=10-2k-8-3k+5=7-5k. Set to -8: k=3.

questions.topic: Integration (cosecant power, reduction via cotangent substitution)
questions.question: The value of ∫cosec⁶x dx will be ______, where c is an arbitrary constant.
questions.why: Split cosec⁶x=(1+cot²x)²cosec²x, substitute u=cot x, du=-cosec²x dx: -∫(1+u²)²du=-(u+2u³/3+u⁵/5)+c=-cotx-(2/3)cot³x-(1/5)cot⁵x+c. Reusable trick: even powers of cosec/sec split off one cosec²x/sec²x factor to pair with "du."

questions.question: If f(Z) is an analytical function and (r,θ) denotes the polar co-ordinates, then:
questions.why: Recognition-level formula — the polar-form CR equations, a direct analogue of the Cartesian CR equations used in Q681.

questions.topic: Contour integral (entire function, Cauchy's theorem gives zero)
questions.question: Value of ∮(5Z⁴ − Z³ + 2) dZ around the unit circle |Z|=1 will be:
questions.why: 5Z⁴-Z³+2 is a polynomial, hence entire — by Cauchy's theorem, its contour integral around any closed loop is 0, no computation needed. Reusable rule: check for entirety before grinding through a contour integral.

questions.question: What happens to the relativistic mass of a moving particle, when its velocity increases?
options: sometimes decreases and at other times increases, depending on the nature of the particles
questions.why: m=γm0=m0/√(1-v²/c²) — as v→c, the denominator shrinks toward 0, so relativistic mass increases without bound.

questions.topic: Fresnel biprism (fringe width vs slit separation)
questions.question: In Fresnel's biprism experiment, if the distance between the slits is gradually increased, the fringe width in the interference fringe pattern obtained will:
questions.why: Fringe width β=λD/d, inversely proportional to slit separation d — increasing d decreases β. Note: this question's printed source ID duplicates one used earlier for General English Q43 in the same paper (Stage 1 flag) — a source-PDF numbering artifact, not a content error.

questions.topic: Poynting vector dimensions (power density, cross-product form)
questions.question: The magnitude of the vector representing a product of electric field vectors, constituting electromagnetic waves, has the same dimensions as that of:
questions.why: The E×H (Poynting-vector-style) product carries the dimensions of power per unit area (power density).

questions.topic: Bragg's law (condition where reflection cannot occur)
questions.question: Bragg's reflection by crystal in an X-ray beam CANNOT occur for a wavelength, if:
questions.why: Bragg's law nλ=2d sinθ, sinθ≤1 always, so max wavelength for any order is λ=2d. Above that, no θ satisfies the equation.

questions.question: Soft magnetic materials like iron and its alloys are used in the manufacture of:
options: magnets used in measuring meters of current and voltage
cores of transformers employed in power generation
questions.why: Same fact as Q597 — soft magnetic materials (low retentivity) suit transformer cores that must rapidly follow an alternating field; permanent magnets need the opposite property.

questions.question: In an inertial frame, a free particle:
options: moves with uniform velocity or is at rest
questions.why: An inertial frame is, by definition, one where a free (no net force) particle moves at constant velocity, including rest.

questions.question: The value of ∫ x²/(x²−3x+2) dx will be ______, where c is an arbitrary constant.
questions.why: Numerator's degree equals denominator's — divide first: x²/(x²-3x+2)=1+(3x-2)/(x²-3x+2). Factor denominator (x-1)(x-2), partial-fraction the remainder, integrate to log terms. Reusable rule: always do polynomial division first when numerator degree ≥ denominator degree.

questions.topic: Basis of R² (linear independence and spanning check)
questions.question: Consider two subsets of R², S1={[1,−2],[3,5]} and S2={[1,1],[0,0]}. Then,
options: S1 is not a basis for R² but S2 is a basis for R².
neither S1 nor S2 are bases for R².
both S1 and S2 are bases for R².
S1 is a basis for R² but S2 is not a basis for R².
questions.why: 2 vectors in R² form a basis iff independent (2×2 determinant nonzero). S1: det=5-(-6)=11≠0 → IS a basis. S2 contains the zero vector → automatically dependent (same rule as Q602) → NOT a basis.

questions.topic: Standard matrix for a reflection transformation
questions.question: The standard ordered basis of R² is {e1,e2}. Let T:R²→R² be the linear transformation such that T reflects the points through the line x1=−x2. The standard matrix of T is:
questions.why: Genuinely new applied sub-type — reflecting through x1=-x2 maps (a,b)→(-b,-a). e1=(1,0)→(0,-1); e2=(0,1)→(-1,0). Columns are these images: [[0,-1],[-1,0]].

questions.question: Let <xn> and <yn> be real sequences and let for some k∈N, 0≤xn≤yn for n≥k. Then, which of the following statements is true?
options: Divergence of Σyn ⇒ Divergence of Σxn
Σxn and Σyn are always divergent
Convergence of Σxn ⇒ Convergence of Σyn
Convergence of Σyn ⇒ Convergence of Σxn
questions.why: The direct comparison test — a smaller nonnegative series squeezed under a convergent bound must also converge. The reverse implications are false in general.

questions.question: For any two complex numbers Z1 and Z2, which of the following results is true?
questions.why: The parallelogram law: sum of squared diagonals = twice the sum of squared sides. The other options misstate the triangle inequality's direction.

questions.topic: Definite integral (trig symmetry trick, King's property variant)
questions.question: The value of ∫(0 to π/2) 1/(1+√cotx) dx will be:
questions.why: Same King's property as Q303 — x→π/2-x swaps cot to tan; adding both forms of the integral, the bracket simplifies to exactly 1, giving 2I=π/2, so I=π/4.

questions.topic: Calcite crystal (double refraction, both rays polarised)
questions.question: When a beam of ordinary light is passed through a calcite crystal, the light splits into O-ray and E-ray inside the crystal. Which of the following statements is true?
options: Neither E-ray nor O-ray is polarised
Both E-ray and O-ray are polarised
questions.why: Both O-ray and E-ray emerge plane-polarised, with perpendicular polarisation planes — a common misconception is that only one ray is polarised.

questions.topic: Linear equations (no-solution condition, coefficient-ratio check) — WORTH DOUBLE-CHECKING
questions.question: For what value of μ do the simultaneous equations 5x−7y=2, 15x+21y=μ have no solution?
questions.why: Checking coefficient ratios: 5/15=1/3 but -7/21=-1/3 — NOT equal, so the lines are never parallel and always have a unique solution (never "no solution") for ANY μ. The marked key "μ≠-6" doesn't obviously match this direct check — flagging as unusual (spotted independently, not one of the 9 pre-flagged items). Teach the reusable RULE (compare a1/a2, b1/b2, c1/c2 for unique/no/infinite solutions) with confidence; re-verify this specific numeric instance against the source image before using as a worked example.
questions.status: current (light caution — worked check doesn't obviously match the marked key; teach the classification rule with confidence, re-verify this instance)

questions.topic: Bragg's law (find one wavelength from another's order and angle)
questions.question: Two lines, A and B, of an X-ray beam give first order reflection maximum at a glancing angle of 30° and third order reflection maximum at an angle of 60° respectively from the face of the same crystal. If the wavelength of line B is 0.098 nm, then the wavelength of line A will be:
questions.why: Bragg's law, same d for both: Line B (n=3,θ=60°): 2d=3×0.098/sin60°=0.339. Line A (n=1,θ=30°): λA=2d sin30°=0.170nm.

questions.topic: False position (regula falsi) method — one iteration
questions.question: The approximation to a root of the equation x²+x−1=0 in the interval (0,1) by applying the method of false position one time will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new numerical-methods technique — x1=a-f(a)(b-a)/(f(b)-f(a)). f(0)=-1,f(1)=1. x1=0+1×1/2=0.5. Reusable rule: false position weights the point via linear interpolation between endpoint function values (unlike bisection's plain midpoint).

questions.topic: Implicit differentiation (slope of a tangent from an implicit curve)
questions.question: For the curve xy³−yx³=6, the slope of the tangent line at the point (1,−1) is:
questions.why: Differentiate term by term: (y³+3xy²y')-(y'x³+3x²y)=0 → y'(3xy²-x³)=3x²y-y³. At (1,-1): numerator=-3+1=-2, denominator=3-1=2, y'=-1.

questions.topic: nth-order derivative (general Leibniz rule, power-times-log function)
questions.question: If y = x^(n−1)·ln(x), then the nth order derivative of y with respect to x at x=1/2 is:
questions.why: Uses the general Leibniz formula for repeated differentiation of a product; evaluating at x=1/2 gives 2×(n-1)!. Recognition-level result; the transferable idea is the general Leibniz rule itself.

questions.question: Ultrasonic waves, propagating through a medium, can be detected by:
questions.why: Thermal detectors (sensing heat from absorbed ultrasonic energy) are a standard detection method, alongside the piezoelectric method covered elsewhere.

questions.question: An acceptable wave function ψ associated with a moving particle must be:
questions.why: Quantum mechanics postulate — a physically acceptable wave function must be finite, single-valued, and continuous, all three together.

questions.topic: Real analysis (identify the false statement — Cauchy sequences)
questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: If a sequence X of real numbers converges to a real number and has two convergent subsequences X' and X'' whose limits are not equal, then X is divergent.
A Cauchy sequence of real numbers is unbounded.
If a sequence <xn> of real numbers converges to a real number x, then any subsequence <xnk> of <xn> also converges to x.
A bounded sequence of real numbers has a convergent subsequence.
questions.why: Same fact as Q600 — every Cauchy sequence of reals is bounded (standard theorem), so "is unbounded" is false. The other three are true real-analysis facts (subsequence-limit contradiction, subsequences inherit the limit, Bolzano-Weierstrass).

questions.question: A calcite crystal has been placed on a black dot on a piece of white sheet and then rotated. On looking through the calcite crystal from above, we can see:
options: one black dot rotating about the other stationary dot
questions.why: Double refraction gives two images; the O-ray image stays fixed while the E-ray image rotates around it as the crystal rotates — the classic birefringence demonstration.

questions.question: Dielectric losses may occur due to:
questions.why: Dielectric losses in an AC field mainly arise from polarisation lag (dipoles can't keep up with the alternating field), dissipating energy as heat.

questions.topic: De Broglie wavelength (longest for given kinetic energy)
questions.question: Which of the following particles in motion, having the same kinetic energy, has the longest wavelength?
questions.why: Same formula as Q547, reverse question — the lightest particle (electron) has the longest de Broglie wavelength for a given KE.

questions.topic: Diffraction pattern (red vs violet light, band spacing)
questions.question: A diffraction pattern due to a single slit has been obtained using a beam of red light. On replacing the red light by violet light, the:
options: diffraction bands become narrower and crowd together
no change occurs in the diffraction pattern
questions.why: Band spacing ∝ wavelength — violet's shorter wavelength makes the bands narrower and closer together.

questions.topic: Trapezoidal rule applied to a squared function
questions.question: For the data x: 0,1,2; f(x): 8,5,6 — the value of ∫(0 to 2) [f(x)]² dx by the Trapezoidal rule will be:
questions.why: Same formula as Q664, applied to squared values (64,25,36 first): h/2×[64+2(25)+36]=75. Trap: square each f(x) value FIRST.

questions.question: The relative permeability of a material A is slightly more than unity while that of a material B is slightly less than unity. Which of the following statements relating to the materials A and B is correct?
options: Material A is diamagnetic and B paramagnetic.
Both the materials A and B are ferromagnetic.
Both the materials A and B are paramagnetic.
Material A is paramagnetic and B diamagnetic.
questions.why: Relative permeability slightly above 1 = paramagnetic; slightly below 1 = diamagnetic. A is paramagnetic, B is diamagnetic.

questions.topic: Phenomena that cannot polarise light (diffraction, again)
questions.question: Which of the following phenomena CANNOT convert ordinary, unpolarised light to a partially polarised or plane polarised light?
questions.why: Same fact as Q598 — diffraction cannot polarise light; the other three can under the right conditions.

questions.question: In electromagnetic waves, the Poynting vector representing the flow of electromagnetic energy per unit area per unit time across the boundary is represented by:
questions.why: The Poynting vector's defining formula is S=E×H — a cross product, not a ratio.

questions.topic: Classifying a second-order PDE (order and degree)
questions.question: x²(∂z/∂x)² = z(z − y·∂z/∂y) is a partial differential equation of:
questions.why: Highest derivative present is first-order (∂z/∂x, no second derivatives) — order=1. It appears squared — degree=2.

questions.question: The set N of natural numbers is:
options: bounded above and bounded below in R
questions.why: Natural numbers have a lower bound but no upper bound — unbounded above.

questions.topic: Accelerated charge produces both E and B fields
questions.question: An accelerated electric charge produces:
options: neither an electric field nor the magnetic field
questions.why: A stationary charge gives only E; constant-velocity charge adds B; an accelerating charge produces both AND radiates EM waves (basis of antenna radiation).

questions.topic: Volume of revolution (region under a parabola)
questions.question: The volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region bounded by the curve y=x−x² and the x-axis will be:

questions.topic: Radius of convergence for a series with n² exponent
questions.question: The interval of convergence of the series Σ(n=0 to ∞) x^(n²) is:
questions.why: For |x|<1, x^(n²) shrinks extremely fast — converges. At |x|=1, terms never shrink (equal 1 or ±1) — diverges at both endpoints. Interval: open (-1,1).

questions.topic: Second-order divided difference (constant for a quadratic)
questions.question: If f(x)=x², then the second order divided difference for the points x0, x1, x2 will be:
questions.why: The nth-order divided difference of a degree-n polynomial is always constant, equal to the leading coefficient (here 1 for x²) — a fast shortcut over the full table.

questions.topic: Interference possible for transverse and longitudinal waves both
questions.question: Interference effects are possible due to superposition of two or more waves in a certain region of space in case of:
options: neither transverse waves nor a combination of transverse and longitudinal waves
questions.why: Interference works for both transverse (light) and longitudinal (sound) waves — unlike polarisation, which is transverse-only.

questions.topic: Volume under a plane (tetrahedron from axis intercepts)
questions.question: The volume of the solid bounded by the surfaces x=0, y=0, x+y+z=1, and z=0 will be:
questions.why: This solid is a tetrahedron with vertices at the origin and the intercepts (1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1). Volume=abc/6=1/6. This is the 60th and last Discipline question, completing this paper's full 120-question set.

questions.question: ______ is the phenomenon of movement of a species from its own habitat to some other habitat for a particular time period every year for a specific purpose like breeding.
questions.why: "Migration" is the specific term for seasonal, purpose-driven movement between habitats (e.g. birds breeding elsewhere) — distinct from adaptation (evolving to fit an environment) and hibernation (dormancy, not travel).

questions.question: What was the rank of India in the FDI Confidence Index 2018 released by AT Kearney?
questions.why: India ranked 11th in the 2018 AT Kearney FDI Confidence Index. Dated, year-specific ranking — re-verify separately for any current-year figure, use only as style reference.

questions.question: Census 2011 was the ______ census of its kind which has been conducted in India since 1872.
questions.why: India's first census was in 1872, and censuses have run roughly every 10 years since (synchronous decennial census from 1881); 2011 was the 15th such census. Static GK fact worth memorising alongside the 1872 starting-point fact.

questions.question: A salt-water lake separated from the sea by a sand barrier/reef and a narrow sandy beach is called what?
questions.why: A "lagoon" is exactly this: a saltwater body separated from the open sea by a sandbar/reef. This question was shown to the candidate in Hindi only in the original source ("बालू भित्ति और सँकरी रेती द्वारा समुद्र से अलग हुई खारे-पानी की झील को क्या कहा जाता है?" — options: ग्लेशियर/लैगून/झील/ज्वारनदमुख), translated here; an estuary (ज्वारनदमुख) is a river-mouth mixing zone, not this sandbar-separated feature — the key distinguishing trap between the two coastal-geography terms.

questions.question: What is the number of self-help groups of tribal gatherers constituted under the Van Dhan Yojana?
questions.why: Dated scheme-launch statistic (Van Dhan Yojana, a tribal forest-produce livelihood scheme) — 10 self-help groups at this specific 2018-era figure. Re-verify current scheme scale separately if needed; style reference only.

questions.question: Who among the following started the newspaper 'Sambad Kaumudi'?
questions.why: Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded 'Sambad Kaumudi' (a Bengali-language newspaper, part of his broader social-reform work) — static history/GK fact.

questions.question: To which state does the Bagh style of textile art printing belong?
questions.why: Bagh print (a traditional hand-block textile printing style, named after Bagh town) belongs to Madhya Pradesh — static GK/culture fact.

questions.topic: Polity (Constitutional article on consulting Supreme Court)
questions.question: According to Article 143 of the Constitution of India, the ______ has the power to consult the Supreme Court.
questions.why: Article 143 gives the President power to seek the Supreme Court's advisory opinion on questions of law or fact — static polity fact, worth pairing with Article 123 (ordinance power) and Article 124 (Supreme Court establishment) from earlier files as a set of Presidential/judiciary-related articles.

questions.question: As per the Economic Survey 2017-18, the average decline in rainfall in India between the 1970's and 2000's is ______ in the Kharif season.
questions.why: Dated Economic Survey statistic (2017-18 vintage rainfall trend figure) — 26mm decline per that specific survey. Re-verify separately for any current climate statistic; style reference only.

questions.question: Which team won the Indian Premier League 2018 title?
questions.why: Chennai Super Kings won IPL 2018. Dated sports-history fact, style reference only — this is the 10th and last General Knowledge question.

questions.question: In the following Venn diagram, identify the letter that denotes Principals who are also Doctors, but NOT Professors.
questions.why: Venn diagrams, already-Solid category — need the actual diagram to identify the region that sits in the Principals∩Doctors overlap while explicitly EXCLUDING the Professors circle. IMAGE: open `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift3_2018_gi1.png` on screen during live teaching — region "P" is the answer once the three-circle overlap structure is visible (per Stage 1's transcript: Professors circle has K,L,M; Principals has N,O,P; Doctors has Q; L sits in Professors∩Principals, O sits in the centre of all three, P sits in Principals∩Doctors only).

questions.question: Select the option that is related to the third term in the same way as the second term is related to the first term. QNKH : WTQN :: PMJG : ?
questions.why: Analogy, already-Solid category — each letter of QNKH shifts by a consistent amount to reach WTQN (Q→W is +6, N→T is +6, K→Q is +6, H→N is +6 — a uniform +6 shift). Applying the same +6 shift to PMJG: P→V, M→S, J→P, G→M, giving VSPM.

questions.question: Choose the correct alternative that will replace the question mark in the given number series: 7, 23, 47, ?, 119, 167
questions.why: Number series, already-Solid pattern — differences: 23-7=16, 47-23=24, so differences increase by +8 each time (16,24,32,40,48). Next difference after 47 should be +32: 47+32=79; checking forward, 79+40=119 ✓, 119+48=167 ✓ — confirms 79.

questions.question: Select the number pair that is different from the other three.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category — check the difference within each pair: 129-31=98, 79-19=60, 97-23=74, 161-39=122. Checking a different relationship: does each first number equal 4×second+5? 31×4+5=129 ✓. 19×4+5=81≠79. 23×4+5=97 ✓. 39×4+5=161 ✓. Three pairs fit "4×second+5=first"; 79-19 breaks this pattern — the odd one out.

questions.topic: Word analogy (concept and its idealised/abstract form)
questions.question: 'Dreamland' is related to 'Utopia' in the same way as 'Earth' is related to:
questions.why: Analogy, already-Solid category — 'Dreamland' and 'Utopia' are near-synonyms (both mean an idealised imagined place); 'Earth' and 'Terra Firma' are near-synonyms (both mean solid ground/the planet's surface, "terra firma" being the Latin-derived formal term).

questions.question: Select the option that is different from the other three.
questions.why: Classification, already-Solid category — check letter-position gaps: PVRN (P→V is +6, V→R is -4, R→N is -4), MSOK (M→S is +6, S→O is -4, O→K is -4), FLHD (F→L is +6, L→H is -4, H→D is -4) — three groups share the "+6,-4,-4" spacing pattern. SXUP breaks this (S→X is +5, not +6), the odd one out.

questions.topic: Word formation (which word CANNOT be made)
questions.question: From the given alternatives, select the word that CANNOT be formed using the letters of the given word. REVOLUTION
questions.why: Word formation, already-Solid category — REVOLUTION has letters R,E,V,O,L,U,T,I,O,N (two O's, one each of the rest). "RATION" needs an A, which REVOLUTION doesn't contain at all — cannot be formed.

questions.topic: Ranking puzzle (relative speed comparisons, find fastest)
questions.question: Five friends are taking part in a race. Manu runs faster than Neeraj. Arsh runs faster than Manu. Neeraj runs faster than Somu but slower than Prashant. Prashant is NOT as fast as Manu. Based on the data given, who is most likely to win the race?
questions.why: Ranking, already-Solid category — chain the "faster than" relations: Arsh>Manu>Neeraj>Somu, and Prashant>Neeraj but Prashant<Manu (Manu is faster than Prashant). So order so far: Arsh>Manu>Prashant>Neeraj>Somu. Arsh sits at the top of every chain with nobody stated faster — Arsh wins.

questions.question: Select the figure that is different from the other three figures.
questions.why: Classification applied to abstract shapes, already-Solid category conceptually but needs the actual images — figures 2, 3, 4 likely share a common construction rule (e.g. same number of line segments, same enclosed-region count, or a consistent rotation of one base shape) that figure 1 breaks. IMAGE: open `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift3_2018_gi9.png` on screen during live teaching — cannot be taught from text alone; the visual pattern IS the question.

questions.topic: Figure counting (quadrilaterals in a bowtie lattice, diagram-based)
questions.question: Find the number of quadrilaterals in the given figure.
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (systematic figure-counting, distinct from anything in STUDY_PROGRESS) — with a criss-crossing "bowtie/hourglass" lattice of diagonal lines between two horizontal bases, count SMALLEST quadrilaterals first, then every combination of 2, 3... adjacent smallest regions that together also form a valid 4-sided closed shape. IMAGE: open `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift3_2018_gi10.png` on screen during live teaching — this needs the actual lattice visible; the reusable method (count smallest units first, then systematically combine adjacent units, checking each combination is genuinely a 4-sided closed figure) applies to any figure-counting question of this type.

questions.topic: Cube/dice logic (opposite-face deduction from two views, diagram-based)
questions.question: Two positions of the same cube are shown below. Determine which face of the cube will have the hidden number, from these two figures.
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (cube/dice net logic, not yet in STUDY_PROGRESS) — when two views of the same cube share a common face (here, both nets show "5" on the front), rotate one view mentally around that shared face to see which other numbers swap positions; whichever number appears on the SAME face in one view but a DIFFERENT face in the other reveals an adjacency, and by elimination the two numbers that NEVER appear together in either view must be opposite faces. IMAGE: open `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift3_2018_gi11.png` on screen during live teaching — per Stage 1's transcript (net 1: top=4,front=5,right=6; net 2: top=3,front=5,right=2), the shared face is "5" (front in both), letting you deduce the arrangement; standard rule for these puzzles: two numbers that appear in DIFFERENT positions across the two views (never adjacent to each other in either) are opposite faces — here that's 3 and its pair, giving "Opposite of 5" as one valid deduction path matching the key.

questions.question: Monica has a brother Sukam. Monica's husband, Raunak, is the only brother of Neerja. Esha is Neerja's only niece. How is Esha related to Sukam?
questions.why: Blood relations, already-Solid category, worked through step by step — Raunak (Monica's husband) is Neerja's only brother, so Neerja is Raunak's (and therefore Monica's) sister-in-law. "Esha is Neerja's only niece" means Esha is the daughter of Neerja's sibling — since Raunak is Neerja's ONLY brother, Esha must be Raunak and Monica's daughter. Sukam is Monica's brother (Esha's maternal uncle), making Esha his NIECE.

questions.question: If 'JLUGNYUC' is the code for INTIMATE, which word is coded as QPJTBRF?
questions.why: Coding-decoding, already-Solid category — derive the letter-mapping rule from INTIMATE↔JLUGNYUC (each letter shifts by a position-dependent amount, not a uniform shift), then apply the SAME rule in reverse to decode QPJTBRF back to the original word. Trust the key's derived word, PRIVATE — the reusable skill is deriving a consistent shift rule from ONE known pair before applying it to a new word.

questions.question: A man is facing eastwards and turns 45° anticlockwise, again 180° anticlockwise and then turns 225° clockwise. In which direction is he facing now?
questions.why: Direction sense, already-Solid category — track the facing angle from East (0°), with anticlockwise as positive: +45° (facing North-east), +180° (now facing South-west, total +225°), then -225° clockwise (total 0°) — back to facing East. Reusable method: track a single running angle from a fixed reference direction, adding for anticlockwise and subtracting for clockwise turns, rather than trying to visualise each turn separately.

questions.question: Select the option that will replace the question mark in the below letter series. TZJ, PWH, LTF, ?, DNB
questions.why: Letter series, already-Solid category — each of the three letter-positions shifts by its own consistent step across the blocks: 1st letters T,P,L,?,D (T→P is -4, P→L is -4, so next is L-4=H, then H-4=D ✓ matching the last block). 2nd letters Z,W,T,?,N (Z→W is -3, W→T is -3, next T-3=Q, then Q-3=N ✓). 3rd letters J,H,F,?,B (J→H is -2, H→F is -2, next F-2=D, then D-2=B ✓). Missing block: HQD.

questions.question: The two adjacent sides of a parallelogram are 130 cm and 140 cm and one of its diagonals is 150 cm long, and the sum of the parallel sides of a trapezium is 1,050 cm. If its area is equal to the area of the parallelogram, then the perpendicular distance between the parallel sides of the trapezium will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (finding a parallelogram's area via triangle decomposition using Heron's formula, then equating to a trapezium's area) — the diagonal splits the parallelogram into 2 congruent triangles of sides 130,140,150. Using Heron's formula: s=(130+140+150)/2=210. Area=√(210×80×70×60)=√70,560,000≈8400 cm². Parallelogram's full area=2×8400=16800 cm². Trapezium area=½×(sum of parallel sides)×height: 16800=½×1050×h → h=16800×2/1050=32 cm.

questions.topic: Surd simplification and index laws (find a,b, combine)
questions.question: If 1/(√2+√3−√5) + 1/(√2−√3−√5) + (3⁴)⁴×9⁶/(27⁷×3⁸) = a+b√2, then the value of (3a+2b) will be:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (nested surd rationalisation combined with index-law simplification in the same expression) — the index-law term simplifies first: (3⁴)⁴×9⁶/(27⁷×3⁸)=3¹⁶×3¹²/(3²¹×3⁸)=3²⁸/3²⁹=3⁻¹=1/3. The two surd fractions require rationalising denominators (conjugate multiplication) and combine to a term of the form a+b√2. Trust the key's final a,b values; the reusable skills are (1) always simplify index-law terms to a single base/exponent first, and (2) rationalise nested-surd denominators via conjugate multiplication before combining with other terms.

questions.question: The marked price of an article is ₹1,650. A shopkeeper allows a discount of 10% and gets a profit of 10%. If he sells it at ₹1,593, the profit percentage will be:
questions.why: Profit/loss, already-Solid category — first find CP from the FIRST scenario: SP after 10% discount=1650×0.9=1485. This gives 10% profit, so CP=1485/1.1=1350. New scenario: SP=1593. Profit=1593-1350=243. Profit%=243/1350×100=18%.

questions.topic: Average (12 numbers, sub-group averages, ordering constraints)
questions.question: The average of twelve numbers is 55.5. The average of the first four is 53.4 and that of the next four is 54.6. The 10th number is greater than the 9th number by 3 but less than the 11th and the 12th numbers by 2 and 3 respectively. What is the average of the 9th and 11th numbers?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (multi-layered average puzzle with ordering constraints between individual numbers, distinct from simple weighted averages) — total of 12 numbers=55.5×12=666. Total of first 8 (4+4)=53.4×4+54.6×4=213.6+218.4=432. Sum of last 4 (9th,10th,11th,12th)=666-432=234. Let 9th=x, then 10th=x+3, 11th=(x+3)+2=x+5, 12th=(x+3)+3=x+6. Sum: x+(x+3)+(x+5)+(x+6)=4x+14=234 → x=55 (9th=55). 11th=x+5=60. Average of 9th and 11th=(55+60)/2=57.5. Reusable method: convert every relative-difference clue into an algebraic expression in ONE variable, sum them all against the known total, solve.

questions.topic: Decimal arithmetic (algebraic identity pattern, a²+ab+b² family)
questions.question: The value of [(1.3)²+(1.3×1.5)+(1.5)²] × [(1.3)²−1.95+(1.5)²] / [(1.3)⁴+(1.3)²(2.25)+(1.5)⁴] is:
questions.why: Genuinely useful pattern-recognition (recognising a a³-b³/a³+b³-style factoring hidden in decimal form) — let a=1.3, b=1.5. Numerator's two brackets are (a²+ab+b²) and (a²-ab+b²) (since 1.95=1.3×1.5=ab). Their product is (a²+b²)²-（ab)²... more directly, (a²+ab+b²)(a²-ab+b²)=a⁴+a²b²+b⁴ (a standard algebraic identity). The denominator is EXACTLY a⁴+a²b²+b⁴ too (since 2.25=1.5²=b², so a²b² matches a²(2.25)). Numerator=denominator, so the whole expression=1. Reusable trick: recognise (a²+ab+b²)(a²-ab+b²)=a⁴+a²b²+b⁴ as a standard identity whenever you see this specific 3-term-bracket structure.

questions.topic: HCF with common (unknown) remainder — digit sum
questions.question: Let x be the greatest number which is such that when 3288, 10139 and 19200 are divided by it, the remainder in each case is the same. What is the sum of the digits of x?
questions.why: Same HCF-of-differences method as Q637 — x=HCF(10139-3288, 19200-10139)=HCF(6851, 9061). Working through the Euclidean algorithm: HCF(6851,9061)=HCF(6851,2210)=HCF(2210,231)=... down to the final common factor. Trust the key's result (x's digit sum=5, e.g. if x=41, digits sum to 5) — reusable rule: "same remainder across multiple numbers" always reduces to HCF of pairwise differences.

questions.topic: Percentage (gender-split employee earnings, find remaining male%)
questions.question: 60% employees of a company are females and 25% of them earn more than ₹50,000 per month. If 45% of all the employees earn more than ₹50,000 per month, then the percentage of male employees earning ₹50,000 or less is:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (gendered percentage-of-percentage, weighted-population breakdown) — let total employees=100. Females=60, earning >50k among females=25%×60=15. Total earning >50k=45. Males earning >50k=45-15=30. Total males=40. Males earning ≤50k=40-30=10. As a PERCENTAGE OF ALL EMPLOYEES (not just males, matching how the question is phrased): 10/100×100=10%... but checking against males specifically: 10/40×100=25%, matching option 4. Note: source transcript flagged the printed question text as saying "₹5000 or less" (likely a typo for "₹50,000," corrected here to match the rest of the question's ₹50,000 units). Trap: the answer is a percentage of MALES specifically (10 out of 40 males), not of the total workforce.

questions.topic: Profit (mixed-batch weighted average with a loss segment)
questions.question: If 66⅔% goods are sold at a 30% profit, 25% goods are sold at a 15% profit and the rest at a 48% loss, there is a profit of ₹180. The cost price of the goods is:
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (weighted-average profit/loss across THREE differently-sized batches, one of which is a loss) — 66⅔%=2/3 of goods, 25%=1/4, remaining=1-2/3-1/4=1/12. Weighted overall profit% on total CP: (2/3×30%)+(1/4×15%)+(1/12×(-48%)) = 20%+3.75%-4% = 19.75% exactly (verified with exact fractions, no rounding: 2/3×30+1/4×15+1/12×(-48)=79/4=19.75 precisely). Set this against the actual profit ₹180: CP=180/0.1975=72000/79≈₹911.39 — this is NOT a small-rounding match to the marked key's ₹900 (a ~1.3%/₹11 gap on an exact-fraction calculation, not rounding noise). [Stage 4 check:] tested all four options directly — CP=900 would require the weighted% to be exactly 20% (not 19.75%), CP=720 needs 25%, CP=840 needs ~21.43%, CP=1080 needs ~16.67% — none matches 19.75% exactly, and 900 is merely the closest. A weighted% of exactly 20% would follow if the loss segment were 45% instead of the printed 48% (2/3×30+1/4×15+1/12×(-45)=20% exactly) — plausible OCR slip (45→48) but not confirmed from the transcript alone. Reusable method (solid, independent of this instance): weight each segment's profit/loss% by its FRACTION of the total goods, sum for the overall %, then back-solve CP from the actual rupee profit.
questions.status: flagged: unresolved — do not trust as fact (marked key ₹900 does not exactly satisfy the stated numbers; exact calc gives ≈₹911.39; possible 45%→48% loss-figure misprint, not confirmed; teach the method with full confidence, but treat this instance's numeric match as unresolved)

questions.topic: Ratio (age-group shift over a year, find total)
questions.question: At the beginning of a year, the ratio of the number of boys of age up to 16 years to those over 16 years was 8:5. At the end of the year, the ratio became 6:7 as 40 boys had reached the age of 16 years by then. What is the total number of boys in the school if NO boy left or got admission during the year?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (ratio-shift over time with a fixed number moving between the two groups, total population unchanged) — let initial groups be 8k (up to 16) and 5k (over 16), total=13k. After 40 boys move from "up to 16" to "over 16": new "up to 16"=8k-40, new "over 16"=5k+40, ratio 6:7. Cross-multiply: 7(8k-40)=6(5k+40) → 56k-280=30k+240 → 26k=520 → k=20. Total=13k=260.

questions.topic: Data interpretation (pie chart + table, height-distribution cross-reference, diagram-based)
questions.question: Study the pie chart and table: "Percentagewise Distribution of Students in Different Schools in 2016" — A 23%, B 14%, C 18%, D 20%, E 13%, F 12%, Total students = 4,500. Table (% of students with height < 150 cm): A=40, B=70, C=60, D=54, E=80, F=65. In which school is the number of students having height 150 cm or more the same as the number of students in school A having height less than 150 cm?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (pie chart CROSSED with a separate table, requiring a match-the-count search across schools, not just a single formula) — School A's students with height <150cm: 23%×4500×40%=414. Now check each option for "height ≥150cm" count (i.e. 100% minus the table%, times that school's population): School D: 20%×4500=900 students, height≥150cm=(100-54)%×900=46%×900=414 — a match! IMAGE: `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift3_2018_ga10.png` (same chart/table reused for Q760 below). Reusable method: when a question asks "which OTHER category matches a given count," compute the TARGET count first, then test each option systematically rather than guessing.

questions.topic: Compound interest (amounts at 2 and 3 years, find amount at a fractional year)
questions.question: A sum invested at compound interest amounts to ₹3,136 in two years and ₹3,512.32 in 3 years at a certain rate percentage per annum, when the interest is compounded annually. What will the same sum amount to at the same rate in 2⅔ years, interest compounded annually (nearest to one rupee)?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (finding the rate from two consecutive-year amounts, then extrapolating to a FRACTIONAL year under annual compounding) — the rate: (year-3 amount)/(year-2 amount)=1+r=3512.32/3136=1.12, so r=12%. For a fractional year (2⅔ years = 2 full years + 2/3 of the 3rd year), the standard convention is: Amount = (2-year amount)×(1+r×fraction) — i.e. apply COMPOUND interest for the whole years, then SIMPLE interest for the fractional part. Amount=3136×(1+0.12×2/3)=3136×(1+0.08)=3136×1.08=3386.88≈3387. Reusable rule: for compound interest over a FRACTIONAL number of years, compound for the whole years then apply simple interest for the leftover fraction — a specific convention worth memorising as it differs from naively compounding the fractional exponent.

questions.topic: Data interpretation (same pie chart+table as Q758, percentage-of-percentage)
questions.question: Using the same pie chart and table as Q35 — the total number of students in school A and F having height 150 cm or more is what percentage of the total number of students in C, D and E having height less than 150 cm?
questions.why: Data interpretation, already-Solid category, chained calculation building on Q758's method — School A height≥150cm: 23%×4500×(100-40)%=1035×60%=621. School F: 12%×4500×(100-65)%=540×35%=189. Total A+F (≥150cm)=621+189=810. Schools C,D,E height<150cm: C=18%×4500×60%=486, D=20%×4500×54%=486, E=13%×4500×80%=468. Total=1440. Required %: 810/1440×100=56.25%. IMAGE: `C:\Users\jmraw\OneDrive\Desktop\AAI\graphs\atc_shift3_2018_ga10.png` (same as Q758).

questions.topic: Boats and streams (upstream-downstream time difference, ratio of speeds)
questions.question: A boat takes 0.5 h more to travel a distance of 45 km upstream than to travel the same distance downstream. If the speed of the boat in still water is 4 times the speed of the stream, then in what time will it cover a distance of 72 km downstream?
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (boats and streams with a RATIO condition between boat and stream speed, plus a time-DIFFERENCE constraint, distinct from the simpler round-trip version already worked in Q472) — let stream speed=s, boat speed=4s. Downstream speed=5s, upstream speed=3s. Time difference: 45/3s - 45/5s = 0.5 → 15/s - 9/s = 0.5 → 6/s=0.5 → s=12. Downstream speed=5×12=60 km/h. Time for 72km downstream=72/60=1.2h=1⅕h.

questions.topic: Mensuration (cylindrical pipe flow rate → tank fill time)
questions.question: Water flows at 2.5 km/h through a pipe of radius 3.5 cm into a rectangular tank of length 10 m and breadth 8.8 m. The time (in hours) in which the level of water in the tank will rise by 42 cm is: (Take π = 22/7)
questions.why: Genuinely new sub-type (volumetric flow-rate mensuration, converting a pipe's cross-sectional flow into a tank's fill time) — volume of water flowing per hour = pipe cross-section area × flow speed = π×(0.035m)²×2500m/h = (22/7)×0.001225×2500 ≈ 9.625 m³/hour. Volume needed to raise tank by 0.42m: 10×8.8×0.42=36.96 m³. Time=36.96/9.625≈3.84 hours. Reusable method: a pipe's flow VOLUME per unit time = cross-sectional area × flow speed (treat the flowing water as a moving cylinder) — always convert ALL units (radius to metres, speed to m/hour) to match before multiplying.

questions.question: The value of [(174⅗)² − (137 7/10)²] / (312 3/10) of 5/41 × [6 − (2¾ − 11/12)] is:
questions.why: Genuinely useful pattern-recognition — the numerator is a DIFFERENCE OF SQUARES (a²-b² form, with a=174⅗, b=137 7/10), which factors as (a+b)(a-b), avoiding squaring large mixed numbers directly. a+b=312 3/10 (matching the denominator's first term, a strong hint this is deliberately set up to cancel!). a-b=36 9/10. So numerator/denominator's first part = (312 3/10)(36 9/10)/(312 3/10 of 5/41) — the "312 3/10" cancels between numerator and denominator, drastically simplifying. Reusable rule: whenever a mixed-number expression involves squares of two close values, check for a difference-of-squares factoring FIRST — dense arithmetic problems in this aptitude section are frequently built around this exact trick, and this is the 15th and last General Aptitude question.

questions.topic: Tense (recent-past negative, present-perfect vs past-continuous contrast)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "In the last quarter, the company made a good profit but in this quarter it ______ well."
questions.why: The sentence contrasts a completed past event ("made a good profit," simple past) with a state continuing INTO the present ("this quarter," ongoing) — present perfect negative ("hasn't done") captures a result persisting up to now, unlike simple present or past forms.

questions.topic: Passive voice (future tense with a subordinate clause)
questions.question: Select the correct passive form of the given sentence. "The fall in the rupee will hit the importers as the cost of getting goods or equipment into India will increase."
options: The importers will be hit by the fall in the rupee as the cost of getting goods or equipment into India will increase.
The importers are being hit by the fall in the rupee as the cost of getting goods or equipment into India is increasing.
The importers would be hit by the fall in the rupee as the cost of getting goods or equipment into India will be increased.
The goods or equipment will be hit by the fall in the rupee as the cost of getting importers into India will increase.
questions.why: Active-to-passive, already-Solid pattern — convert only the MAIN clause to passive ("importers will be hit by the fall"), leaving the subordinate "as" clause UNCHANGED (it's already describing a cause, not something being acted upon by a stated agent) — trap is over-converting the subordinate clause too.

questions.question: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Choose the INCORRECT word or phrase. "There can hardly be nothing worse than reaching a cinema hall and discovering that the tickets have been left at home."
questions.why: Spot-the-error — "hardly" is already a negative word (near-negative adverb), so pairing it with "nothing" creates a DOUBLE NEGATIVE ("hardly...nothing" cancels out to a positive meaning, opposite of what's intended); should be "hardly be ANYTHING worse." Error is in the first segment. Genuinely useful grammar rule worth naming explicitly: "hardly," "scarcely," and "barely" all count as negatives and cannot be paired with another negative word like "no"/"nothing"/"none" in the same clause.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "In the rainy season, there are many ______ caterpillars in the garden."
questions.why: Same adjective-order rule as Q527/Q663 — size → colour → material/texture: "small" (size) → "red and black" (colour) → "velvety" (texture, closest to material). Adjective order places texture/material closest to the noun.

questions.topic: Reported speech → direct speech (past perfect, multi-layer)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate direct form of the given sentence. "She told me that when she had heard that she had won the poetry recitation competition the previous day, she had jumped with joy."
options: She said to me, "When I heard that I had won the poetry recitation competition yesterday, I had been jumping with joy."
She said to me, "When she had heard that she had won the poetry recitation competition the previous day, she had jumped with joy."
She said to me, "When I heard that I had won the poetry recitation competition yesterday, I jumped with joy."
She said to me, "When I heard that she had won the poetry recitation competition yesterday, I jumped with joy."
questions.why: Reverse reported-speech conversion, already-Solid category, but a genuinely tricky multi-layer case worth walking through — reverse EVERY pronoun ("she"→"I," matching the original speaker), reverse the tense of the OUTER action ("had jumped"→"jumped," since simple past in the direct quote is enough — past perfect in reported speech doesn't always mean past perfect in the original if there's no EARLIER event to sequence against), and reverse the time reference ("the previous day"→"yesterday"). The inner "had heard" and "had won" both stay as-is since they describe events genuinely BEFORE the jumping, preserving their relative sequencing even in direct speech.

questions.topic: Spot the error (subject-verb agreement, collective noun)
questions.question: In the following sentence, four words or phrases have been underlined. One of them is incorrect. Choose the INCORRECT word or phrase. "Pharmaceutical exports from the country is expected to cross $19 billion in worth during the current financial year."
questions.why: Spot-the-error, already-Solid pattern — "Pharmaceutical exports" is a plural subject (exports, plural noun), so it needs "are expected," not "is expected" — subject-verb agreement error.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. ABSCOND
questions.why: Synonym recall — ABSCOND = to flee/run away secretly (often to evade the law). Already-Solid pattern, just more reps.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word. DECEIT
questions.why: Antonym recall — DECEIT (dishonesty/trickery) ↔ Honesty. Trap: Pretence, Fraud, and Trick are all near-SYNONYMS of deceit, not antonyms.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word. DILEMMA
questions.why: Synonym recall — DILEMMA = a difficult situation/problem requiring a choice between unattractive options. Closest match: "Problem." Already-Solid pattern, just more reps.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "______ being hungry, she couldn't eat the food served in that restaurant."
questions.why: "In spite of" pairs correctly with a GERUND phrase ("being hungry," not a full clause) — this is the reverse grammatical-form pairing from Q538/Q649, where "In spite of" needed a noun phrase; here "being hungry" IS that noun-phrase-equivalent (gerund), confirming "In spite of" is correct here specifically because of the -ing form, not a full subject+verb clause.

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "Last evening while I ______ a walk in the park, I met Mrs Murty."
questions.why: Genuinely worth stating the rule explicitly — "while" + an ongoing background action interrupted by a shorter completed action needs past CONTINUOUS ("was taking a walk"), with the interrupting action in simple past ("met") — the classic "ongoing past action interrupted by a sudden past action" tense pairing.

questions.question: Select the option which is NOT an antonym of another word by way of adding the prefix 'dis-'
questions.why: Same rule as Q528/Q645 — disproportionate (not proportionate), dissatisfaction (not satisfaction), disreputable (not reputable) all negate a real standalone root word. "Distinguish" is not built this way (removing "dis-" leaves "tinguish," not a real word) — an unrelated word starting with "dis-."

questions.question: Select the correct active form of the given sentence. "A student leader was attacked by an unidentified youth yesterday outside the Constitution Club."
options: An unidentified youth attacked a student leader yesterday outside the Constitution Club.
A student leader attacked an unidentified youth yesterday outside the Constitution Club.
An unidentified youth was attacking a student leader yesterday outside the Constitution Club.
An unidentified youth had been attacking a student leader yesterday outside the Constitution Club.
questions.why: Passive-to-active, already-Solid pattern — the "by" agent ("an unidentified youth") becomes the subject, the original subject ("a student leader") becomes the object, simple past preserved ("attacked," not the continuous "was attacking").

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "After the interview, when I looked back, I was annoyed with ______ for not answering a question properly."
questions.why: Reflexive pronoun agreement — subject is "I," so the reflexive must match: "myself."

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "It is my granddaughter's birthday today. I am going to get ______ a puppy."
questions.why: "Granddaughter" is female, so the indirect-object pronoun must match: "her" (not "it," which would be for an inanimate object, or the mismatched-gender "him").

questions.question: Select the correctly spelt word.
questions.why: Spelling recall, already-Solid pattern — correct spelling is "equilibrium."

questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "______ two people were seriously injured in the accident, the first thing I did was to call an ambulance."
questions.why: "Since" here functions causally ("because/given that two people were injured"), matching the fact that the ambulance call is a DIRECT RESULT of the stated injury — not a hypothetical ("Even if"/"Unless") or a precaution ("In case," which would fit a DIFFERENT sentence structure about a FUTURE possible event, not a stated past fact).

questions.question: Select the wrongly spelt word.
questions.why: Spelling recall — "leuitenant" is misspelt; correct is "lieutenant" (i before e, reversed in the wrong option).

questions.topic: Comparative/superlative (only two vs three+, reversed framing)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank. "The youngest child of the family was the ______."
questions.why: "The youngest child OF THE FAMILY" implies comparison among potentially MANY siblings (a family, not just two people), so the superlative "most successful" fits — same underlying rule as the comparative-vs-superlative-for-two trap (Q316/Q530), just applied in the superlative direction this time since "family" implies 3+.

questions.topic: Reported speech (future tense with plural "them" mismatch)
questions.question: Select the most appropriate INDIRECT form of the given sentence. I said to him, "In winter, I am going to visit Cambodia with my family."
options: I told them that in winter I would be going to visit Cambodia with my family.
I told them that in winter he was going to visit Cambodia with his family.
I told them that in winter I am going to visit Cambodia with my family.
I told them that in winter I was going to visit Cambodia with my family.
questions.why: Reported speech, already-Solid pattern — "said to him" (past tense) triggers full backward shift: "am going"→"was going" (present continuous with future meaning → past continuous). Pronoun "I" stays "I" (the SPEAKER doesn't change, only "him" becomes "them" per the marked key's context). This is the 20th and last General English question, completing the paper's four "general" sections.

questions.topic: De Broglie wavelength ratio (proton vs electron, same kinetic energy)
questions.question: An electron and a proton have the same kinetic energy. Then, the ratio of de Broglie wavelengths of proton and electron will be nearly:
questions.why: Same core formula as Q547/Q710 (λ=h/√(2mKE)) — for equal KE, λ ratio is inverse of √mass ratio. Proton is ~1836× heavier than electron, so √1836≈43. λ_proton/λ_electron=1/√(mass ratio)=1/43, i.e. ratio 1:43.

questions.topic: De Broglie wavelength (shortest, same velocity not same KE)
questions.question: Which of the following particles, moving with the same velocity, has the shortest wavelength?
questions.why: Genuinely important contrast with Q547/Q784 — here the particles share the SAME VELOCITY, not the same kinetic energy, so λ=h/(mv) is now DIRECTLY inversely proportional to mass alone (not √mass). The heaviest particle (alpha, ~4 atomic mass units) has the shortest wavelength. Trap: don't apply the "same KE" formula (λ∝1/√m) when the question specifies "same velocity" instead — the mass dependence is different (λ∝1/m) in that case.

questions.question: The value of lim(x→0) (e^x − 1)/x³ is:
questions.why: Genuinely useful limit-technique — expand e^x-1≈x+x²/2+x³/6+... near x=0, so (e^x-1)/x³≈(x+x²/2+...)/x³=1/x²+1/(2x)+1/6+..., and as x→0 the 1/x² term dominates and blows up. Since the numerator approaches a nonzero constant relative to x's rate (e^x-1~x, a FIRST-order term) while the denominator is THIRD-order (x³), the ratio diverges to infinity, not a finite value. Reusable rule: when comparing the "order" of the numerator and denominator near a limit point, a lower-order numerator over a higher-order denominator (in terms of powers of the vanishing variable) diverges, not converges — check orders before assuming L'Hopital gives a clean finite answer.

questions.question: In a dielectric material, the polarisation vector P, the displacement vector D and the electric field vector E are related as:
questions.why: Same underlying relation as Q668 (D=ε0E+P), rearranged to solve for P: P=D-ε0E.

questions.topic: Linear independence (constant multiples and the zero vector)
questions.question: Consider two subsets of R³ given as S1={[7,7,7]} and S2={[0,0,0]}. Then,
options: Both S1 and S2 are linearly independent.
S1 is linearly independent but S2 is linearly dependent.
S1 is linearly dependent but S2 is linearly independent.
Both S1 and S2 are linearly dependent.
questions.why: Genuinely worth stating the single-vector rule explicitly — a set containing exactly ONE nonzero vector is ALWAYS linearly independent (there's no other vector to combine it with to get zero, except the trivial zero coefficient). S1={[7,7,7]} is nonzero → independent. A set containing ONLY the zero vector is ALWAYS dependent (0×anything nonzero gives the zero vector trivially, but more precisely, a nonzero scalar times the zero vector still gives zero, violating independence's definition). S2={[0,0,0]} → dependent.

questions.question: A general solution of the differential equation (x+y)·dy/dx − x − y = 0 will be ______, where c is a constant.
questions.why: Rearranging: (x+y)dy/dx=x+y, wait — check carefully: the equation as given is (x+y)dy/dx-(x+y)=0, i.e. dy/dx=1 if x+y≠0, which would give a trivial linear solution — but the marked answer is a quadratic form, suggesting the actual equation (perhaps a scan/transcription nuance) is homogeneous in x,y with dy/dx=(x+y)/(x-y) or similar. Trust the key's quadratic-form answer (x²-2xy-y²=c) as the standard solution shape for a homogeneous first-order ODE (substituting y=vx reduces it to a separable equation in v and x) — the reusable technique is: whenever dy/dx is a ratio of same-degree expressions in x,y, substitute y=vx to make it separable.

questions.topic: Relativistic speed of light (observer moving toward a light source)
questions.question: An observer moves with a speed of 0.86 C towards a stationary source of light in air. The speed of light would appear to the observer to be:
questions.why: Genuinely important relativity principle worth stating explicitly — the speed of light is INVARIANT (always exactly c) in every inertial reference frame, regardless of the observer's own motion toward or away from the source. This is Einstein's second postulate of special relativity — unlike classical velocity addition (which would naively suggest c+0.86c), relativistic velocity addition always caps the result at c.

questions.question: The resolving power of a plane transmission diffraction grating will increase on increasing:
options: the total number of rulings on the grating only
both order of the spectrum and total number of rulings on the grating
the order of the spectrum only
questions.why: The resolving power formula R=nN (n=order of spectrum, N=total number of rulings) shows resolving power depends on BOTH factors together — increasing either alone increases R, but the formula explicitly involves their PRODUCT, so "both" is the complete/correct answer over either single factor.

questions.topic: Relative permeability (from magnetisation and flux density)
questions.question: A magnetic material has a magnetization of 2350 A/m and produces a flux density of 3.142 mWb/m². Then the relative permeability of the material is:
questions.why: Genuinely new applied formula — B=μ0(H+M), where H is the applied field, M is magnetisation. Rearranging to find H: H=B/μ0-M=3.142×10⁻³/(4π×10⁻⁷)-2350≈2500-2350=150 A/m (approx, working through the exact numbers). Relative permeability μr=B/(μ0H)=1+M/H≈1+2350/150≈16.67, matching option 4. Reusable formula: relative permeability μr=1+M/H (or equivalently B/(μ0H)) — connects magnetisation, applied field, and flux density.

questions.topic: X-rays cannot be deflected by fields (uncharged)
questions.question: X-rays can be deflected by:
questions.why: X-rays are electromagnetic radiation (uncharged photons), so they are NOT deflected by electric or magnetic fields at all — unlike charged particle beams (electrons, alpha particles), which DO deflect in such fields. This distinguishes X-rays (particle-nature aside, still fundamentally uncharged photons) from charged-particle radiation.

questions.topic: Squeeze theorem for sequences (bounded between two sequences with equal limits)
questions.question: Suppose that X=<xn>, Y=<yn>, Z=<zn> are sequences of real numbers such that xn≤yn≤zn for all n∈N, and that lim<xn>=lim<zn>. Then:
options: Y is convergent and lim<zn> < lim<yn> < lim<xn>
Y is convergent and lim<xn> < lim<yn> < lim<zn>
Y is convergent and lim<xn> = lim<yn> = lim<zn>
questions.why: This is the squeeze/sandwich theorem for SEQUENCES, direct analogue of the squeeze theorem for limits used in Q568 — if Y is sandwiched between X and Z, and X and Z converge to the SAME limit, Y is forced to converge to that identical limit too (it can't be higher or lower, since it's squeezed on both sides).

questions.question: The concept of displacement current was proposed by:
questions.why: Maxwell introduced the displacement current term to fix an inconsistency in Ampere's law for time-varying fields (particularly for capacitor circuits), leading to the complete set of Maxwell's equations — static physics-history fact.

questions.topic: Real analysis (identify the false statement — open/closed set operations)
questions.question: Which of the following statements is FALSE?
options: The intersection of an arbitrary non-empty collection of closed sets is a closed set.
The union of an arbitrary collection of non-empty open sets is an open set.
The union of an arbitrary non-empty collection of closed sets is closed.
The intersection of a finite collection of open sets is an open set.
questions.why: Genuinely important topology fact worth stating precisely — ARBITRARY (possibly infinite) unions of closed sets are NOT necessarily closed (this is the FALSE statement, option 3) — only FINITE unions of closed sets are guaranteed closed. By contrast: arbitrary intersections of closed sets ARE always closed (option 1, true), arbitrary unions of open sets ARE always open (option 2, true), and finite intersections of open sets ARE always open (option 4, true). Reusable rule: "closed sets are well-behaved under intersection (any size) and finite union; open sets are well-behaved under union (any size) and finite intersection" — the classic asymmetry in point-set topology.

questions.topic: Fresnel biprism (thickness from fringe shift count)
questions.question: In a Fresnel's biprism arrangement, monochromatic light of wavelength 550 nm is used to obtain an interference fringe pattern on the screen. When a thin, transparent glass sheet of refractive index 1.52 is introduced in the path of one of the interfering beams, ten interference fringes are found to be shifted. Then the thickness of the glass sheet is nearly:
questions.why: Same fringe-shift formula family as Q275/Q553/Q673, solved for thickness this time — shift=(μ-1)t/λ. 10=(0.52)×t/550nm → t=10×550/0.52≈10,577nm≈10.6μm.

questions.topic: Quartz for ultrasonic generation (piezoelectric, reversed framing)
questions.question: Which of the following materials is used for the generation of ultrasonic waves by using the piezoelectric effect?
questions.why: Quartz generates ultrasonic waves via the PIEZOELECTRIC effect (applying an AC voltage causes mechanical oscillation) — a complementary generation method to the magnetostriction effect (used with ferromagnetic materials like iron, covered in Q544) for the same underlying application.

questions.topic: Standard integral forms (identify the correct formula among four)
questions.question: Which of the following statements is true?
questions.why: Genuinely useful to have all three standard "square root of a quadratic" integral formulas together as a reference set: ∫√(a²-x²)dx=x√(a²-x²)/2+(a²/2)sin⁻¹(x/a)+c; ∫√(x²-a²)dx=x√(x²-a²)/2-(a²/2)cosh⁻¹(x/a)+c (or equivalent log form); ∫√(a²+x²)dx=x√(a²+x²)/2+(a²/2)sinh⁻¹(x/a)+c. Option 4 correctly matches this last standard form. Reusable rule: these three integrals all follow the SAME structural pattern (x·√(...)/2 + a²/2 × an inverse-trig-or-hyperbolic term), differing only in which inverse function matches which sign combination — memorise the pattern, not three separate formulas.

questions.topic: Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions (irrational-degree case)
questions.question: If sin(u) = (x³+y³)/(√x+√y), then x·ux + y·uy will be equal to:
questions.why: Genuinely new degree-calculation twist on Euler's theorem (already introduced in Q396) — sin(u)=(x³+y³)/(√x+√y): numerator has degree 3, denominator has degree 1/2 (since √x scales as x^(1/2)), so sin(u) is homogeneous of degree 3-1/2=5/2. Euler's theorem: x·(sin u)_x+y·(sin u)_y = n·sin(u). By chain rule, (sin u)_x=cos(u)·ux, so cos(u)·(x·ux+y·uy)=n·sin(u), giving x·ux+y·uy = n·tan(u) (NOT cot — dividing sin(u) by cos(u), from the g(u)/g'(u) form with g=sin, g'=cos, gives tan directly). Here n=5/2, so x·ux+y·uy=(5/2)tan u — this exactly matches the marked key (option 2). [Verified independently by Stage 4 via sympy/direct differentiation: the earlier draft of this Why field second-guessed itself into "cot" by mistake; the correct chain-rule derivation gives tan(u) cleanly, with no ambiguity.] Reusable general rule: for F(x,y)=g(u) homogeneous of degree n, x·ux+y·uy = n×g(u)/g'(u) — for g=sin, g'=cos, so g/g'=tan.
questions.status: current — Stage 4 independently re-derived and confirmed (5/2)tan u exactly, resolving the earlier hand-wavy note

questions.topic: Wave packet (quantum mechanical description of a moving particle)
questions.question: According to quantum mechanics, a moving material particle is associated with:
questions.why: Definitional recall — a moving particle in quantum mechanics is represented by a WAVE PACKET (a superposition of many waves of slightly different wavelengths, localised in space), not a single pure wave (which would be infinitely spread out) or a physical acoustic/light wave.

questions.topic: Integration (rational function, partial fractions with quadratic factors)
questions.question: The value of ∫ 2x/((x²+1)(x²+3)) dx will be ______, where c is an arbitrary constant.
questions.why: Genuinely useful substitution trick — let u=x², du=2x dx, transforming the integral to ∫du/((u+1)(u+3)), a standard partial-fractions form: 1/((u+1)(u+3))=½[1/(u+1)-1/(u+3)]. Integrating: ½[log|u+1|-log|u+3|]+c=½log|(u+1)/(u+3)|+c=½log[(x²+1)/(x²+3)]+c. Reusable trick: when 2x appears alongside x² terms in the numerator, substitute u=x² to turn it into a simpler rational-function integral in u.

questions.topic: Convergence/divergence of alternating sequences (bounded oscillation vs approaching zero)
questions.question: Consider the following two sequences, X={−1,1,−1,1,...} and Y={1,½,3,¼,...}. Then:
options: both X and Y are divergent.
both X and Y are convergent.
X is divergent but Y is convergent.
X is convergent but Y is divergent.
questions.why: Genuinely useful contrast worth spelling out — X oscillates forever between -1 and 1 without settling on any single value, so it's DIVERGENT (bounded but oscillating, a classic non-convergent sequence). Y interleaves two sub-patterns: the odd-indexed terms (1,3,5,...) GROW without bound while the even-indexed terms (½,¼,⅛,...) shrink to 0 — having a SUBSEQUENCE that diverges to infinity means Y as a whole is also DIVERGENT (a convergent sequence must be bounded, but Y's odd terms are unbounded). Both divergent, for two DIFFERENT reasons (oscillation vs unboundedness).

questions.question: Consider two functions y1(x)=x and y2(x)=|x|. Then:
options: both functions are linearly dependent on the real line.
y1(x) is linearly independent but y2(x) is linearly dependent on the real line.
y1(x) is linearly dependent but y2(x) is linearly independent on the real line.
both functions are linearly independent on the real line.
questions.why: Genuinely new applied concept (linear independence of FUNCTIONS, not vectors — the ODE-theory extension of the vector concept already covered) — two functions are linearly dependent if one is a CONSTANT multiple of the other EVERYWHERE. For x>0, |x|=x (so y2=y1 there), but for x<0, |x|=-x (so y2=-y1 there) — no SINGLE constant k works for ALL x (k would need to be both +1 and -1 simultaneously), so no constant multiple relationship holds everywhere. Both x and |x| are therefore linearly independent as functions on the whole real line — even though they "agree" on half the domain, that's not enough for dependence.

questions.topic: Diffraction (light through gaps in leaves, circular patches)
questions.question: Circular patches are often observed on the ground when sunlight filters through the space between the leaves of a tree. This arises due to the optical phenomenon of:
questions.why: The small, roughly-circular gaps between leaves act like tiny apertures, and light diffracting through them produces the characteristic bright circular patches (in fact, these patches are pinhole-camera-like images of the sun itself, especially noticeable during a partial solar eclipse) — a diffraction/small-aperture phenomenon, not scattering or interference.

questions.topic: De Broglie wavelength (accelerated by a potential, standard formula)
questions.question: The de Broglie wavelength λ associated with an electron of mass m and accelerated by an electric potential V is:
questions.why: Standard formula worth memorising — kinetic energy gained from potential V is eV, and de Broglie wavelength λ=h/p=h/√(2m×KE)=h/√(2meV). Note the square root covers the WHOLE denominator (2meV), matching option 2's structure exactly.

questions.topic: Forming a PDE from a product-of-quadratics relation
questions.question: A partial differential equation formed from the relation z=(x²+a)(y²+b) will be:
questions.why: Differentiate z=(x²+a)(y²+b) partially: ∂z/∂x=2x(y²+b), ∂z/∂y=2y(x²+a). Product: (∂z/∂x)(∂z/∂y)=4xy(x²+a)(y²+b)=4xy×z (since z=(x²+a)(y²+b) itself). This directly gives (∂z/∂x)(∂z/∂y)=4xyz, eliminating the constants a,b without needing to solve for them individually first.

questions.topic: Alternating series convergence test (p-series comparison, absolute vs conditional)
questions.question: Consider two series Σ(−1)^(n−1)an and Σ(−1)^(n−1)bn, where an=1/√n, bn=xⁿ/(n(n+1)), 0<x<1. Then:
options: Σ(−1)^(n−1)an is divergent but Σ(−1)^(n−1)bn is convergent.
Σ(−1)^(n−1)an is convergent but Σ(−1)^(n−1)bn is divergent.
questions.why: Genuinely new applied combination — the an series is an alternating p-series with p=1/2≤1, which would DIVERGE if not alternating, but the alternating (Leibniz) test still applies since 1/√n→0 monotonically — so Σ(-1)^(n-1)an CONVERGES (conditionally, not absolutely).
